News.title: Two men re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran.

Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated.

Seven men in total have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on 27 September.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles.

Petrol was found in three vans near the airbase and five men were arrested.

They had been initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Police later said they did not find "improvised explosive devices".

The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially arrested on 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in the borough of Westminster.

The other five men - who also include a 22-year-old British national arrested in Westminster on 6 October - remain on police bail.

The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it."

The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature.

"Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident.

He did not provide further details at the time.

Iran has previously denied any involvement.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

In the week after the incident, it emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

Vice-President JD Vance said it was done out of an "abundance of caution".

News.title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
News.content:
The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made.

The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months.

Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea.

Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw.

News.title: Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
News.content:
Conservative MP Alicia Kearns has raised concerns over whether Jonathan Powell, the National Security Advisor, can remain in his post following his wife's references to Palestine Action on social media.

The shadow home affairs minister has written to the prime minister questioning whether Powell's position is still tenable, despite the Metropolitan Police concluding no action was necessary over his wife's, Sarah Helm, comments.

A Downing Street spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."

Posting on X last Thursday, Helm wrote: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney.

The Normal People writer announced last week that her books will not be supplied to UK booksellers after she announced she would use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

The Met investigation into Helm's post found "it did not meet the criminal threshold" and the matter was dropped on Saturday.

But Kearns has written to Andy Burnham about the handling of sensitive national security information, asking whether the government has investigated the posts and whether he retains full confidence in his adviser.

She told the BBC: "We cannot have the NSA's wife tweeting about what decisions her husband has or hasn't made."

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation last year, making it a a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years imprisonment to belong to or support the group.

An appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action is due to be heard by the Supreme Court next month, external, in a battle that has now gone on for more than year.

News.title: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
News.content:
The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran in February, killing the country's supreme leader and sparking the ongoing Iran war.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital shipping lanes, has been effectively closed since then.

King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William and Catherine and Princess Anne were among the royals on duty at Windsor for the state visit.

It was the first state banquet for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was seated next to the Omani academic and novelist, Jokha Alharthi.

It was a table laden with elaborate candelabra and polished decorations, with five glasses per setting, and even the surface of the salt had an imprint of the cypher of King Charles.

The hot summer meant a bumper crop of pomegranates in the Windsor Castle gardens, and the fruits were placed on the table alongside the floral decorations.

The King's speech, delivered to 160 guests in English with some quotes in Arabic, expressed his approval that his son Prince William had worked on an expedition project alongside the Sultan's son.

"There can be few happier symbols of success than a living relationship being passed from one generation to the next," said the King.

News.title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
News.content:
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.

The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.

There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.

The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.

It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.

Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.

Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.

Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".

"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.

"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."

News.title: Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says
News.content:
Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot."

Staff and pupils told the BBC they have become so used to these measures that they barely notice them anymore.

Lock-in - or "in-vacuation" - drills for dealing with intruders have become second nature, even to the youngest pupils.

"It's a bit scary sometimes, but you know you're safe," said Livi, a Year 6 pupil.

"It's sad that we can't be equal to everyone else, but people don't like us just because of the way we are," added her classmate, Sadie.

A group of a dozen older pupils who spoke to the BBC said that while they feel safe inside school, hearing about antisemitic attacks in the UK, including reports of pupils at other Jewish schools being harassed on their commute and at sports fixtures, has left them feeling targeted.

Some said that they were reluctant to wear skullcaps or necklaces featuring the Star of David â a Jewish symbol â outside school.

"Other religions get to be out and wear their necklaces and be proud - I don't get why Jewish people can't do it as much," said Year 9 pupil Ilan.

In response to the recommendations, the government is also expected to encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

He added: "We have advocated these measures be accompanied by other steps including improving education about Jewish life and ensuring schools maintain their duties in relation to political impartiality."

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

The Department for Education has declined to comment before the review is published.

News.title: Woman says she 'couldn't speak or breathe' during alleged rape by Russell Brand
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who says Russell Brand raped her at his home in London told police she "couldn't speak or breathe" during the alleged attack, a jury has heard.

The 51-year-old entertainer is accused of raping the woman in 2009 after meeting her at London's Hammersmith Apollo, where he had been performing as a stand-up comedian.

Brand faces seven charges in the trial in total - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.

In video evidence of her speaking to a police officer, the woman said she performed a sex act on Brand at the London theatre after being invited for drinks following the show.

She said she gave him her phone number, explaining she was "a massive Russell Brand fan" and a "massive comedy fan" at the time.

After that night, she said Brand messaged her and she went to his house in Hampstead knowing they would have sex.

But she said a consensual encounter became rape when Brand started having anal sex with her and ignored her pleas for him to stop.

She said when she arrived at his home, Brand told her she needed to have a shower "because my hair smelled funny". He then asked her to brush her teeth.

"I was trying to make a joke of what he was making me do", she said. "All of those things made me feel, 'I don't like this'."

The woman said a short while after getting on his bed, she was turned over. It was then she said she was allegedly raped.

She told police: "From the very moment it happened, I felt I had willingly gone there and from what his reputation was, what did I expect?"

She said Brand "hurt me and harmed me, and when I asked him to stop, he didn't". She added: "The horror in anyone that I told was not enough to make me believe I didn't deserve it."

The woman said she told friends and family afterwards, and went through sexual health tests - believing that she had contracted a disease from Brand.

Earlier on Tuesday, another woman who claims Brand sexually assaulted her described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".

That complainant alleges Brand assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.

She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside.

"He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury. "He grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."

The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on.

"He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."

From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack.

"His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."

The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.

She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.

The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.

She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck.

"His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."

She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."

News.title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
News.content:
BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag, Normal People and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022.

BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.

However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.

Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.

The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes.

Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.

While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.

Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chairman of ITV and production company Endemol, told BBC News: "This is a modest and pretty well-judged package.

"The essence of it is it protects the spending on content, it really cuts money in the distribution of programmes, and it really had to happen because the BBC has lost 30% of its revenue in 10 years."

But entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".

Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.

The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.

The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further Â£5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles.

Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks.

RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and Radio 4âs The World Tonight and You & Yours are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far.

News.title: Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong
News.content:
Only properly trained professionals will be allowed to offer high-risk cosmetic procedures like liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), vampire facials and chemical peels, under long-awaited government plans for England in 2027.

The government said it wanted to "drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market" and shield people from treatments "that can go badly wrong".

Currently, there are no restrictions over who can carry out these 'no scalpel' procedures, which can harm or kill if not performed safely.

Under the new rules, high-risk procedures for under-18s will also be banned, and rogue providers will face new criminal offences and fixed fines of up to Â£4,000.

News.title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
News.content:
The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City.

The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September.

No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case.

It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than Â£900m. City are appealing the verdict.

The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs.

The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules.

It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies.

BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm.

The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme.

Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases.

He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules.

"This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account.

"The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability."

BDO declined to comment.

News.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
News.content:
Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.

The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.

The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.

"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

"Services have been restored."

They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard, external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.

Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.

In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.

It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.

These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.

The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.

News.title: Man, 26, charged with woman's murder
News.content:
A man has been charged with the murder of a woman who was stabbed to death in a street in Manchester.

Lawrence Johnson, 26, of Dorking Avenue, has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels, also 26, and the attempted murder of a man following the incident on Thursday.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Det Ch Insp Justin Bryant said officers were continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ms Samuels' death and to provide answers for her family.

Police are still appealing for information.

Det Ch Insp Bryant said: "I'd like to thank those that have called and supported our investigation thus far. Your reports are always taken seriously and prove vital to our work.

"I urge others who may have information, no matter how small, to please come forward."

News.title: Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to repair his complicated relationships with his father and brother, in a magazine interview.

"Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point," Prince Harry told GQ in New York.

"Scars stick around forever. But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past, that's something that I would encourage everybody to do," said Prince Harry.

Last week Prince Harry and Meghan carried out their first public engagement together since their return to the UK in the summer.

The GQ interview with Prince Harry was conducted last month and released as the Royal Family were on duty in Windsor welcoming the Sultan of Oman at the start of a state visit.

But a spokesman for the Sussexes said the interview was recorded in late September and it was the entirely the publishers' decision when to run it - and that nothing should be read into the timing.

The spokesman also said that the reference to "some people don't want it to work out" was not a swipe at his brother Prince William or any other member of his family.

Prince Harry and Meghan moved from the UK to the United States in 2020, stepping down as working royals in what was an acrimonious departure.

Harry's memoir, Spare, showed the depth of the family fall out and the damaged relationship with his brother William.

Despite Prince Harry now being physically nearer to his family in the UK, there hasn't seemed to be any more emotional closeness with his brother Prince William, and in this interview Harry seems to be open to reconciliation.

It was a message of wanting to build bridges that he had previously sent in a BBC interview in May 2025, when he had been living in the US.

News.title: Second Labour MP suspended over Covid loan repayments
News.content:
A second Labour MP, Perran Moon, has been suspended over Covid loan repayments, after voluntarily referring himself for investigation.

Moon, the MP for Camborne and Redruth, is listed on Companies House as the co-director of a training company called Autoswot, external, which last filed accounts in June 2021.

Government Bounce Back Loans of up to Â£50,000 were made available to support small businesses during the pandemic, but a government report found the scheme was vulnerable to fraud and error.

In August, Labour MP Bayo Alaba was suspended after queries about a Covid-era loan, and a third MP, James McMurdock, quit Reform in 2025 after questions about eligibility for loans he received.

Bounce back loans worth a total of Â£46bn were issued when the scheme was launched in May 2020, making it the biggest of the government's pandemic-era loan schemes.

Each one had a 100% government guarantee, meaning taxpayers' cash was used to pay back banks if the companies failed, but the Covid counter-fraud commissioner later found total fraud and error estimated at up to Â£2.8bn to the public purse.

Autoswot had been set up in June 2019, a year before the loans became available, and at that time had forecast revenues of more than Â£200,000.

Moon stressed he had applied for the maximum loan of Â£50,000 within the rules, regularly seeking professional advice about its obligations, and would provide documents to the Labour Party investigation into the matter.

He said the loan was used to pay for "staffing and other essential business costs" during the pandemic and partial repayments were made until the company ceased trading in late 2022.

The BBC understands that Moon was repeatedly assured in writing by Companies House that no accounts needed to be filed after the company applied to be struck off, but that guidance was incorrect.

Moon, who was first elected in the 2024 Labour landslide following a career in communications and marketing, said the business folded due to unforeseen external market pressures and "despite the best efforts of staff".

He said: "In order for these matters to be looked into, I have voluntarily referred myself to the Labour Party's investigations process and will cooperate fully with this process.

"The loan application was made in good faith, and the information provided, including the company's turnover forecast, was accurate and properly based.

"I will continue to work hard every day representing my constituents while this party process is ongoing."

A Labour Party spokesperson confirmed Moon had referred himself for investigation.

"The Labour Party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and we have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld," they said.

"We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing."

This is the second investigation the Labour Party has launched into the loans, with Alaba, the MP for Southend East and Rochford, also referring himself for investigation over loans made to a real estate company, Alaba Properties.

At the time, Alaba said: "There has been no attempt to avoid my financial obligations, and I am wholeheartedly committed to ensuring that the liability is met in full."

McMurdock, who now sits as an independent, was the first MP to be questioned over bounce back loans given to two fitness companies worth Â£70,000.

In 2025 McMurdock said all his business dealings had been compliant with the rules, adding that after taking "specialist legal advice" he had decided "to continue my parliamentary career as an independent MP".

News.title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
News.content:
The UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the government has said.

The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure - a move authorised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham - against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group.

It follows Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast.

"These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a written statement on Tuesday.

News.title: Student who stabbed housemate 30 times admits murder
News.content:
A student who stabbed his housemate more than 30 times in a masked ambush has changed his murder plea to guilty.

Zack Coughlan, 23, attacked Jamie Collins, 21, in an alleyway near the garden of their home on 8 April and then left his body outside for eight hours before calling police.

A murder trial had been under way at Bristol Crown Court because Coughlan initially denied the charge, although he did admit killing Collins. He told jurors he stabbed Collins because he feared his housemate would kill him.

However, Coughlan, of Cleve Road, Filton, has now changed his plea to guilty and will be sentenced for murder on Wednesday.

Describing him as "a sensitive and caring young man", Collins' family said he had been "looking forward to finishing his journey" at the University of the West of England (UWE) and returning home to Swansea "in a matter of weeks".

"His passion for equality stood out to everyone who knew him. His unapologetic inclusivity will be his legacy for all of us. We know he was heading for a hugely successful future following his engineering and robotics degree," they added.

News.title: Dancing with the Stars LIVE: Dedication Night opens with Val Chmerkovskiy’s suspension addressed
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

News.title: New UN initiative will aim to tackle the military uses of AI
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The United Nations is launching a new initiative on the military uses of artificial intelligence, aimed at addressing some dire concerns about the threat the rapidly developing technology could pose to humanity.

The initiative by the U.N. Institute for Disarmament Research plans to launch Thursday, establishing the first international forum for key players to try to tackle the issue.

Robin Geiss, head of the Geneva-based institute known as UNIDIR, warned at a U.N. press conference Tuesday that “the margin for human judgment is increasingly narrow, including in the nuclear domain.”

It’s difficult to assess how close the world is to machines possibly acting outside of human control, Geiss said, and that uncertainty “is the issue we’re trying to resolve here.”

One problem is that AI is increasingly creeping into so many areas — early warning systems, information gathering and reconnaissance, to name a few — “and it’s quite difficult to say at which point we’re actually really losing control,” he said.

For a long time, he said, there was widespread reluctance to deal with AI guardrails, but the proliferation of its capabilities and the potential impact have led to “a growing realization that we stand at a crossroad — that now is the time to act, including on military AI.”

Geiss said the U.N. recognizes that global competition to lead on AI poses serious obstacles.

“But concerns about AI’s impact are already transcending geopolitical blocs, and they’re prompting action from major powers,” he said, pointing to a proposal last month for the U.S. and China to set up an AI safety alert system for issues that could threaten national security.

The risks posed by AI were a major topic in speeches by leaders of many of the U.N.’s 193 member nations at their annual high-level meeting last month.

UNIDIR this summer established a Center of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, the first permanent platform by the world body focused on those issues. Geiss said it received funding from all five major nuclear powers — the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France.

On Thursday, UNIDIR will launch a new forum as part of the center to bring together “actors from every relevant sector and all over the world” to work on AI in military uses.

Geiss was vague on exactly what the initiative will do, but he said it will be part of other AI efforts being launched by the center this week. Another will focus on the role of industry and aims to develop “a framework for responsible industry behavior,” he said.

Decisions by companies on design and development “determine whether AI-enabled military capabilities are ultimately reliable, predictable and whether they can operate in line with international law,” Geiss said.

For that reason, he said, UNIDIR is developing a framework of responsible industry behavior that will “provide practical, voluntary guidelines" that follow international law and ensure human rights.

The U.N. agency will hold consultations this week with defense technology companies, software developers, subcontractors, investors and others that will work alongside governments, civil society, academia and experts, Geiss said.

UNIDIR also is launching an initiative focused on the risks of AI misuse by armed groups, he said, warning that such actors are already using the technology to support operational planning, execution and logistics.

“The urgent issue of AI in the military domain will certainly no longer be allowed to linger in the shadows,” Geiss said. “The time has come to pull our strengths and confront AI in the military head-on.”

News.content:

A 76-year-old woman faces murder and assault charges after allegedly shooting her ex-husband and two other people on Monday afternoon in Toombs County, Georgia.

Deputies responded to 188 McNatt Falls Road around 2:19 p.m. following a 911 call reporting three gunshot victims, according to the Toombs County Sheriff’s Office.

Inside the residence, officers discovered 75-year-old Wallace Truman Edge and 40-year-old Pamela Cook dead from gunshot wounds. A third victim, 55-year-old Diane Cook, was treated for a non-life-threatening gunshot injury.

Authorities identified Grace Edge, the former spouse of Wallace Edge, as a primary person of interest shortly after arriving at the scene.

She was arrested and charged with two counts of malice murder, two counts of felony murder and three counts of aggravated assault. She is currently held at the Toombs County Detention Center pending an initial court appearance.

open image in gallery Grace Edge, 76, faces murder and assault charges after allegedly shooting her ex-husband and two other people on Monday afternoon in Toombs County, Georgia ( Toombs County Sheriff's Office )

Police have not officially confirmed or commented on whether past domestic disputes or abuse were documented prior to the shooting or may have been a motive.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation’s Region 12 office joined the inquiry at the request of local officials, who said there was no ongoing threat to the public.

“A person of strong interest is currently in custody,” the Sheriff's Office stated regarding the inquiry. “Further information will be released as the investigation allows.”

News.title: Trump’s first press secretary warns him to stop focusing on looks for his next pick
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Sean Spicer, Donald Trump’s first press secretary and the only one who was a man, has warned the president to stop focusing on looks when he picks the next person to stand behind the podium.

Trump has gone through six press secretaries throughout in first and second terms so far. Karoline Leavitt was tapped to be the administration’s voice at the start of Trump’s second term, but left her post at the end of August to spend time with family. Trump then tapped Katie Zacharia, another blonde woman, to replace Leavitt — she only lasted five days.

“What does this whole fiasco say about White House vetting and whether Donald Trump chooses people who look pretty and just agree with him instead of people who are competent at the job?” Andrew Bolt from the Australian outlet News24 asked Spicer.

Spicer defended Zacharia’s intelligence, but noted that it would serve Trump well to understand what it takes to be a successful White House press secretary.

He said Zacharia “does a great job of fighting for the America First agenda,” but he added that it’s only “about 20 percent” of the job.

open image in gallery Sean Spicer, Donald Trump’s first press secretary and the only one who was a man, has warned the president to stop focusing on looks when he picks someone to replace Katie Zacharia, who only lasted five days behind the podium ( Getty Images )

“I caution the White House and the president, in particular, for just focusing on that part of the duties,” Spicer said. He then listed other duties that he says are “critical” to the job, such as handling the “logistical nature of dealing with the media.”

Zacharia gave such a disastrous press briefing last Tuesday that social media users started comparing her to Trump’s one-time communications director Anthony Scaramucci for his record-short 11 days on the job.

Even Scaramucci joined in the mockery, writing on X, “The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci.”

Zacharia, who previously served as senior communications advisor for Trump’s Truth Social platform, stumbled through her first press briefing. She was visibly nervous and at one point, accidentally called her husband “my president” — a sharp contrast to Leavitt, who was well-spoken and often sparred with journalists while defending Trump’s agenda.

open image in gallery Spicer said Zacharia ‘does a great job of fighting for the America First agenda,’ but said, ‘I caution the White House and the president, in particular, for just focusing on that part of the duties’ ( Getty Images )

News broke on Friday that Zacharia was canned. Trump said that he told her to reconsider the job after media outlets were “so nasty to her.”

“I said to her honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider,” Trump told reporters. “She's got a beautiful husband and family ... maybe it's not for her.”

Spicer, who resigned as Trump’s press secretary after six months on the job, spoke about the gravity of the role.

“You’re talking about being the point person for the government of the United States through all the agencies and the departments, coordinating with outside stakeholders in Congress, and I don’t think some people fully appreciate that aspect of the job,” Spicer told Bolt.

“And secondly, Andrew, it’s incumbent upon the candidates who want to put themselves out there for this job to recognize their own strengths and weaknesses.”

News.title: University of Arizona student alleges she was sexually assaulted by 2 men at fraternity house
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A sorority member at the University of Arizona has alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house during a night of drinking in late August.

The student told the university’s police department that she consensually kissed one of the men at one point while at the Sigma Phi Epsilon house on Aug. 26 but doesn’t remember agreeing to sex, according to search warrant records posted Monday night by KOLD-TV in Tucson.

The sexual assault allegations surfaced two weeks after the university had suspended activities for its 21 fraternities amid reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing and drug- and alcohol-related behavior. Suspensions on all but five fraternities have since been lifted after they had mandatory meetings with the dean of students.

In speaking with an investigator, the sorority member recalled consuming tequila, including sharing a cup of the beverage with friends; witnessing two men sexually assaulting her, even feeling one man’s breath on her face; awakening the next morning without pants and underwear on; and noticing a difficulty in swallowing, a possible sign of strangulation, according to the records.

Later that day, she reported the allegations to police and underwent a forensic exam at a hospital.

In a recorded call with the sorority member two days after the encounter, one of the men acknowledged he had sex with her, but he said she had agreed to it and denied that another man had sex with her. He said he had been drunk and “fuzzy” on what happened. He said people took video of the sorority member and him kissing in a bathroom, according to the records.

The Associated Press left email and phone messages with the university Tuesday seeking comment. Its police department said the investigation is ongoing and declined to say if any arrests had been made. The Pima County Attorney’s Office said the case hasn’t been referred to it for prosecution.

Sigma Phi Epsilon at the University of Arizona didn’t respond to requests for comment from the AP, nor did the national fraternity organization.

The university had put Sigma Phi Epsilon on probation from July until May of next year after a hazing complaint. Sigma Phi Epsilon isn’t among the five fraternities that are currently listed as suspended.

Meanwhile, at Cornell University, a former student alleged that multiple Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted her in October 2024. The allegations have sparked campus protests, renewed scrutiny of the Ivy League school's disciplinary system and a state investigation into the alleged assault. Several of the men have denied that they engaged in any nonconsensual sex or denied they touched the woman at all.

News.title: Burnham and Sultan of Oman set to sign new investment agreement at Downing Street
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Burnham will host the Sultan of Oman at Downing Street on Wednesday as part of the Middle Eastern leader’s three-day state visit to the United Kingdom.

Ahead of receiving Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said at No 10, the Prime Minister praised "a friendship which generates real benefits" between Britain and Oman.

The visit comes as the United States continues its war against Iran, with Oman serving as a key UK ally in the Middle East.

Off the Omani coast lies the crucial Strait of Hormuz shipping route, which effectively remains shut to oil tankers due to a blockade orchestrated by Tehran.

Ahead of the Downing Street talks, Mr Burnham said: "I’m delighted to welcome His Majesty The Sultan to the UK – the UK and Oman have built a friendship which generates real benefits for people at home, and I look forward to shaping the next chapter of our relationship.

"Economic growth, security, defence, education: these are just some of the priorities we share as we plot a course through an increasingly complex world.

open image in gallery The Sultan of Oman joined King Charles at a state banquet on Tuesday ( Getty )

"Working together, we are leading with our values and creating opportunities for people in both our countries."

During the bilateral meeting, both leaders are anticipated to formalise a new two-way investment agreement alongside a maritime security pact intended to increase information sharing.

Furthermore, the UK is expected to declare the return of the Chevening educational scholarship programme to Oman.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will also hold talks with their Omani counterparts as part of the broader cross-government schedule.

Mr Miliband said: "The UK-Oman relationship spans almost four centuries and is built on trust and collaboration. His majesty the sultan’s visit to the United Kingdom reinforces this partnership for the future age.

"At what is a critical time for the Middle East, our close collaboration has never been more vital. Oman continues to play a valued diplomatic role in supporting the dialogue necessary to support a pathway to peace and regional stability – essential for the global economy and global security.

"Driving closer working across defence, trade and investment, and education, ensures that our long-standing friendship is a modern partnership that delivers for both the British and Omani people."

The King and Queen welcomed the Sultan to Windsor Castle on Tuesday at the start of the trip.

This marks the first state visit to the UK by a Sultan of Oman in 44 years.

News.title: Campaigners hit out at ‘cynical’ scheme to remove front-of-shirt sponsors as Premier League gambling ads soar
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Campaigners have criticised the Premier League’s “cynical” front-of-shirt gambling sponsor ban as new research shows football fans continue to be bombarded with adverts.

Researchers from the University of Bristol recorded 15,571 gambling advertising messages during the Premier League’s opening weekend.

This is a 42 per cent rise since 2023 when footballing authorities first decided to bring in a ban on gambling logos on the front of matchday shirts. The voluntary agreement came into force for the 2026/27 season, after a three-year transition period.

Analysis shows that the front-of-shirt ban has contributed to only a 10.5 per cent reduction in gambling , which has simply moved onto shirt sleeves and training kits. Gambling branding appeared on shirt sleeves and training kits 362 per cent more than in previous years, the report concluded.

Nick Harvey, spokesperson for the Coalition to End Gambling Ads (CEGA), said that the figures showed that the front-of-shirt ban was a “cynical move” from the Premier League which ultimately was ineffective.

open image in gallery Gambling companies use football shirts to advertise through sponsorship ( Getty )

"I think it was a cynical move from the Premier League to voluntarily remove the gambling ads from the front of shirts because I think they knew that they could easily move them to the sleeves, to training kits and around stadiums, which is exactly what's happened,” he said.

“So the exposure from these ads hasn't been reduced by anywhere near as much as it could have been. I think the only way to do this properly is to end all gambling advertising in football, and that's something which the government can do."

Meanwhile, pitchside advertising continued to dominate, accounting for 72 per cent of all messages during live matches.

Dr Raffaello Rossi, a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol Business School and Co-Director of Bristol Hub for Gambling Harms Research, said that the findings raised questions about the Premier League’s ability to self-regulate its relationship with the gambling industry.

He said: "The findings raise serious questions about the effectiveness of the Premier League’s front-of-shirt restriction and football’s voluntary Sponsorship Code of Conduct. The gambling and football industries have repeatedly promised to get a grip on the massive volume of gambling marketing surrounding the Premier League.”

open image in gallery Gambling advertising visible in the background of Brentford and Aston Villa’s Premier League match at the Gtech Community Stadium, London (Jonathan Brady/PA) ( PA Wire )

Dr Rossi has been tracking the number of gambling messages for four years and said that they remained pervasive despite widespread recognition of the issue.

He said: “This cannot be presented as a success for self-regulation. Premier League broadcasts contained more gambling messages per game than every other jurisdiction in our comparison, including Germany, Canada and the United States. Gambling marketing remains an unavoidable part of watching Premier League football and the issue needs to be tackled more effectively.”

Mr Harvey called on the prime minister to root out gambling advertising in football.

“I believe Andy Burnham has the will and the ability to do that. Otherwise it's like squeezing a balloon; you squeeze it in one place, it'll just pop up somewhere else, and that's what's happened with gambling advertising in football.”

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Dr Rossi is set to present the findings on Wednesday to the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Gambling Reform in a session questioning if current regulations fall short and whether the government should do more to prevent gambling-related harms.

Sir Iain Duncan Smith MP, Co-Chair of the APPG for Gambling Reform, said the research was proof that the voluntary approach to gambling advertising in football wasn’t working.

“After repeated promises of reform, fans continue to be exposed to thousands of gambling messages during Premier League coverage. The front-of-shirt restriction has barely scratched the surface of the issue.

“We cannot continue to rely on the gambling and football industries to regulate themselves. That is why the APPG on Gambling Reform is calling on the Government for more stringent regulation of gambling advertising and to close the loopholes in the current system."

Around 1.3 million people in the UK are estimated to suffer from problem gambling, many of whom go on to suffer serious harm, according to the Gambling Commission.

Mr Harvey is set to present a petition to Downing Street on Thursday, signed by more than 27,000 people who want to see an end to gambling advertising in football.

A Premier League spokesperson said: “The Premier League and our clubs take their responsibilities around gambling sponsorship seriously and fully recognise the importance of protecting children and people at risk of gambling-related harm.

“From this season gambling sponsorships no longer appear on the front of matchday shirts, making the Premier League the first UK sports league to take this step voluntarily.

“This forms part of a broader approach that includes football’s Gambling Code of Conduct, annual monitoring of clubs’ compliance and specific protections for children. We will continue working constructively with government, other football bodies and wider sport."

A DCMS spokesperson said: “We welcome the Premier League’s move to voluntarily ban all gambling sponsorship from the front of shirts from this season, which complements the Codes of Conduct already in place to ensure gambling advertising and sponsorship in sport is socially responsible.

“However, we are concerned that unlicensed gambling operators can still sponsor some of our biggest football clubs in other ways.

“That is why we are now working on banning unlicensed operators from sponsorship deals in British sport.”

News.title: Government’s long-awaited decision on Jackdaw gas field to be announced
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Government is widely expected to approve a long-awaited new gas drilling operation off the coast of Aberdeen on Wednesday.

A decision on the Jackdaw gas field will be announced following months of speculation about its future.

The North Sea project is one of two – alongside the Rosebank oil field – which the Labour Government must decide the fate of, after their approval by the previous Conservative administration was halted because of a legal challenge last year.

open image in gallery (PA Graphics) ( PA Graphics )

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will “take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea” since coming to power in the summer.

He has faced pressure from environmental groups to “stick to the spirit” of Labour’s manifesto and refuse consent for either of the schemes.

The 2024 manifesto committed to issuing no new oil and gas licences for the North Sea.

However, proponents of Jackdaw and Rosebank within the party have argued that neither are new fossil fuel fields, given the wheels were in motion to tap them ahead of Labour winning power.

The Prime Minister’s political opponents have argued further North Sea drilling will increase domestic energy supplies amid global price spikes triggered by the US war with Iran.

Analysts have, however, said that approving the oil and gas fields would have very little impact on energy prices for UK households and businesses.

Mr Burnham has also faced pressure from across the Atlantic to maximise oil and gas production from the North Sea.

US President Donald Trump has claimed the UK is “sitting on top of gold”, and has urged Mr Burnham to approve more drilling in the basin, as he did to former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has said a decision on Rosebank, the largest untapped oil field in the North Sea, will take “a bit longer”, and will not be made alongside one on Jackdaw.

open image in gallery Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh (Maja Smiejkowska/PA) ( PA Wire )

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said the Jackdaw decision “should be the start, not the end”.

He added: “Labour must approve Rosebank, end the ban on licences, and scrap the Energy Profits Levy. That is what a Conservative Government would do, and it is what this Prime Minister should do if he wants anyone to believe he is serious.”

Gary Smith, GMB general secretary also welcomed the coming decision as “great news”, and said his union would “continue to press for further, essential measures that increase our domestic energy capacity, such as granting permission for Rosebank”.

He added: “For too long, this and other vital decisions on our gas supplies and storage have been put off, risking the UK’s energy security at a time of worrying international volatility.

Elsewhere, climate campaigner for Friends of the Earth, Danny Gross, said: “Is the Prime Minister living in a parallel universe? One where we haven’t just endured our hottest summer on record, with droughts, wildfires and, in all likelihood, the most heat-related deaths on record? And where the UN hasn’t warned that we’re on the brink of breaching the all-important 1.5 degree warming limit?

“Against this backdrop, there’s nothing that justifies giving the go-ahead to a colossal new fossil fuel project in North Sea. The disconnect is absolutely maddening.”

Rosemary Harris, Oil Change International North Sea senior campaigner, said: “It is a shame that one of the first big decisions for the new Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has been to approve more fossil fuel drilling.

“At a time where the impacts of climate breakdown are so clearly felt, from the loss of livelihoods, homes and lives in the UK over the summer, to the devastating floods in Nepal, our government should look to the future, not cling to the past.

“All eyes are now on Rosebank, and the hope that Andy Burnham and his Energy Secretary have the courage and vision to push back against the industry and plot a path to an energy transition that provides more security, lower bills and a safe climate.”

News.title: Rio Ngumoha dazzles with coming-of-age night in Europe
News.content:
Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way [against Villarreal] or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

News.title: England dealt harsh lesson in Pakistan collapse
News.content:
Brendon McCullum wants his team to learn how to adapt as they prepare for the World Cup and this was a lesson in how not to master a run chase.

Failing to overhaul 302 is not an embarrassment, but the way England threw away a good start with some brittle batting gives McCullum plenty to ponder.

Spin exposed familiar failings as left-armer Arafat Minhas added six for 40 to his 59 from 58 with the bat, but it was also short balls from the seamers that hurt England. A two-paced pitch made the back-of-a-length delivery tricky, as it had in the match between Sri Lanka and Pakistan on the same ground at the weekend, but England failed to find a way to adjust their tempo.

Ben Duckett, Joe Root and Sam Curran were all dismissed by seamers hitting the pitch hard and forcing them to play square while Arafat exposed limitations against spin. He bowled Harry Brook for five with a beauty that dipped and straightened as he mixed up his arm ball with consistent accuracy to deadly effect.

News.title: Fried chicken and sugary drinks: Tanzania battles a growing obesity problem
News.content:
In early 2025, Said Shukuru, 31, was experiencing life-threatening health concerns. He weighed 150 kg (over 20 stone); his body mass index (BMI) was over 40 and he had a blood pressure of 190/100.

“It was very serious,” says Shukuru. In April last year, he underwent a successful mini gastric bypass operation at the Aga Khan Specialised Polyclinic in Masaki, Dar Es Salaam. His weight has since halved.

Shukuru’s case may be extreme, but his story serves as a warning. Overweight and obesity levels are increasing fast across East Africa, and particularly in Tanzania. Unless the government responds properly, the country faces a looming public health crisis.

Overweight and obesity in Tanzania have grown over the past 40 years because of economic development and liberalisation, urbanisation and increasingly sedentary lifestyles. Traditional diets, based on whole foods, are being replaced by refined and processed products. To make matters worse, chicken and chips, known as kuku chips, and sugary drinks are everywhere.

“When you live in an urban area like Dar (Es Salaam),” says Shukuru, “junk food is cheaper than groceries.”

The origins of these developments lie in Tanzania’s economic history. During the colonial period, fruits and legumes were exported while high-energy, starchy foods like maize were produced for domestic consumption, says Joyce Kinabo, professor of nutrition at Sokoine University.

“Food security was considered as having a lot of maize,” says Kinabo.

News.title: US warns over travel in Kenya as Ebola cases mount
News.content:
The United States has urged citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya, raising its travel alert level after the country reported an eighth case of Ebola.

The East African nation has recorded a rash of cases linked to a Kenyan businessman who died after travelling from Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

DRC is currently enduring the second worst Ebola outbreak on record with more than 4,000 deaths since May, though the true toll is thought to be far higher.

“The level was changed from Level 2 to Level 3 due to health risks,” the US embassy in Kenya said, a day after the State Department issued renewed travel advice for its citizens.

“Reconsider travel in Kenya due to risk of health, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and traffic safety. Some areas have increased risk,” it said.

The alert came as Kenyan doctors leaders demanded better protective equipment against the highly infectious virus.

Three of the confirmed Ebola cases are reported to be health staff who cared for the businessman and the others are thought to be relatives who visited him.

News.title: US records first human case of H5N1 this year
News.content:
A man in Washington has tested positive for H5N1, marking the first human case of bird flu in the US this year.

The patient, who works on a dairy farm, was reportedly infected after being exposed to two infected cows.

H5N1 has become endemic on US dairy farms after ‘spilling over’ from birds in 2024, and has since infected more than 1,000 herds across dozens of states.

The person is not seriously ill and is isolating at home, according to the Washington State Department of Health.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 mutates and gains the ability to spread person-to-person, it could trigger the next global pandemic – and each new infection gives the virus more opportunities to replicate and change.

Last week, a 50-year-old man in Taiwan was infected with a different strain of bird flu, H7N7, genetic analysis of which showed the virus had undergone adaptations to spread more effectively between mammals.

Of the more than 1,000 people who have contracted H5N1 since it was first detected in the late 1990s, almost half have died.

Its “extraordinarily high” mortality rate means that, were it to gain the ability to spread between people, it would be of “enormous concern”, the World Health Organization (WHO) previously warned.

However, the strain circulating among US dairy cattle, clade 2.3.4.4b, has proven less lethal to humans.

News.title: French bond sell-off spreads across Europe
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The cost of French government borrowing has risen at the fastest pace among G7 nations after a second night of riots.

The yield on 10-year French bonds, known as OATs, climbed from 4.80pc to 4.85pc on Monday, the steepest increase among major world economies.

Bond yields are effectively the interest rate paid by governments when they borrow money by issuing bonds to financial markets.

Emmanuel Macron is facing a crisis after shops were looted and vandalised across the country.

More than 2,300 people were arrested on Saturday after protests against the cost of living and poor school conditions.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “This won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs, so the modest recovery in French spreads over the last week or so will be tested today.

“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Burnham seeks EU embrace over AI | UK presses for access to a scheme that will prioritise investment in sovereign technology

2) Larry Ellison’s TikTok bans ad account for Musk documentary | Social media company blocks promotion for the film because of its political content

3) Profit warnings rise ahead of Budget | Most companies blame government policy and geopolitical uncertainty for worsening outlook

4) Istanbul airport stockpiles jet fuel over shortage fears | Turkish hub can sustain flights for three weeks without topping up tanks

5) GB News to launch ‘all-British’ radio station | New broadcast venture will attempt to win market share from BBC

What happened overnight

Oil prices fell more than 1pc after Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia.

On Friday, the President signed an executive order that delayed a wave of fresh sanctions and tariffs as they were set to take effect.

Brent crude edged down by nearly 1pc to just under $109 a barrel, with West Texas Intermediate hovered at around $101 a barrel.

Asian shares were mixed as volatility in technology stocks persisted.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index was up 1.1pc to 5,729.58 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 18pc over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 0.8pc to 64,799.03. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron lost 2.1pc, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 3.6pc.

Hong Kong’s stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.2pc higher to 3,722.20, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5pc for its economy in the third quarter.

CXMT, China’s leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7pc despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months.

China’s official growth data is set to be issued on Monday, giving the markets a glimpse into how the world’s second-biggest economy is faring.

The data is expected to show that China’s economy expanded by 4.4pc in the third quarter, improving on a multi-year low in Q2 but still falling just short of its annual target.

Beijing is aiming for growth of around 4.5pc to 5pc this year, which is its lowest goal in decades.

However, experts think China is on course to miss its annual economic target, weighed down by the Iran war energy shock.

China’s economy has been under pressure from mounting energy costs and faltering domestic demand. Researchers polled by AFP suggested exports were its sole outperformer.

Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1pc. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, were down 0.6pc. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 0.3pc higher at 8,832.20. India’s Sensex edged down 0.1pc.

Indonesia’s benchmark stock index fell another 5pc to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11pc on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its “emerging market” status.

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Huge points deduction leaked as EFL 'ready to agree' punishment
Sports.content:
A statement from the Premier League at the end of September read: "An independent Commission has found Manchester City FC guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation.

"The independent Commission found that between Seasons 2009/10 and 2017/18: - Manchester City arranged ‘sham’ contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on ‘sham’ agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs - The club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators - Manchester City was significantly in breach of both the Premier League’s and UEFA’s spending limits - During the Premier League’s investigation, Manchester City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and utmost good faith towards the League (three of the four alleged breaches were upheld)

"The independent Commission found that Manchester City arranged ‘sham’ commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club. As part of the scheme, further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, were entered into to enable the club to record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred, as well as a ‘sham’ circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG.

"The purpose of these schemes was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900 million during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules. The consequence of this, as the Commission found, was that the club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators. The Commission concluded that ‘by its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent the PL Rules‘.

"As a result, Manchester City failed to accurately report its income and expenditure for the purposes of the Premier League’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules and UEFA’s Club Licensing and Financial Fair Play Rules. The Commission found that, had all of the relevant agreements been reported accurately in the club’s accounts, it would have been in breach of both the League’s and UEFA’s spending limits by a very substantial amount.

"In addition, during the course of the four-year investigation conducted by the Premier League, the club committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and utmost good faith towards the League. The Commission concluded that the club had ‘made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation’."

City continue to insist they are innocent.

Sports.title: Rio Ngumoha breaks Liverpool record in Villarreal win and hails 'dream' night
Sports.content:
Rio Ngumoha breaks Liverpool record in Villarreal win and hails 'dream' night

Goals from Alexis Mac Allister, Ronald Araujo and Florian Wirtz helped Liverpool beat Villarreal 4-3, but Rio Ngumoha was the star of the show by producing an outstanding display

View Image Rio Ngumoha lit up Anfield (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

Rio Ngumoha said it was a “dream” come true after inspiring Liverpool’s Champions League fightback at Anfield. Ngumoha, 18, provided two assists as Liverpool came back from 2-0 down to win with Alexis Mac Allister twice on the score sheet in a seven-goal thriller.

‌



‌



Liverpool starlet Ngumoha became the club’s youngest player to provide an assist in the competition as they made it three straight wins in the league phase. England winger Ngumoha went off to a standing ovation when he was substituted and he told Amazon Prime: “We have the best fans in the world and to hear my name chanted is a dream.

‌



“These records are amazing to break but winning is the most important. It was a top performance from the boys. We were two goals down but the mentality was always there. We knew we were going to win.

‌



“It's up there with one of the best I've played. I enjoyed myself and the team helped me a lot. Whenever I get the ball and there's an opportunity to go one-v-one or two-v-one, I believe in myself. I'll just keep going and be ruthless.”

Sports.title: PSG earn statement Barcelona win as Phil Foden continues hot streak for Man City
Sports.content:
PSG earn statement Barcelona win as Phil Foden continues hot streak for Man City

CHAMPIONS LEAGUE ROUND-UP: There was a six-goal thriller in Paris as the holders faced Barcelona, as the Champions League delivered on a mouth-watering set of fixtures

View 3 Images Paris Saint-Germain are still on top (Image: Mustafa Yalcin/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Paris Saint-Germain showed once again why they're the kings in Europe by beating in-form Barcelona 4-2 in a back-and-forth bout. There were also high-scoring wins for Manchester City and Liverpool - but in vastly different circumstances.

‌



‌



Topping the bill was the clash in Paris, and it was the hosts who took the lead first when Desire Doue capitalised on a mistake from Lamine Yamal and curled in a sumptuous finish. Barcelona nearly hit back through Fermin Lopez, who'd replaced the injured Dani Olmo in the first half, but he was denied by a combination of Matvei Safonov and Willian Pacho.

‌



Barca didn't take long to level things, though. 10 minutes into the second half, 19-year-old Xavi Espart driving down the right and beating Safonov for power just after Achraf Hakimi had missed a golden opportunity. But for all the technical quality on the pitch, it was a set piece that decided the game.

‌



After Ferran Torres missed a chance from close range against his former club, Lucas Hernandez powered home a header from the resulting corner. But Yamal still had something to say.
