Sports.title: How Brazil’s election result could shape women’s football in the country
Sports.content:
The day before the first round of Brazilian elections, the Estádio do Morumbi hosted the second leg of the Brazilian Women’s Championship final, in which São Paulo drew 1-1 with Corinthians to win 3-2 on aggregate and secure the Brasileirão Women’s title.

It had been an incredible final but after the game the goalkeeper Carlinha used an interview to appeal to her fans: “Never again Bolsonaro in power,” she shouted to a record-breaking TV audience of 23 million people.

Having lost her grandmother during the Covid-19 pandemic, Carlinha recalls the challenges faced by hundreds of thousands of Brazilian families when the far-right president Jair Bolsonaro spread fake information about the virus while ignoring public appeals for the government to buy and distribute vaccinations. More than 700,000 Brazilians died during the pandemic. Now his son, Flávio, is standing against the 80-year-old incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

“I didn’t just think of [my grandmother] when I gave that interview, I think about her and miss her every single day,” Carlinha tells Moving the Goalposts. “I felt relieved after talking about my personal opinion in such an important moment of Brazilian democracy. I’m a journalism student and I know the impact if the right wins the elections.”

Carlinha is one of several female football players who have used social media and their visibility to speak up before and during the presidential election, which will come to an end on Sunday with a second-round vote. The father of the Bolsonaro dynasty is currently under “humanitarian house arrest”, serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt.

Carlinha’s club and international teammate, Tayla Carolina, went viral the weekend after discussing her family’s background and how public policies implemented during Lula’s government were important for her mother and grandmother, who have worked as cleaners throughout their lives and have since passed. “I’m from a very humble family, I’m a Black woman. I’ve studied in public schools and used the national healthcare system … my mum, dona Dora, worked for over a decade for someone who never paid her labour rights … and she worked until she couldn’t walk any more due to the cancer that took her from us. She never saw me play because she never had the time, she never rested,” she wrote. Her story resonates with many Brazilians who fought for shorter working weeks, approved earlier this week in congress.

View image in fullscreen The Brazil international Tayla Carolina has expressed her support for Lula’s policies. Photograph: Aude Alcover/Icon Sport/Getty Images

Tayla elaborates her point: “I’m from a country where most of the people are poor but the country is not seen as poor. It shows there are huge inequalities, which come from exploitation. Years have passed and there’s still a lot of inequality and I come from it … as a public figure, and someone who has lived similar lives to the majority of Brazilians, I feel the responsibility to speak up.”

The player organisation Fifpro has just released a new study showing that nearly half of female football players think of early retirement owing to the psychological and financial pressures of the women’s game (800 professional players took part). With the Women’s World Cup being staged in Brazil next year both Carlinha and Tayla feel the election will have a huge impact on the game going forward.

“There is one side that makes it quite clear how they feel about women’s rights,” says Carlinha, referring to, among other things, politicians such as Eduarda Campopiano, one of the most voted members of the São Paulo Assembly, who calls herself an “enemy of feminists” and has said she does not believe in femicide – that women and girls can be killed because they are women. Tayla also feels the need for policies to support the women’s game at a crucial moment. “We still need government incentives, so it may not be immediate, but the game will be affected, positively or negatively, depending on how the elections go.”

Lula approved the World Cup law in June 2026, which regulates many aspects of the tournament, including how ministries, the Brazilian FA (CBF), state federations and clubs will commit to developing a legacy and supporting the women’s game in the country. The legacy plan, divided into four strands, proposes supporting access and permanence of girls and women in football, developing and professionalising the game, fighting gender- and racial-based discrimination, and enhancing the economic and cultural aspects of women’s football in Brazil. The commitment to the tournament is stated in Lula’s government plan. Bolsonaro’s proposals for women’s sport do not mention the World Cup; instead, he proposes “ensuring that women’s categories, from youth to elite, are played by athletes of the female sex, protecting women and tournaments from ideological agendas”.

Brazilian football, men’s and women’s, has been heavily politicised for decades, and the rise of social media has led to an increase in players publicly supporting their political candidates. In the men’s game, the far right is often championed by the Santos and Brazil forward Neymar, who has showed support for the Bolsonaro family on many occasions. Tottenham’s Richarlison, meanwhile, is positioned on the left and this week accused Flávio Bolsonaro of “taking possession” of an island he says he bought a few years back.

The country’s female players do not have the same number of followers on social media and cannot influence a big audience in the same way as the men. However, it is true that the result of the election is likely to have more of an impact on the women’s game than on the men’s.

View image in fullscreen Brazilian students and activists march in downtown Rio de Janeiro to support Lula and protest against the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro. Photograph: Ellan Lustosa/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Kely Nascimento, the daughter of late football legend Pelé and founder and executive director of the Nascimento Foundation, says: “Female players, female athletes, they don’t have the protection of wealth. What feeds the brilliance of Brazilian football are the players, and they mostly come from communities, favelas and other places that are going to be hugely affected by these elections. Women are more affected by all this, right?”

Carlinha, who played in one of the two recent friendlies against Argentina, says playing for the national team at home is “one of the best feelings ever”. At both stadiums, in Porto Alegre and Recife, the crowd predominantly chanted in support of Lula, which could be heard over the TV commentary during the broadcast.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The politicisation of women’s football is not new, as Brazilian women’s football historian and author Aira Bonfim explains. “This is a hundred-year-old history, because we have episodes of women playing football in Brazil since 1915, and the women’s game reveals different perspectives of gender inequalities, racial inequalities, class, territory, which will affect the progress of the women’s game,” she says. “By knowing women’s football history, we can look at episodes which are equally as political, such as the ban on the women’s game [between 1941 and 1979], the persecution of women, and lies that were told so that female players would give up on it.”

One of the pieces of history that she has uncovered in her research became a short film, which debuted earlier this month at the Rio Film Festival, The House of Dona Carlota, produced by Mymama Entertainment and directed by Lili Fialho and Bruna Linzmeyer, which tells the story of a woman who was arrested and persecuted because she led a women’s football team, Primavera Atlético Clube.

It shows women’s football as a space of socialisation, sport and resistance to the Estado Novo dictatorship in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The women’s game was banned in Brazil for decades, and the World Cup in 2027 is where many hope its renewed development will be consolidated.

“What’s at risk [in this election] is a waste of all of the human investments in building social legacy plans. There is also the risk of dismantling all political communication that has been done to support [the World Cup] through the ministries, cities and state governments. If you elect someone who did not make any commitments towards it, who did not commit to the World Cup or what it represents to women, it can be a huge loss,” Bonfim says. “Just the fact that during Jair Bolsonaro’s government he removed the status of the ministry of sports reveals how he feels about the sector.”

The hosting of a Women’s World Cup is key in developing public policies and attracting investment and support. As Nascimento says: “There are girls all over Brazil for whom football is not just their dream, but it’s also how they get out of very awful situations. And there are amazing people doing God’s work all over Brazil just to get girls to play, to be educated in another way … for some reason, Brazil just makes football magic, and that’s not gender-specific. And there’s an enormous Brazil that is being ignored and taken advantage of.”

There are many reasons for the international community to look closer at the second round of Brazil’s elections on Sunday, from how it can affect climate change, foreign policy and financial markets to many other issues. Women’s football, and all it represents, is one of them.

Sports.title: As Harry Kane aims to haunt Arsenal again, and with the Ballon d'Or on the horizon, this is the story of his remarkable rise - and what English football must do to unearth its next superstar
Sports.content:
As Harry Kane closes in on some of football’s most prestigious accolades, the man who gave him his big Premier League break fears Tottenham have failed their next generation. Kane’s success, competing for the Ballon d’Or and becoming England’s most-capped player, reflects well upon Spurs, the club where he came through the youth ranks and scored a club-record 280 goals before leaving for Bayern Munich three years ago. At least, it does to a point. For Tim Sherwood, the brilliant rise of Kane serves to highlight how English clubs can produce more world-class talent if they are prepared to show more faith. ‘The academy side of that club is unrecognisable now,’ Sherwood, 57, tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘They might as well close it up and batten down the doors. ‘You can’t tell me there’s not been one player through that academy who has not been good enough to play for Tottenham on a regular basis since Harry Kane. ‘Either they have let whoever has been the manager close them off or they have not been banging down the door like we used to do. They have failed them.’ Harry Kane will look to take down Arsenal with Bayern Munich and could be crowned as the Ballon d’Or winner next week Kane scored his first Premier League start for Tottenham in 2014 against Sunderland Tim Sherwood, who gave Kane his break, fears Tottenham are failing to give chances to the next generation Kane’s career might have taken a very different route without Sherwood’s 148 days in charge of Spurs after Andre Villas-Boas was sacked in December 2013. It was Sherwood who thrust him into the team for his first Premier League start against Sunderland aged 20, the first of six successive starts at the end of the season. Having spent four seasons there as a player, Sherwood joined Harry Redknapp’s Spurs coaching staff in 2008 and later become technical director, working with Les Ferdinand and Chris Ramsey to oversee the academy. When he took over from Villas-Boas, his instinct was to trust his young players. ‘I didn’t do it because I was on an ego trip trying to put in as many academy boys as possible,’ says Sherwood. ‘I judged everyone on a level playing field. I was qualified to make that judgment because I knew those boys and I’d walked that path as a kid who was awful when he first went into the team and was kept in for long enough to become average and then very good. I know how vital it is for someone to trust you and give you an opportunity.’ When Mauricio Pochettino replaced Sherwood, Kane knew what was required to score in the Premier League. But amid seven different managers in seven years since Pochettino, such opportunities have vanished. The only academy graduate to play in the Premier League for Spurs this season is Mikey Moore, now on loan at Cologne in Germany. ‘I know how important it is for the Tottenham manager to get results,’ says Sherwood. ‘They tend not to look at the academy. Or they’re waiting for a Lionel Messi to fall from the tree, but it doesn’t happen like that. ‘They tend to look at the transfer market or try to get a tune from experienced players. They would argue they haven’t got time to wait and I’d argue back because those players who cost £50million, £75m or £100m, they will let you down as well.’ Sherwood cites Florian Wirtz, who cost Liverpool £116million from Bayer Leverkusen in 2025 and is yet to make an impact. Sherwood and others on Tottenham's coaching staff worked closely with Kane as he developed during loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich and Leicester When Pochettino replaced Sherwood, Kane knew what was required to score goals in the Premier League and thrive ‘We all know Wirtz has ability,’ he says. ‘He is a wonderful talent. But he has played more than 50 games now for Liverpool. Are you telling me an academy kid would have had 50 games if he was playing as bad as Wirtz? Never.’ Sherwood’s passion is clear. ‘Recruitment has not been good enough,’ he says. ‘Kids have found the pathway blocked by bang-average players who get more opportunity because of their reputation and their prices tags. It’s just not on.’ When Kane’s chance came, he seized it and did not look back. ‘Harry’s mentality was special,’ says Sherwood. ‘I can see his mentality is the same now as when he was 16-18. He doesn’t think he has reached his ceiling. He is still looking to improve. He was never afraid to ask questions if he didn’t understand something and once he understood, he did whatever he could to improve. ‘We had individual programmes to make him better — as we did with all those boys. Now we have too many coaches interested in enhancing their own careers rather than the boys’ careers. ‘It’s geared towards winning. They are applauded by the hierarchy for winning Under 21 leagues. Who cares? No one cares who wins those leagues. ‘I’m a firm believer that if they are not in the first team at 18, you need to find them a pathway. They need to go and play games, but if no one is fighting for those kids they will never make it. ‘All that stuff you hear about, “If they’re good enough they’ll make it in the end”, is the biggest load of b*****ks I’ve heard. There are sliding-doors moments and it’s about getting the opportunity and grasping it.’ Ramsey, Ferdinand and others on the Spurs coaching staff shared this belief and they worked closely with Kane as he developed, supporting him through loans at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich and Leicester. Kane scored a club-record 280 goals for Tottenham before leaving for Bayern Munich three years ago Sherwood questioned Tottenham's sales of Troy Parrott and Will Lankshear, who he believes should have been given the same opportunity as Kane to establish themselves at Tottenham ‘People would say to me, “I know you like Harry but he’s at Orient and it’s not exactly the Premier League”,’ Sherwood recalls. ‘I’d say, “Well, send Luka Modric there and let’s see how he gets on”. It’s f***ing hard at that level. It’s almost a different sport. ‘Just because he didn’t score bundles of goals everywhere he went doesn’t mean he failed. It was just about progression, and it was far better for his development than Mickey Mouse U21s football where no one cares who wins or loses. ‘We weren’t normal in the way we fought for those kids. I have enormous pride in the work put in by me, Chris and Les and everyone else who helped develop Harry Kane.’ Spurs have struggled for goals since Kane and in the summer they sold 21-year-old Will Lankshear to Middlesbrough, where he has scored 11 in 14 games. ‘There are clear parallels,’ says Sherwood. ‘I knew Harry and the other boys like they were my own. I knew how their hearts would beat and how to work them. I don’t know Will Lankshear but if I’d worked with him, I would know him and know if I felt he had the drive and determination and ability to play for Tottenham. I would not have let them sell him for £10m. ‘Put an arm around him and give him a chance. Tell him, “Don’t worry what the crowd are thinking, you’ve got the opportunity and if you do well they’re going to love you”. ‘Big him up. Tell him he can be the next Harry Kane. There’s no reason he can’t be. What are you selling Will Lankshear for when you’ve got strikers who can’t score a goal? Troy Parrott is another I would not have let go.’ Sherwood hailed Kane's mentality and believes the forward would genuinely rather win the Champions League with Bayern Munich than win the Ballon d’Or for himself Parrott made two brief Premier League appearances for Spurs before he was sold aged 22 to AZ Alkmaar, where 51 goals in 97 games earned him a £17million move this year to Real Betis. Kane, meanwhile, forges on towards his dreams. ‘If he can win the Champions League or the Ballon d’Or I know what he will say,’ says Sherwood. ‘And it won’t be a stock answer, it will be a genuine answer. The genuine answer is he would rather win the Champions League with Bayern Munich than win the Ballon d’Or for himself. ‘That’s the mentality we’re talking about. That’s why he’s the best. That’s why I’ll have a lot of respect for the Ballon d’Or if he wins and I won’t if he doesn’t. ‘Kane is a total team man. That’s why he’s a great example to any kid coming through but those kids will not get the same opportunities unless there are people inside these academies fighting for them.’

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo's night to forget: Star, 41, misses huge chance AND a penalty in Al-Nassr win, hours after being attacked by Erik ten Hag for 'letting down' Man United
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo's night to forget: Star, 41, misses huge chance AND a penalty in Al-Nassr win, hours after being attacked by Erik ten Hag for 'letting down' Man United

Cristiano Ronaldo endured a nightmare evening as he missed a penalty and squandered another huge chance for Al-Nassr.

Ronaldo's misery started in first-half stoppage time when he failed to hit the target with a spot kick after Joao Felix was brought down inside the box, much to the shock of those in the stadium.

Ronaldo, 41, went even closer in the second half when he was teed up for an open goal by Sadio Mane just yards out, but he inexplicably volleyed the ball over the bar.

The 41-year-old cut a frustrated figure after that as he threw his hands up in the air and looked to the sky in exasperation, before he bowed his head to the ground.

Thankfully for the global superstar, his side still won the match, beating Neom 1-0 after Felix's second-half strike.

The victory left Al-Nassr in third place in the Saudi Pro League, three points behind table-toppers Al-Qadsiah having played a game fewer.

Ronaldo It’s time to say goodbye to football 🙄 pic.twitter.com/hPCR3Nugdq https://t.co/B6obI4G0d7 — The Final Whistle (@Rufus_45) October 20, 2026

Cristiano Ronaldo endured a night to forget as Al-Nassr held on for a 1-0 victory over Neom

Ronaldo's difficult evening capped a tricky day for the Portuguese forward after former Man United boss Erik ten Hag hit out at his attitude in a wide-ranging interview with The Athletic.

Reflecting on his time at Old Trafford, the Dutchman accused Ronaldo of letting United down by failing to prepare himself for matches, with the former Red Devils boss claiming the forward pulled out of training sessions and encouraged team-mates to 'save their legs'.

Ronaldo left Man United by mutual consent in November 2022 after a bombshell interview with Piers Morgan, in which he claimed he had been 'betrayed' by Ten Hag.

Ten Hag claimed Ronaldo did not get himself to the 'right fitness levels' after withdrawing from training sessions and failed to get his heart rate raised to the required level when he did train.

'He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,' Ten Hag said. 'Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.

'Many times I say, "Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score".

'He was not capable to do this. It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself.'

Ten Hag continued: 'Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

'He was telling the players, "Save your legs at the training". I understand it when you are top fit; you have sessions, you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels.'

Ronaldo missed a first-half penalty and also squandered an open goal from a few yards out

Meanwhile, on Monday, Ronaldo received a strangely light punishment by Portugal despite walking out on their camp during the recent international break.

The forward was provisionally suspended by the country's FA after leaving the squad following a dispute with head coach Jorge Jesus.

Ronaldo had claimed Jesus broke promises when he was kept on the bench for their game against Norway.

Despite his misdemeanour, the Portuguese FA announced that he has been fined just £215 and is free to play again in next month's international break.

The superstar, 41, has technically been banned for a month by Portuguese football chiefs - but that punishment is backdated to his strop on September 30, reports in his homeland claim.

That means his ban will be served by the time Portugal's next fixture against Denmark rolls around on November 14.

Meanwhile, his piddling fine of £215 will take the billionaire approximately 38 seconds to recoup on his £488,000-per-day salary at Al-Nassr.

Sports.title: The night Rio Ngumoha cemented his status as a future world-beater: Liverpool had a £400m attack at their disposal but it was the 18-year-old who shone brightest in chaotic comeback win, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
They used to call it 'Pep roulette' at Manchester City. A phrase coined by fantasy football nerds about Pep Guardiola's tendency to chop and change his front line every week to devastating effect. We haven't refined our snazzy phrase for Andoni Iraola yet – the working drafts are 'AI Bingo' or 'Iraola tombola' – but the Liverpool boss has a devastating depth of attacking talent that, if they all fulfil their potential, can lead this team to dizzying heights. That is caveated with a reminder that Iraola's Reds are simultaneously plagued by many teething problems in other areas and are far from complete. We will discuss that in due course but first, a word on Iraola's deck of cards that contains multiple aces and jokers. With the best part of half a billion pounds worth of attackers not starting this comeback victory against VIllarreal, it was left to others to step up and no one caught the eye more than the potential world-beater but lesser-heralded Rio Ngumoha. At just 18, Ngumoha already has three England caps and is well on the radar of Thomas Tuchel, but he is not yet guaranteed a starting berth at Liverpool and has had to bide his time due to competition and having been asked to swap wings by Iraola after the arrival of left-winger Bradley Barcola. The teenager, who was poached from Chelsea in 2024 to much fury at Stamford Bridge, will cost a maximum of £6.8million but his ceiling is just as high as £125m Alexander Isak, £123m Barcola or £116m Florian Wirtz. Liverpool beat Villarreal 4-3 in a chaotic Champions League encounter at Anfield on Tuesday Alexis Mac Allister was Liverpool's hero, scoring twice as the Reds came from behind to win But it was Rio Ngumoha's display that was most impressive as he showed all of his quality Ngumoha is yet to score this season but was the shining light here with two assists in a spell-binding performance that helped tilt the game in Liverpool's favour. That was far from guaranteed after a shoddy, uncharacteristic and worrying first half an hour. Liverpool 4-3 Villarreal: MATCH FACTS LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 6; Araujo 7 (Wirtz 46, 7), Jacquet 6 (Gomez 74, 6), Van Dijk 5, Tsimikas 6; Nyoni 7 (McConnell 81), Mac Allister 8; Ngumoha 8 (Barcola 74, 6), Gravenberch 6; Gakpo 6; Koumas 6. Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Kerkez, Isak, Chambers, Danns, Laffey. Booked: None. Scorers: Mac Allister 36, 65, Araujo 45+2, Wirtz 68. Manager: Andoni Iraola 7. VILLARREAL (4-2-3-1): Gulacsi 5; Mourino 5, Navarro 5, Veiga 6, Cardona 6; Saliba 7 (Oluwaseyi 46, 7), Gueye 6; Buchanan 5 (Freeman 60, 6), Comesana 6 (Moreno 78), Moleiro 6 (Foyth 54, 6); Mikautadze 7 (Perez 60, 6). Subs not used: Luiz Junior, Akhomach, Costa, Diatta, El Jmili, Gaitan, Macia. Booked: Moleiro, Mourino. Scorers: Mikautadze 4, Cardona 29, Oluwaseyi 87. Manager: Inigo Perez 7. Referee: Szymon Marciniak (Pol) 7. Attendance: not provided. Alexis Mac Allister is also worthy of vast praise as the Argentine struck a brace to continue his resurgence and stellar season after a year-long dip, while Ronald Araujo and substitute Wirtz also scored. As the scoreline suggests, Liverpool's defence was all at sea and that will provide a headache for Iraola in the coming days, especially given they have conceded 10 in their last four games, also shipping three to Manchester City and Austrian side LASK. But while the boss agonises over fixing the defence, he knows he has cracked it at the other end. Ngumoha can trouble any defence, Isak can win any game with his instinctive poacher-like finishing, Wirtz and Barcola are starting to show signs they can unlock stubborn sides. Then there is Cody Gakpo, who returned from injury and showed signs he is picking up where he left off, and the energetic Victor Munoz, who missed this game but was described as a 'Formula One car' in these pages yesterday. And don't forget £79m injured striker Hugo Ekitike. Liverpool's array of weapons in attack were needed to help them get over the mess of the first half an hour, as Iraola was being taught a lesson by his former right-hand man, Inigo Perez, who was the No 2 during the Basque's formative years at Rayo Vallecano. Perez could not move to England when Iraola did because some wise cracks at the Home Office said he was not skilled enough for a work permit. The 38-year-old has made a mockery of that since, leading Rayo to the Conference League final after taking over from Iraola as head coach and now managing in the Champions League, where, for 35 minutes at least, his team played six-time European kings Liverpool off the park. Liverpool fought back after a dreadful first 30 minutes that saw Villarreal go 2-0 ahead Ronald Araujo scored his second goal in a week and celebrated by jumping into the stands Florian Wirtz (right) was also on the scoresheet to cap off a good few days for the German RIO: ONE OF THE BEST I'VE PLAYED Rio Ngumoha said his virtuoso performance against Villarreal was up there with the best in his budding career. The 18-year-old registered two assists and was the star man as Liverpool put a worrying start behind them to come from 2-0 down to beat their Spanish opposition. And the three-time England cap said: 'It's up there with one of the best I've played, I think. I enjoyed myself out there. The team helped me as well a lot. I enjoyed today. 'Like I always say, we have the best fans in the world. To hear my name being chanted is a dream.' Boss Andoni Iraola added: 'The good thing with Rio is he is still 18, he is not the full package, he can add things fortunately for us. 'Hopefully he can continue in the same way. He's not always going to be like this, he will have ups and downs in the process. 'But I'm happy because attitude-wise I think he's in a great place.' Alexis Mac Allister was also a shining light and scored twice. The Argentine said: 'Look at Rio, he was amazing tonight. He made the difference. He was really important and I'm glad for him. 'It's clear the quality Rio has. Everyone knows. It's easy to say he's a really good player but he needs to focus on other things. He worked really hard off the ball.' On his fine headed goal, Mac Allister added: 'It's not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it's something I got from him. 'Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn't right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don't like to compare. I'm feeling good.' By Lewis Steele Villarreal were magic, Liverpool tragic. This was by far the worst half hour of the Iraola era, more worrying than the capitulation against Manchester City. At least that time they had the defence of going down to 10 men. No excuse on this occasion, apprentice Perez was simply schooling master Iraola. Villarreal, nicknamed El Submarino Amarillo or The Yellow Submarine, were enjoying themselves in the land of the Beatles – whose song inspired that tag and is played before games at Estadio de la Ceramica. They were ahead after just four minutes. Virgil van Dijk made a honking error to head a long ball straight to the path of Georges Mikautadze, who could not believe his luck and scored. Van Dijk barely makes one wrong step, never mind a catastrophic mistake like this, and everyone at Anfield looked shellshocked. The 1,500 or so away fans and sea of vibrant yellow shirts were soon jumping for joy again on 29 minutes when Sergi Cardona sprung through a shoddy offside trap and waltzed through on goal to slot past a helpless Alisson for 2-0. Iraola was left scratching his head and probably regretting the six changes he made from the team that fought from behind to beat Brentford on Saturday. But out of nowhere, his team found something and started the comeback, through a Mac Allister header on 36 minutes. The Argentine may be small but is as good as most in the air and connected well with Kostas Tsimikas's corner to score. Anfield found its voice and the Reds responded. Ngumoha made the equaliser with a fine ball that was headed home by Ronald Araujo for his second goal in a week after scoring at LASK. The Uruguayan loanee, here for the season from Barcelona, is quickly becoming a cult hero and is being affectionately referred to as 'Big Ron'. He jumped into the Anfield Road End and made the night of one lucky lady, who received a bear hug. There was never any looking back from there, and Mac Allister put Liverpool ahead on 65 minutes after a dancing run from Ngumoha, before Wirtz came on and put gloss on the victory with a fine finish to continue an eye-catching week for the much-criticised German. Tani Oluwaseyi made it a nervy finish with an 87th-minute goal which highlighted Liverpool's defensive issues once more, but at least they can follow the old mantra of 'you can score, we will just score more'. How long that will last, who knows, but it is certainly not going to be boring this year.
