World.title: Number Of The Day | 78.9% | 20 October 2026
World.content:
South Africa's Debt Problem Is Also a Public Spending Problem

Government debt is often discussed as a percentage of GDP, but the greater danger lies in what borrowing costs take away from the country's ability to invest in its future.

South Africa's debt debate is frequently reduced to whether a particular number is too high. The country has committed to stabilising government debt at 78.9% of gross domestic product, a threshold that has become an important test of fiscal policy. Yet the significance of that promise cannot be understood through the debt ratio alone. The more revealing question is how much it costs to carry the debt, and what those payments prevent government from doing.

A debt-to-GDP ratio compares the stock of government debt with the size of the economy. It gives an indication of the burden the country carries relative to its economic capacity, but it does not tell us everything about affordability. Interest rates, revenue collection, economic growth and the terms of existing borrowing all influence whether that burden becomes manageable or increasingly expensive.

For South Africa, this distinction matters because servicing debt competes directly with other spending priorities. In the 20 October edition of Number of the Day, Francis Herd highlights a striking measure of that pressure: according to the Finance Ministry figures he cites, more than 21 cents of every rand collected in tax revenue has been going towards debt-interest costs.

That is money required to meet obligations arising from previous borrowing, rather than to build something new. It reduces the fiscal space available for education, housing, infrastructure and other services. Debt-interest payments are a necessary part of government finance, but when they consume a substantial share of revenue, they make difficult spending choices even harder.

Why the cost of debt matters as much as its size

Governments routinely borrow to finance their activities, and borrowing is not inherently a sign of failure. Debt can help fund infrastructure and other investments that support future economic growth. The problem arises when borrowing grows faster than the economy's capacity to support it, or when the interest bill leaves too little room for productive expenditure.

Investor confidence plays an important role in that equation. A government viewed as financially risky may have to offer higher interest rates to attract lenders. Those higher costs can place further pressure on the budget, potentially creating a cycle in which expensive debt makes the debt problem more difficult to solve.

The opposite process is possible too. Credible fiscal management can support confidence and help contain borrowing costs. But confidence does not follow automatically from announcing a target. Lenders and rating agencies also examine whether budgets, economic assumptions and subsequent outcomes make that target believable.

The consequences reach beyond financial markets. When debt service absorbs revenue, the trade-off becomes visible in public infrastructure that needs maintenance, services facing pressure and development plans competing for scarce resources. The central economic issue is therefore not simply whether South Africa owes a large amount. It is whether the country can finance its obligations without continually sacrificing the investments needed to strengthen future growth.

A target is a starting point, not a solution

The Medium-Term Budget provides an opportunity to examine the credibility of government's debt plans. Stabilising debt at 78.9% of GDP would be significant if achieved, particularly after the long increase discussed by Herd. But the target is only meaningful if the underlying revenue, expenditure and growth assumptions can sustain it.

Slower economic growth can make a debt ratio harder to reduce even when spending is restrained. Higher borrowing costs can undermine improvements in revenue. Unexpected economic shocks can also derail forecasts. None of these risks makes fiscal commitments pointless; they make transparent assumptions and consistent implementation essential.

South Africa's challenge is ultimately to create a more sustainable relationship between what the state owes and what the economy produces. Reducing the burden of debt service would not resolve every development problem, nor would it guarantee better public services. It would, however, create more room for government to make choices about the future rather than continually paying for the past.

The real test of fiscal progress is not the announcement of a percentage. It is whether that percentage eventually translates into lower financial pressure and greater capacity to invest in the country.

References

· Number of the Day, 20 October 2026. Francis Herd, episode transcript. Source for the 78.9% debt target and the discussion of debt-interest costs.

· General public-finance explanations concerning debt sustainability, borrowing costs and spending trade-offs are analytical context, not additional verified claims about the October 2026 budget outcome.

World.title: WATCH | Cellphones, dagga, salt, correctional service raid Klerksdorp prison
World.content:
KLERKSDORP - Correctional Services has stepped up security at its facilities ahead of the festive season.

On Tuesday night, National Commissioner Makgothi Thobakgale led a search operation at Klerksdorp Correctional Centre.

The operation is aiming to remove illegal items and improve safety inside the facility.

Among those items found are cellphones, chargers, dagga and salt, which Thobakgala said will be tested.

"According to indication there is still more that we will find because some of the offenders are actually declaring what they have to the search team," he said.

In an article published on eNCA in August, Correctional Services Minister Pieter Groenewald painted a grim picture of facilities in South Africa.

READ | 'All of us must get rid of this evil of gangsterism' - Groenewald

This was amid growing debate over whether they are actually disrupting organised crime or simply relocating its leadership behind bars.

Groenewald previously indicated that several gang members have never been in prison, which also points to poor communities being used as breeding grounds where they then begin to recruit individuals.

Some of these individuals, he said, have access to prisoners, with Groenewald admitting that gang leaders continue directing criminal activity from prison, particularly through illegally obtained cellphones.

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua hosts Edwin Sifuna and Linda Mwananchi leaders at his Wamunyoro residence on October 20, 2026. [Kibata Kihu, Standard]

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua returned quietly from the United States but hours later generated political shockwaves by hosting Linda Mwananchi leaders led by Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna at his Wamunyoro home in Nyeri.

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Trump calls on New Mexico to change its name to ‘New America’
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Monday called on New Mexico to change its name to “New America” — the latest example of him seeking geographical name changes that fit his political agenda.

“New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!” Trump wrote on Truth Social, shortly before departing the White House for a midterm rally in Kansas.

His comments about New Mexico — a blue state he lost by 6 points in 2024 — come as Republicans are anxious about holding their congressional majorities in November, with voters saying in polling that the president isn’t paying enough attention to the country’s most pressing problems.

Trump claimed, without citing any evidence, that “home values and incomes would rise” because of a name change. And he repeated his baseless claims about rigged elections by adding, “Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!”

Trump has previously suggested renaming New Mexico, although not so forcefully. In September, he posted to social media a map of the state with the word “Mexico” crossed out and “America” written underneath — an image that was reposted by the White House X account.

It’s just the latest renaming push from Trump. He signed an executive order in August to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as part of his ongoing trade war with Canada. He took similar action last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America.” The president has also repeatedly floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait.”

But while Trump has the power to rename what geographic landmarks, such as bodies of water, are called in the Geographic Names Information System, he doesn’t have the constitutional ability to legally rename states. That process would need to happen within the state.

New Mexico’s name predates the founding of the United States back to the 16th century, according to a fact sheet on the origin of state names from the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

New Mexico Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Monday evening dismissed Trump’s comments.

“Let me repeat: New Mexico was New Mexico long before the United States existed and we’ll be New Mexico forevermore,” she wrote in a post on X.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico wrote in a social post that the state’s name “carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are.”

“We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico,” he continued.

World.title: France’s crisis sounds familiar. Is America next?
World.content:
France is on fire, and it faces a political and an economic reckoning that feels dangerously familiar to Americans.

The country is nearing a fiscal crisis, because it spent more than it can afford to pay back. The bill is coming due much faster than expected after bond rates surged in recent months, boosted by rising energy costs. Raising taxes and reducing government spending are part of a potential solution, but those would be politically unpopular decisions that could risk further angering an already livid public. Any workable solution faces a steep climb in an uncertain budget battle in a sharply divided government.

Does that ring a bell?

A growing number of countries are facing struggles similar to France’s — in particular, the United Kingdom — where rapidly growing debt, surging costs to finance that borrowing and insufficient political will to make the uncomfortable decisions to solve the problem are the story of Western economics right now. That includes the United States.

But similarities can be superficial.

France’s financial stress is particularly acute. The risk of contagion throughout Europe is low. France’s enormous public safety net represents a much larger share of government spending than that in the United States. And the unique dynamics of the American economy means the United States faces no imminent danger of becoming the next France.

The problem

These are not new problems: Europe’s social safety net has been on an unsustainable path for decades, and economists and some politicians have warned for years that the bill would eventually come due.

But they’re getting worse. The Iran war exacerbated the West’s fiscal problems.

Since February, the G7 economies’ average 10-year government bond yield grew more than 1 percentage point, reaching the highest level in nearly 20 years, the International Monetary Fund reported last week.

By the end of the decade, those seven economies’ public debt loads are expected to collectively exceed their economic production, the IMF predicts. That would be the first time since World War II.

France’s public debt is around 119% of its GDP, double the European Union’s target, and its annual budget deficit is 5.4% of its gross domestic product.

“In Europe, people are increasingly scared of the bond market and the interest rates that governments need to pay to borrow,” said Peter Taylor-Gooby, a social policy professor at the University of Kent. “It’s come to a point where you can’t ignore it anymore. If we do, we’ll reach a serious crisis.”

On paper, America doesn’t look dissimilar: Its $32 trillion public debt is roughly equal to annual US GDP, and the $2 trillion budget deficit that it just closed the books on is more than 6% of GDP. The cost to finance America’s public debt just crossed $1 trillion a year, an astounding 14% of the total federal budget.

In other words, one in every seven tax dollars is used just to pay interest on the amount of money the United States is borrowing.

But the serious conversations about cutting back on spending and raising taxes taking place in Europe are considerably less serious in the United States. So why isn’t the United States facing the same problems as France?

Why it won’t happen in the US…yet

The United States’ biggest advantage is that it prints the world’s reserve currency. The majority of global transactions are conducted in US dollars, including key commodities like oil and gold.

Demand for dollars remains robust in large part because they’re considered safe: The United States’ transparency and commitment to the rule of law make the dollar the cornerstone of the global financial system — even if some of the shine has worn off over the past decade.

That also fuels demand for US Treasuries, widely considered the safest of safe-haven assets. Even in the midst of a global government bond sell-off, US bond rates remain lower than those of other Western economies. And when stocks went on a skid last week, investors were unafraid to turn to their traditional place of refuge, sending Treasury yields sharply lower in the process.

But the difference between France and the United States really comes down to one thing. As James Carville said: It’s the economy, stupid.

The United States also has a uniquely large and diverse economy that is far less susceptible to shocks than many of its smaller peers. AI in particular is producing an investment boom in the United States that is lifting the economy when several other sectors appear to be stagnating or in decline.

One key way to make deficits less relevant is to keep the economy growing strong. That makes the debt look puny by comparison.

So countries need to ask: What is the rate we’re paying — and is it sustainable for us to keep paying it based on our expected economic growth?”

“France and the UK are pretty close,” noted Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “But in the US, AI’s contributions to growth make it more likely we’ll manage our debts and navigate it much more gracefully.”

Economists warn: Don’t confuse the lack of a looming debt crisis in the United States with fiscal responsibility. It’s just that it can handle the problem better than France or the UK.

“That doesn’t mean we should take any solace in that,” added Zandi. “We’re just in a different place.”

Could it happen elsewhere?

Any time a European country faces a fiscal problem, it raises concerns about a contagion that could spread across the continent. But economists widely view France’s problems as contained within the country.

A shopper pays with a five Euro bank note for fruits at a local market in Paris on September 10, 2026. Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters

The European Central Bank has signaled it would not need to intervene in France’s fiscal situation. But it could if it had to, and it is well-positioned to buy up a bunch of bonds of its member countries to limit any potential contagion effects, noted Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.

Other European economies’ deficits are also much smaller by comparison. Some are expected to run surpluses this year.

And French political parties across the left and right have said they want to remain with the European Union — including French presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, a far-right candidate who once championed “Frexit” but has since backed off that pledge. Although Germany’s AfD party has advocated leaving the EU, it isn’t close to forming a government yet, Kenningham noted.

But an X factor could lead to a debt crisis outside France: the US “X date.” At some point next year, the United States will hit its debt ceiling again, and the new Congress will need to negotiate with President Donald Trump to raise it — a political football that could be particularly challenged by a lame duck president and a potentially Democratic-controlled Congress less willing to give in.

A failure to raise the debt ceiling threatens to force the United States to manufacture a default on its debt, even if it otherwise would be able to pay.

“You could construct a scenario in which we breach the debt limit by Halloween next year,” said Zandi. “And then you’ve got other issues.”

World.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks
World.content:
The United Kingdom said Tuesday it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The UK will fly “defensive counter-air missions” using Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the defense ministry said in a statement.

Over the past month, the Houthis have intensified their targets on Saudi Arabia, launching ballistic missiles and drones at key infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, in response to the kingdom’s support for the Yemeni government.

“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in the statement. “The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region.”

“This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” he added.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: GOP attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith come to a head in heated town hall exchange
World.content:
The Muslim Brotherhood has become a flashpoint in Michigan’s Senate race, with Republicans trying to cast Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror and El-Sayed arguing that he is being unfairly accused of the same “dual loyalties” that former Presidents John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama once were.

El-Sayed this weekend denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement founded in Egypt in 1928 — first in a heated exchange with a voter, and later when speaking with reporters — after Republicans have sought to highlight his family’s ties to the group and his past comments about it.

“I do want to talk about why they want to make this their closing argument,” El-Sayed told reporters after a rally Sunday in Flint. “They want to speak to a certain implicit dual loyalty. This has a long history in our politics, that notion that people might pray a little bit differently, have a dual loyalty. It was the same thing they did to JFK when he ran for president, the notion that because he was Catholic that he somehow had dual loyalties. They did the same thing to President Obama simply because his father was of Muslim origin, even though his father is an avowed Christian.”

He added: “This is nothing new. This is what they do when they have no message about the real issues in people’s lives.”

GOP attacks on El-Sayed

Republicans have increasingly drawn attention to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith in the closing weeks of one of the most important Senate races on the 2026 midterm election map.

President Donald Trump, at a campaign rally Friday night, referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and falsely declared that the Democratic former public health official is a “jihadist.” Those comments have become staples of recent Trump rallies and social media comments.

El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, said Sunday on CNN that he has “never called him a terrorist” and said he does not “speak for the president.”

But Rogers accused El-Sayed of aligning with the Muslim Brotherhood.

The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist movement with global offshoots that once wielded significant political power in Egypt, where it was founded. The movement officially rejects the use of violent means to secure its goals. However, offshoots of the group have been linked to attacks in the past.

Trump signed an executive order in November that initiated a process by which certain chapters or other subdivisions of the Muslim Brotherhood could be considered for designation as Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

“You know, he wants to play the victim. This is not about that. This is about the way you think, not the way you pray,” Rogers told CNN’s Dana Bash. “This is about your ideology and how dangerous it is.”

El-Sayed’s town hall exchange

The GOP efforts to tie El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Islamic extremism, burst into the open this weekend at a town hall in Caro.

An attendee repeatedly pressed El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he had yet to hear the candidate reject the organization.

“Abdul, will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” the man shouted from the crowd.

El-Sayed, after disavowing the movement, blasted the man for implicitly assuming his “dual loyalty.”

“You assume … that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution,” El-Sayed said. He later added, “For me, that Constitution is the guiding light.”

The audience member walked out after the exchange as the crowd cheered for El-Sayed.

Family history scrutinized

The GOP attacks come after old tweets from El-Sayed’s half-sister resurfaced online, including a post from 2012 in which she described having “an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.”

El-Sayed has said he does not know what his mother was doing in Egypt during the 1970s, explaining he was 3 when his parents divorced and didn’t see his mother for years. He was primarily raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother.

El-Sayed in 2012 also signed an open letter supporting then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who had been elected earlier that year with the support of the Muslim Brotherhood after the overthrow of the country’s authoritarian government.

A year earlier, he penned a Huffington Post op-ed calling on the United States to support young Arab protesters in Egypt, and downplaying concerns that supporting democracy there would lead to Muslim Brotherhood control of the nation.

During a recent debate, Rogers pointed out that El-Sayed’s mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a non-profit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism.

“Are you going after my mom?” said El-Sayed.

“I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to Al Qaeda,” Rogers said. “Look, that’s your mom. My mom worked at a small chamber of commerce. I’ll put my mom up any day for that.”

El-Sayed responded he is a “dad and a doctor” who wants to “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for All.” He said Rogers “wants this to be about anything but his own record.”

El-Sayed in recent days also addressed his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, being placed on the federal Terrorism Screening Database — a situation she challenged as part of a 2016 class action lawsuit. It’s not clear why Jukaku, who was once president of UCLA’s Muslim Student Association and is now a home-school teacher and writer in California, was added to the list.

“She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off,” El-Sayed told Fox News when asked about his wife’s sister being placed on the terrorist watchlist, which was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001, attacks. “You’ve got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they’ve got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up.”

World.title: PM: Egypt Forum 2026 will be for citizen, who is ‘hero of the story’
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly emphasized that the “Egypt Forum 2026” will be dedicated to the citizen, quoting the President that the citizen is the “hero of the story,” and noting that the Egyptian citizen is the one who bore with the state the full burden of economic reform, structural reforms, difficult conditions, and the unprecedented challenges the country has witnessed over the past fifteen years.

This came during the speech delivered by Madbouly at the opening session of the “Egypt Forum 2026,” held under the slogan “A Look at Today… A Vision for Tomorrow,” in the presence of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.

At the beginning of his address, the prime minister welcomed the attendees and expressed his sincere thanks and appreciation to President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for directing the government to convene this forum.

He highlighted that it brings together various segments of Egyptian society and stakeholders in Egyptian affairs, including cabinet ministers, governors, heads of affiliated authorities and agencies, as well as representatives of civil society organizations, experts, thinkers, specialists across numerous fields, public figures, politicians, opposition members, and citizens from all walks of life.

The Prime Minister pointed out that this forum aims to engage in a serious and constructive dialogue regarding the reality and future of our beloved homeland, Egypt.

He explained that the forum presents an opportunity to review what has been accomplished across numerous sectors and fields over the course of a 12-year journey of construction and development, amidst unprecedented conditions and challenges that faced Egypt and which the world has experienced and continues to face.

The Prime Minister noted that the forum is not solely intended to display achievements made within the framework of this development journey achievements of which much has been accomplished and will be presented across the forum’s various sessions.

Rather, he explained that the presentation will take place within a framework of listening and responding to the concerns, criticisms, and proposals of society and citizens, stating: “The forum is not a one-way dialogue, but rather a two-way dialogue.”

Consequently, the government will not speak alone while citizens merely listen; instead, the opposite is true: “The citizen speaks as well, and the government listens.”

He noted in this regard that this principle was reflected in determining the themes and sessions of this forum, adding: “The government did not set these themes and sessions on its own; rather, a scientific methodology was applied to identify the concerns and priorities of citizens.”

Madbouly explained that during the 15 days following President Sisi’s call to hold this forum, public opinion surveys were conducted involving citizens, youth, investors, and private sector representatives.

These surveys addressed their vision regarding the most pressing issues, their needs, and their level of satisfaction with the services provided to them by the Egyptian state.

The Prime Minister noted that listening sessions for citizens were also held at the National Training Academy (NTA), in which more than 450 citizens participated and presented around 150 ideas and proposals.

This took place alongside active engagement from Egyptian universities and think tanks, as over 4,000 academics, researchers, and experts participated in 30 preparatory sessions held across 28 Egyptian universities including prestigious institutions such as Cairo, Ain Shams, and Alexandria Universities, alongside capital, national, and private universities.

Furthermore, around 13 preparatory sessions were organized with the participation of nearly 16 think tanks, represented by various public figures and intellectuals, inside the Information and Decision Support Center (IDSC) at the Cabinet headquarters.

Following these steps came the most crucial measure: launching the forum’s official website.

Madbouly explained that when the website was launched, there were apprehensions regarding the level of engagement.

However, he noted that up to this moment, the site has recorded 17 million views, and over 61,000 individuals have registered, submitting more than 16,000 ideas and proposals. Most importantly, 50% of the participants and registered users on the platform belong to the 18–35 age bracket meaning we are talking about our youth—including more than 5,000 students, some of whom are school students.

He pointed out that this interaction resulted in gathering more than 42 pressing public opinion questions, currently displayed on the hall’s screen, reflecting significant diversity.

He emphasized that this forum will serve as an opportunity for ministers and officials, alongside presenting what has been accomplished in the Egyptian state, to address the questions being raised, such as: Why did you build the New Capital? Was the scale of road and bridge projects a necessity, or should the focus have been on health and education? What is the future vision for the Egyptian economy after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) program phase? How will the state move to face external and regional challenges facing Egypt? What steps will the state take regarding the debt portfolio? All these questions will find answers during the forum’s sessions.

Madbouly affirmed that “Egypt Forum 2026” represents a vital opportunity to review the state’s efforts and achievements across various sectors and to answer all citizen inquiries with complete frankness and transparency without withholding any information.

This reflects the state’s keenness to keep citizens informed of the facts and to clarify the outcomes of the policies and measures taken, as well as their real-world impact.

The Prime Minister explained that the forum aims to review different experiences and achievements while also discussing the challenges or setbacks encountered along certain paths, in light of emerging circumstances and variables that sometimes necessitated re-evaluating certain directions and courses.

He stressed the importance of evaluating the experience objectively, recognizing what has been achieved so far, assessing what the situation might have become had necessary measures not been taken, and ultimately establishing work priorities for the coming phase.

Madbouly indicated that the upcoming phase, extending through 2030, requires transitioning from presenting general visions and ambitions to setting clear targets and precise executive plans, focusing on what will be accomplished over the next three years and clarifying the scheduled measures to achieve these targets, thereby allowing for precise performance evaluation and monitoring of implementation rates.

In a related context, the prime minister explained that the results of monitoring citizens’ opinions and proposals showed that five main issues topped the concerns of nearly 70% of participants: education, prices and controlling inflation, improving healthcare services, wages and pensions, and maintaining security and stability.

He added that citizen proposals also reflected interest in several other files, including education, culture and media, strengthening Egyptian national identity, the labor market, youth and sports, and information and communications technology (ICT), stressing that youth represent a fundamental pillar for the nation’s future, which was reflected in drafting the forum’s themes and selecting topics for discussion.

The Prime Minister confirmed that the forum’s events, continuing over the coming days, will address a major theme each day to allow for a comprehensive discussion of priority issues, review achieved results, identify existing challenges, and present the state’s targets and plans to address them in the coming period.

Madbouly explained that the first day of the forum discusses the theme “Human Building” through three plenary sessions alongside parallel workshops, tackling issues of education, youth and innovation, culture, and the social values system.

He noted that discussions under this theme aim to answer a key question regarding how to build upon the progress made in educational facilities and services, expanding opportunities for education, empowerment, and participation, ultimately improving the quality of educational outcomes and building the Egyptian individual who is capable of continuous learning and innovation, thereby enhancing their ability to actively participate in development efforts.

The Prime Minister added that the second day addresses the theme “Integrated Development and Quality of Life for Citizens” through three main plenary sessions, discussing urban development, citizen health, Digital Egypt, and the digital transformation of government services.

He stressed that discussions under this theme aim to explore ways to maximize the benefit from national projects implemented by the state and enhance their direct impact on improving citizens’ quality of life, alongside developing and increasing the efficiency of government services and facilitating citizen access to them through expanded digital transformation applications, contributing to higher service standards and achieving integrated development goals.

Madbouly then spoke about the third theme, represented by social protection and community security, which covers sessions on citizen security, the social protection system, food and water security, current challenges, and the future vision. It addresses how to strengthen the protection of citizens from economic and social pressures.

At the same time, he noted that the fourth theme covers the economic aspect through plenary sessions such as: investment, industry, and sustainable job opportunities; features of the national economic transformation program (the “post-IMF program”); and a report to public opinion on how to double our foreign currency resources and manage the debt portfolio, moving on to the energy sector, over which the world is currently witnessing wars and conflicts.

The Prime Minister stated that discussions on this matter will focus on how to transition from economic stability to more productive and competitive growth, led by private sector investment, to positively reflect on employment, income, and living standards.

He added: “We have dedicated Friday to the citizen to speak directly about the issues concerning public opinion, such as prices, reconciliation in building violations, as well as urban greening, regulating the real estate market, concerns of Egyptians abroad, in addition to any public issues that have drawn attention for a period, including stray dogs.”

The Prime Minister pointed out that the goal is not merely to issue outputs and recommendations from the forum, but rather to establish national priorities that everyone works toward, reaching actionable and trackable solutions with clear responsibilities, where each entity will be accountable for implementing its part, supported by measurement indicators to establish an executive work program for the Egyptian state over the next four years until 2030.

These are the goals aimed for from this forum in order to achieve a larger objective: working to improve living conditions in accordance with current circumstances and realities.

In conclusion, the Prime Minister quoted a thinker, stating: “Building any nation is a long and arduous marathon in which those seeking quick glory do not succeed; the progress of any state does not depend on those who make promises, but on pure and sincere effort exerted by every citizen of this nation.”

World.title: FM welcomes convening of UfM Economic Forum in Cairo
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty welcomed the convening of the Union for the Mediterranean (UfM) Economic Forum in Cairo on Tuesday, highlighting its focus on strengthening the private sector’s role as a key driver of sustainable economic development and growth across the region.

Abdelatty made the remarks during a meeting on Monday, October 19, 2026, with Fadi Hajali, Acting Secretary General of the Union for the Mediterranean, according to Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Nader Zaki.

The Foreign Minister said the forum comes at a critical time as the region faces unprecedented economic, security, and environmental challenges.

He underscored the need for UfM member states to intensify joint efforts to address these challenges and mitigate their negative impact on member countries.

The meeting also discussed ways to strengthen cooperation among UfM member states as a framework for collaboration between the two shores of the Mediterranean.

Abdelatty highlighted the importance of encouraging further joint projects and expressed Egypt’s readiness to deepen its engagement with the union, particularly in energy, water studies, and technological solutions.

The talks also addressed regional developments and ongoing efforts to restore calm and stability.

Abdelatty emphasized that the Palestinian issue remains at the heart of the region’s conflict, pointing to the international community’s responsibility to address the humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip and ensure the unrestricted delivery of aid.

The two sides further discussed efforts to contain tensions and reduce escalation amid regional challenges affecting communities on both shores of the Mediterranean.

World.title: Investment Minister urges youth to embrace technology, continuous learning to seize job opportunities
World.content:
Rapid advances in technology, artificial intelligence and digital services are opening new opportunities for young people to launch businesses and develop their skills, Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Mohamed Farid Saleh said on Monday, October 19, 2026, stressing the importance of continuous learning and gaining the experience needed to benefit from emerging job market opportunities.

Farid made the remarks during an open meeting with 150 students from universities across Egypt, attended by Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom.

The meeting discussed the future of the labor market and entrepreneurship, opportunities available to young people, and ways to prepare for technological and economic changes.

Farid said people’s career paths are shaped by various factors and circumstances, but continuous learning, acquiring knowledge and skills, and applying them in practice are essential to preparing for opportunities and turning them into practical experience.

He stressed that young people should strive to make a meaningful difference in any job they undertake, regardless of its nature or the level of responsibility involved. Excellence, he said, begins with taking assigned tasks seriously, improving work methods and delivering better results.

Learning, he added, does not end with earning a university degree or reaching a particular position. Gaining experience helps individuals identify the skills they need to develop and supports their professional growth.

On launching businesses with limited capital, Farid said the first step is to understand market needs and identify problems that can be addressed with practical solutions, while using modern technology to develop ideas and turn them into viable ventures.

Investment opportunities span productive, service and technology sectors, he said, adding that business success depends on meeting genuine market needs, offering competitive products or services, and adapting business models to customer requirements.

Farid also highlighted the importance of tapping foreign markets to support the growth of Egyptian businesses, particularly as advances in digital marketing and e-commerce enable young entrepreneurs to reach new markets and expand their operations.

He urged students to continue learning, develop their capabilities and prepare for available opportunities, stressing that gaining experience is an ongoing process that requires perseverance and a commitment to achieving tangible results across different responsibilities.

World.title: PM: President al-Sisi has made education top priority since taking office
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has made education a top priority since taking office, noting that significant steps have been taken to reform the sector.

Madbouly made the remarks during a session titled “What Are Our Children Learning, and Does It Prepare Them for the Future?” on the first day of Egypt Forum 2026, held under the theme “A Look at Today, a Vision for Tomorrow” under the auspices of President al-Sisi.E

The session was attended by Minister of Education and Technical Education Mohamed Abdel Latif, Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research and Acting Minister of Culture Abdel Aziz Konsowa, House of Representatives Education and Scientific Research Committee Chairman Ashraf al-Shehy, as well as university presidents, heads of educational institutions, academics, education experts, private-sector and civil society representatives, students and parents.

At the beginning, Madbouly welcomed the participants, stressing that education is a top priority for the Egyptian state, which recognizes that a country’s progress is measured by the quality of its education system and its ability to prepare young people to meet the demands of the modern era.

He noted that improving education was a major challenge worldwide, not just in Egypt, pointing out that even advanced countries were taking measures to address problems in their education systems, despite not facing the same scale of challenges that Egypt had encountered and continued to face.

Madbouly said education reform had been particularly challenging in Egypt, citing classrooms that previously accommodated between 100 and 150 students, a situation that made meaningful improvements in educational outcomes difficult to achieve.

He also noted that, according to international benchmarks cited during the discussion, there should be approximately one university for every million people. Egypt had around 50 universities in 2014, compared with approximately 131 today, serving a population of about 110 million.

He said the expansion represented significant progress in increasing access to higher education, while emphasizing that infrastructure development must go hand in hand with improvements in educational quality.

The Prime Minister added that curriculum reform had also been constrained by teacher shortages and the lack of adequate preparation among some teachers to deliver new curricula.

He stressed that education reform required sustained effort and could not be achieved overnight, particularly given the challenges that had accumulated over decades.

Madbouly said Egypt had made considerable progress in addressing fundamental problems in the education system, adding that the next phase would focus increasingly on improving educational quality and preparing young people to meet the rapidly evolving demands of the modern world.

He also discussed the new Baccalaureate system, noting that private and international schools had long offered students internationally recognized qualifications, including the International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE) and American diplomas, which provide multiple opportunities to improve academic results.

By contrast, students in public schools following the traditional General Secondary Education Certificate system have generally had only one opportunity to determine their academic future.

Madbouly questioned the consequences for students who might be unable to perform well in examinations because of illness, accidents or other unforeseen circumstances.

He said he was deeply saddened each year by reports of students taking their own lives after failing to achieve their desired results in the secondary school examinations, which had come to be viewed by some as determining their entire future.

Acknowledging the considerable psychological pressure the system places on students and their families, Madbouly said the new Baccalaureate system seeks to provide public-school students with opportunities comparable to those available to their counterparts in private schools.

He also stressed the need for continuous curriculum development in response to rapid advances in scientific knowledge. Whereas curricula could previously remain unchanged for 10, 15 or even 20 years, the pace of change today requires regular review and updating.

He said curricula should be reassessed every three to four years to determine whether revisions are necessary, reiterating that improving educational quality would be a central priority in the coming period.

Madbouly said the government would continue developing all components of the education system, including educational projects, institutes and the teaching workforce.

He stressed that reform must produce tangible results and that education policies should respond to citizens’ concerns and address the challenges they face.

The prime minister also referred to concerns raised by citizens during his field visits regarding the status of Arabic and religious education in international schools and whether grades in these subjects should count towards students’ overall scores.

He said these concerns reflected parents’ anxieties about their children’s education, emphasizing that the issue extended beyond educational regulations to encompass the preservation of Egypt’s national identity and national security.

He questioned whether students in international schools had sufficient command of Arabic, describing it as the national language and the language of Egyptian society. He warned that declining attention to Arabic posed a challenge that required serious consideration because of its implications for national identity and security.

Madbouly stressed the need for state intervention to protect younger generations, strengthen their ties to their language and national culture, and reinforce Egyptian identity, while balancing openness to international education systems with the preservation of national values.

Turning to higher education, Madbouly addressed public concerns over the admission of international students to Egyptian universities and the potential implications for Egyptian students seeking places in highly competitive faculties, particularly medicine.

He said some parents questioned the fairness of admitting international students when Egyptian applicants with high grades were unable to secure places in certain faculties. He emphasized the importance of explaining the rules governing international student admissions to the public.

Referring to the higher education minister’s remarks, Madbouly said attracting international students was part of Egypt’s efforts to strengthen the global standing and international rankings of its universities. He noted that international student enrollment was among the factors considered in global university rankings, in accordance with the relevant assessment criteria.

He added that international students helped enhance the academic standing of Egyptian universities and strengthen their regional and global competitiveness, thereby supporting the international recognition of their degrees and their value in overseas labor markets.

Citing the German University in Cairo as an example of a university featured in international rankings, Madbouly said strengthening the global recognition of Egyptian universities and their qualifications required attention to ranking criteria as part of a comprehensive approach to higher education development.

He reaffirmed that these considerations should be taken into account when reviewing regulations governing international student admissions, while maintaining a balance between enhancing the global competitiveness of Egyptian universities and preserving opportunities for Egyptian students to enroll in various faculties.

Madbouly also described education as a key pillar of Egypt’s soft power, stressing the importance of developing Egyptian universities and attracting international students.

He said the benefits extended beyond education to strengthening Egypt’s relations with other countries by enabling international graduates to develop cultural and personal ties with Egyptian society and carry positive impressions of their studies and experiences in the country.

He noted that graduates of Egyptian universities might go on to occupy senior positions in their home countries, including as presidents, prime ministers and ministers, highlighting education’s role in building lasting relationships between Egypt and countries around the world.

Madbouly added that graduates who assume leadership positions in their home countries could help strengthen ties with Egypt, as the relationships and connections they develop during their years of study and residence in the country may endure long after graduation.

He concluded by stressing that education is a major component of a country’s soft power and that enhancing Egyptian universities’ ability to attract international students would help strengthen Egypt’s international presence.

World.title: Liberia Bets Its Future on Iron, Gold and Power
World.content:
MONROVIA — For most of the past half-century, Liberia’s mineral wealth has been a story told in the past tense. In the 1960s and 1970s, iron ore from the Nimba and Bong ranges made this small West African nation one of the world’s leading exporters of the steelmaking ingredient. Then came 14 years of civil war, and the mines, railways and ports fell silent.

By Rodney D. Sieh

This month, the government is staking its economic future on rewriting that story in the present tense.



On October 28 and 29, Liberia will host the first Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference & Expo, known as LIMEC 2026, a gathering of ministers, mining executives, energy developers, financiers and development partners. Organized jointly by the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the Liberia Chamber of Mines and the London-based events firm AME Trade Ltd, the conference will be held at the Farmington Hotel under the theme “Powering Prosperity: Sustainable Mining and Energy as Catalysts for Liberia’s Economic Transformation.” Organizers say ongoing and planned projects could draw more than $3 billion in new investment.

Launching the event at a news conference over the weekend, Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban framed it as a turning point.

“Our message to the international investment community is clear: Liberia is open for responsible business, committed to reform, and ready to build mutually beneficial partnerships,” he said.

But he attached a condition that will be closely watched by the companies already operating here. “Our natural resources must serve not only the interests of investors but also the broader aspirations of the Liberian people,” he said.

That tension — between courting capital and capturing a fairer share of its rewards — runs through every part of Liberia’s resource economy today.

From boom to ruin, and back

Liberia, founded in 1847 and Africa’s oldest republic, built much of its post-war-era economy on concessions: rubber, timber and, above all, iron ore. The Liberian American-Swedish Minerals Company (LAMCO) in Nimba County and the German-backed Bong Mines were among the largest mining operations in Africa, linked by dedicated railways to the ports of Buchanan and Monrovia.

The civil wars of 1989 to 2003 destroyed that system. Rail lines were stripped for scrap, ports decayed, and an industry that once underpinned the national budget vanished.

The revival began in 2005, when Mittal Steel — now ArcelorMittal, the world’s second-largest steelmaker — signed a Mineral Development Agreement to restart mining in Nimba and rebuild the 250-kilometer (155-mile) railway to Buchanan. First exports followed in 2011. But the Ebola epidemic of 2014-15 and a collapse in iron ore prices slowed ambitions, and for more than a decade the company shipped around 5 million metric tons a year.

Liberia also opened its first commercial gold mine, New Liberty in Grand Cape Mount County, which began production in 2016 after Turkey’s MNG Gold rescued the Ebola-stricken project.

What has changed in the past 18 months is scale.

The ArcelorMittal factor

ArcelorMittal Liberia remains the anchor of the sector, accounting for roughly 90 percent of the country’s iron ore exports. Its $1.8 billion expansion, built around a new concentrator at Tokadeh in Nimba County, lifts the company’s total investment in Liberia to about $3.5 billion — the largest foreign direct investment since the war.

In January, lawmakers ratified a third amendment to the company’s agreement, extending it to 2050 with an option to renew for a further 25 years. In return, ArcelorMittal agreed to pay $200 million upfront for the extended mining rights and reserved rail capacity, and annual license fees rose tenfold, from $50,000 to $500,000. The payment alone represented roughly 16 percent of the national budget, according to the credit insurer Coface.

The results are already visible. ArcelorMittal Liberia set production and shipment records in 2025, shipping about 10 million tons. The company initially targeted 20 million tons for 2026 but now guides to 18 million, citing heavy rains that slowed mining and port operations in the second quarter. It is also upgrading the railway to carry up to 30 million tons a year should it decide to expand further.

For the government, the deal secured long-term certainty from its largest investor. For ArcelorMittal, LIMEC is likely to be a stage on which it can present itself as a partner in Liberia’s ambitions — while watching carefully how far the reform agenda reaches into existing contracts.

Breaking the rail monopoly

The most consequential structural change in Liberia’s mining economy may not be a mine at all, but a railway.

For two decades, ArcelorMittal held exclusive use of the Yekepa-to-Buchanan line. Under President Joseph Boakai’s multi-user rail policy, that is ending. In December 2025, the Legislature ratified a 25-year Concession and Access Agreement with Ivanhoe Atlantic, a U.S. company founded by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, valued at $1.8 billion.

The deal allows Ivanhoe to haul ultra-high-grade iron ore from its Kon Kweni project in neighboring Guinea — which holds about 752 million tons of direct-shipping ore, including 209 million tons grading 67.8 percent iron — across Liberia to Buchanan. The company plans initial output of 2 million to 5 million tons a year, with exports through Liberia expected from 2027, and an eventual second phase of up to 30 million tons.

The amended ArcelorMittal agreement now requires new rail users to invest in expanding capacity to meet their own needs, an arrangement designed to turn the corridor into shared national infrastructure rather than a private asset.

The stakes are geopolitical as well as commercial. Ivanhoe markets Kon Kweni as a source of high-grade ore for Western supply chains, an alternative to the China-led Simandou mega-project elsewhere in Guinea, and the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia has publicly endorsed the deal. The corridor sits atop an estimated 12 billion tons of iron ore reserves straddling the border, much of it still under exploration licenses.

If the model works, Liberia could become a transit hub for Guinea’s landlocked southeastern deposits — earning fees, jobs and port traffic from minerals it does not even own.

Gold, grievances and the 3 percent question

If iron ore is Liberia’s success story, gold is its flashpoint.

Bea Mountain Mining Corporation, controlled by Turkish businessman Murathan Günal through Avesoro Resources, is the country’s largest industrial gold producer. It plans to double plant capacity and says the expansion will create more than 2,000 jobs. But the company has faced mounting scrutiny. A joint investigation by The Associated Press and The Gecko Project published in January documented cyanide spills into waterways, 2,200 hectares (5,436 acres) of cleared rainforest and community anger that turned deadly during 2024 protests. The company says it has reinforced its tailings dam and points to its record of rescuing the mine and safeguarding more than 1,200 Liberian jobs.

Politically, the sharpest issue is money. With gold prices near record highs — approaching $4,200 an ounce earlier this year — both senators from Grand Cape Mount County have called for the company’s agreement to be renegotiated, arguing that its flat 3 percent royalty no longer reflects the value leaving the country. The government holds a 5 percent stake in the operation. A visit by Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, at which figures of about $1.6 billion in company revenue were discussed, stirred public outrage over the gap between that wealth and conditions in host communities.

Liberia remains a modest gold producer, at roughly 10 tons a year, and an estimated 70 percent of gold activity is informal, according to Senator Francis Dopoh, who has co-sponsored a bill to create a state-owned National Gold Company and a domestic refinery.

Rewriting the rules

These pressures have converged on a single question: Liberia’s mining law, written in 2000, is widely seen as out of date.

In February, Minister Tingban told Reuters at the Mining Indaba conference in Cape Town that a new mining code would be ready within three months. It would create a national mining company entitled to a free-carried equity stake of 10 to 15 percent in new projects, rising over time to 25 percent. Royalties would remain at 4.5 percent for iron ore and 3 percent for gold, with a new 8 percent rate for heavy mineral sands.

“We are moving from a royalty-only approach to equity participation to maximise returns,” Tingban said at the time. Whether the new equity terms would apply to existing projects, he added, would be determined by the Ministry of Justice.

Eight months on, the overhaul is still working its way through the Legislature. The House of Representatives opened public hearings in July, where the minister pressed for tougher penalties against illegal mining and mineral smuggling. The Senate has advanced an amendment reserving small-scale Class B licenses for Liberians. The Liberia Chamber of Mines, which represents the industry, has urged lawmakers to pursue a comprehensive rewrite rather than piecemeal fixes, saying investors expect fairness, consistency and transparency.

For existing operators, LIMEC arrives at a moment of regulatory uncertainty. The government’s message — welcome, but on better terms — will be tested by how it treats contracts already signed.

Power: the missing ingredient

The “energy” half of LIMEC’s title addresses what may be Liberia’s biggest structural handicap. Only about a third of Liberians — 32.7 percent — have access to electricity.

The government aims to raise that to 75 percent by 2030 under a national energy compact backed by the World Bank, while lifting renewables to 75 percent of the power mix.

There has been progress. The 88-megawatt Mount Coffee hydropower plant, rebuilt after the war, supplies nearly 70 percent of the country’s electricity. In June, President Boakai inaugurated the country’s first utility-scale solar plant, a 20-megawatt park at the Mount Coffee site, and signed a $57 million World Bank financing agreement to expand it and add battery storage. With Mount Coffee’s full capacity restored, the state utility has begun cutting costly imports from Côte d’Ivoire and Guinea through the regional CLSG power line.

For miners, reliable grid power would lower costs and make processing — and the value addition Tingban champions — more viable.

Without it, ambitions to refine gold or process ore at home will remain largely aspirational.

What it means for the economy

The macroeconomic picture is encouraging. The International Monetary Fund estimates Liberia’s economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, up from 4 percent in 2024, and projects 5.5 percent growth this year, driven chiefly by iron ore, with support from manufacturing and construction. Inflation stood at 5.3 percent in May, and the country remains on a $210 million IMF Extended Credit Facility running through 2027.

Mining’s weight is growing fast. Extractives already accounted for more than 21 percent of domestic revenue in 2023, according to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, and mining drove roughly two-thirds of economic growth in the first three quarters of 2025, Coface estimates.

Tingban has projected that mining’s share of national output could climb from 15 percent in 2024 to as much as 50 percent as new producers — including Cavalla Resources, Westcrest, Zodiac and a revived Bao Chico — come online, with national iron ore output potentially reaching 25 million to 30 million tons.

That concentration is also the risk. The IMF projects Liberia’s current account deficit will widen sharply this year, to 18 percent of GDP from 7 percent, as fuel and mining equipment imports surge. A single company still dominates exports, and the country’s fortunes are tightly bound to iron ore prices — and therefore to Chinese steel demand — at a time when vast new supply from Guinea’s Simandou is coming to market.

And Liberia’s history offers a sobering lesson: in the decades of the LAMCO era, iron ore generated enormous export earnings while much of the population remained poor, a disparity that fed the grievances behind the country’s collapse.

The real test

Tingban himself has set the bar. “LIMEC 2026 must be measured not only by the quality of its discussions,” he said, “but also by the investments it attracts, the partnerships it builds, the jobs it helps create, and the lasting benefits it delivers to the Liberian people.”

For international investors, Liberia offers rare advantages: a rebuilt rail corridor, deep-water access, a stable currency, an IMF-backed reform program and a government openly courting capital. For Liberians, the questions are older and harder — whether this boom will build schools and power lines in Nimba and Grand Cape Mount, whether communities will be heard, and whether the country can finally turn the wealth beneath its soil into prosperity above it.

Next week’s conference will not answer those questions. But it will show whether Liberia, a generation after the guns fell silent, is ready to be judged by them.
