World.title: Royce White exploring legal avenues after WNBA tells Congress he is ineligible to play
World.content:
Former NBA player Royce White says he plans to explore legal avenues against the WNBA after Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told Congress that he and Enes Kanter Freedom are ineligible to play because they are men.

White told OutKick that Engelbert’s response does not resolve his challenge to the league’s eligibility standards, calling on the WNBA to explain how it defines men and women.

"We plan to explore every legal avenue possible to hold the WNBA and NBA community to their stated standards and values," White said.

FORMER NBA PLAYER ROYCE WHITE SAYS HE IS DECLARING FOR NEXT WNBA DRAFT AFTER ENES KANTER ANNOUNCEMENT

Asked whether Engelbert’s letter had officially triggered a previously discussed discrimination lawsuit, White said he could not discuss particulars. He did not announce a filing or provide a timetable for taking legal action.

The dispute centers on White’s and Freedom’s efforts to enter the 2027 WNBA draft after declaring that they identify as women. During the interview, White agreed when asked whether his declaration was "for basketball purposes."

In an Oct. 16 letter responding to Republican lawmakers, Engelbert stated the league’s position directly.

"With respect to your questions regarding eligibility, only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men," Engelbert wrote.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The response followed a Sept. 17 inquiry from Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., and four Republican colleagues asking how the WNBA defines "women" under its collective bargaining agreement and why White and Freedom had been deemed ineligible. The lawmakers requested answers by Oct. 16.

The agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but does not specify language concerning gender identity or sex assigned at birth, Front Office Sports reported in August.

Engelbert’s response did not supply a definition of "women" or explain the criteria used to classify White and Freedom as men.

White said that distinction remains central to his challenge.

"No, we’re not letting them off that easy," he said when asked whether Engelbert’s statement represented a step in the right direction.

"She has to define, and the WNBA has to define, what a man and a woman is and why."

White also called for NBA Commissioner Adam Silver to address the dispute.

ENES FREEDOM RIPS CHERYL REEVE FOR SAYING WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES 'DON’T WANT TRANSGENDER PEOPLE TO EXIST'

"I’d like Adam Silver and the NBA to weigh in," he said.

The league had already rejected the two former NBA players’ eligibility through statements attributed to league sources in August.

ROYCE WHITE SHOWS UP TO INDIANA FEVER GAME IN BLONDE WIG AMID WNBA DRAFT PURSUIT

White described himself as a longtime fan of women’s basketball, saying he grew up watching older female relatives play sports and learned from local girls’ basketball players.

"I’m a fan of the WNBA. I think the women have come a long way," White said. "I’d love to see it not as politicized as it is, because I think it takes away from the beauty of the game."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

White added that he has been watching the WNBA Finals and is considering attending games, although he declined to identify which ones, citing security concerns.

"I have my eyes on a few games for sure, and I’ve been watching," he said, describing himself as "scoping the competition."

Eight years after she was fired from her hit reboot of "Roseanne," Roseanne Barr is looking for a second chance.

The 73-year-old has self-financed a new show called "Meemaw: A Modern Day Fable."

Barr told The Hollywood Reporter this week that she's shopping the sitcom to "Anybody who wants a number one show and is smart enough to take a number one show."

ETHAN HAWKE BLASTS HOLLYWOOD'S 'GREEDY BASTARDS,' PREDICTS MASSIVE REBELLION AGAINST POWERFUL ELITES

"I don’t know why they don’t want a number one show and why they hate a number one show and why they would destroy a number one show," she said of Hollywood. "But if they do want a number one show, I got it."

The "Roseanne" reboot was a huge hit with tens of millions of viewers each week, and it finished its first season as the number one primetime sitcom in the 18-49 demographic, according to Variety.

ROSEANNE BARR CALLS FORMER CO-STAR A 'BRAINWASHED BIGOT' AFTER HE SAID REBOOT WAS 'RIGHTFULLY CANCELED'

She’s also pitched "Meemaw" to Elon Musk but without success.

"I don’t know why he hasn’t called me or returned my calls," she admitted of the trillionaire. "I mean, of all people on earth, I’m the one he should call, but I don’t know."

HOW ELON MUSK GOT BACK IN TRUMP'S ORBIT AFTER NUCLEAR FALLOUT, INSIDERS REVEAL: 'WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE'

"Meemaw" is about the matriarch of a mixed-race family in Texas who are preppers, which she describes as "Somebody who’s prepared of the end of the world."

It’s partially based on her life.

"I’m a prepper. I live in Texas. Everybody’s a prepper here," she said.

The show also stars Drea de Matteo, Omar Gooding and Randy Quaid who plays Barr’s love interest.

JOHN GOODMAN ADMITS HE FELT 'FRIGHTENED' AFTER THE SUDDEN FAME HE EXPERIENCED FROM 'ROSEANNE'

"I’m in love with him and I wish he would leave his wife and marry me," she joked. "I enjoyed making out with him so much that I wrote extra scenes where we would make out."

Barr said she hasn’t shown the sitcom to anyone yet.

"But it is so funny," she said. "It’s the funniest s--- I’ve ever done, and I had a ball and I play a really wacky old lady this time."

On her firing from the reboot, Barr insists she didn’t intend her infamous tweet about former Obama aide Valerie Jarrett to be racist.

After the tweet, she apologized, and she claimed ABC gave her a choice of signing off on the rights to the show so it could continue as "The Conners" or it would be canceled and everyone would lose their jobs.

She continued, "The only thing that mattered to me at the time is I said, ‘I want you to say I’m not a racist and that you know I’m not a racist and that my whole life has been about fighting racism and that you know it.’"

Ohio State head coach Ryan Day delivered bad news for his Buckeyes football program, as quarterback Julian Sayin will be out "indefinitely" because of a shoulder injury.

Day initially said that Sayin would miss "several weeks" after injury his throwing shoulder following Ohio State’s 19-15 win over Indiana this past weekend.

Several weeks have now turned into an indefinite amount of time away from the Buckeyes, and Day admitted the team is preparing as if Sayin won’t be available for the remainder of the regular season, and even worse, the College Football Playoff.

"First off, we’re not going to put any timeline on his recovery, but he is out indefinitely," he told reporters. "So, what we’re trying to do is give Julian and his family some privacy to go through this process. But based on the nature of the injury, we are putting together a plan for him not being available for the regular season and also him not being available for the postseason.

Luke Fahey, the true freshman who took over after Sayin went down in the fourth quarter of last week’s victory, will remain the Buckeyes’ starter moving forward. The injury also comes with Ohio State on a bye this weekend before traveling to No. 16 USC for a Halloween matchup.

"When Luke's in there, we just may need to do things just a little bit differently, but the bye week gives us a chance to regroup on that and put our heads together," Day said on Saturday.

Sayin’s injury came after Hoosiers defender Mario Landino hit his throwing shoulder while sacking him. The hit forced Sayin to fumble, and he went to the locker room to look at his ailment. Sayin later returned to the sideline in a sling.

There has not been a specific injury for Sayin, but one can imply just how serious it could be if Day and his coaching staff are preparing as if he might not be available for the entire rest of the season.

World.title: Ana Navarro clashes with 'The View' co-hosts, declares there's 'no way in hell' she would meet with Trump
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The View" co-host Ana Navarro said Tuesday there was "no way in hell" that she would meet with President Donald Trump.

During a segment on the ABC daytime talk show, the panel discussed Trump's Thursday night dinner with comedian Bill Maher, sports commentator Stephen A. Smith and musician Kid Rock at the White House. This led to a discussion among the co-hosts about whether they would accept an invitation to dinner with the president.

While co-hosts Sara Haines and Alyssa Farah Griffin, who previously worked for Trump, said they would accept an invitation, Navarro responded, "Hell to the no."

"There is no way in hell, no way in hell I would want to break bread or be in the same room with a man whose administration is hunting Latinos," Navarro said.

TRUMP HOSTED A DINNER WITH – WAIT FOR IT – STEPHEN A SMITH, KID ROCK AND BILL MAHER

"It’s not 'Lady and the Tramp.' You’re not going to slurp pasta," Haines replied jokingly.

"No, but, listen, stop, this is not funny!" Navarro responded. "What he’s doing to Latinos is criminal."

She clarified that she had no interest in meeting with Trump because it would make "zero difference" to his administration.

"I know that he has seen the polls of Latinos going against him, that he’s lost 50 points of support with Latinos, and his administration has doubled down on their cruelty," Navarro said. "They are killing Latinos, chasing them, hunting them, racially profiling them, torturing them, sending them to places in far-off Africa. You think I’m going to go share a meal with him?"

Haines pointed out that Navarro has met with and questioned other Republican politicians, including Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., but Navarro suggested that there were other ways to push back against political figures.

"You know who’s going to hold him accountable? The people who are going to vote in the midterm elections," Navarro said.

'THE VIEW' CO-HOST DEMANDS 25TH AMENDMENT BE USED AGAINST TRUMP, SUGGESTS CABINET COULD DO IT AFTER MIDTERMS

Co-hosts Sunny Hostin and Whoopi Goldberg agreed with Navarro, saying there was no real reason to sit down with Trump.

"He’s the criminal-in-chief," Hostin said. "I think that he would not listen, and I don’t think this is a normal presidency. I think it’s abhorrent, and I think it’s abnormal. I think what he’s doing to Latinos, I think what he’s doing to African Americans, I think what he’s doing to the LGBTQ+ community, I think the fact that he’s enriching himself, it’s so disgusting and abhorrent. I don't think I would meet with him."

"This is a man who started out racially profiling people," Goldberg said. "It’s not the first time he’s done it. He’s done it for years, and I cannot, in good conscience, try to reason with someone who has decided that I’m barely human."

Fox News Digital reached out to ABC and the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response from either.

Despite several co-hosts' refusal to meet with Trump, fellow co-host Joy Behar said in a New York Magazine interview published Friday that she would like to see the president appear on the show.

"I’d love Donald Trump to take the heat," Behar said.

Vice President JD Vance appeared on "The View" in June and sparred with the co-hosts on issues including immigration.

In an interview with "Fox & Friends" Friday, Kid Rock praised the dinner with Trump, Maher and Smith, saying the group had a great conversation despite having different political leanings.

"It was epic," he said. "And the thing that was the greatest, there's so many points, I could do an hour on it, is that, you know, two Democrats, two Republicans sit down, break bread, have laughs, talk about, have tough conversations on a lot of the issues."

World.title: Supermotocross champion Levi Kitchen wants to try tournament bass fishing when he hangs up his helmet
World.content:
Levi Kitchen just won the 2026 Monster Energy SMX 250 Class World Championship. But the 25-year-old already has his eye on another competitive pursuit for whenever he decides to hang up his helmet.

Professional bass fishing.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

The Monster Energy Pro Circuit Kawasaki rider is an avid angler who spends much of his downtime on the water. And while he's got plenty left to accomplish on a dirt bike, Kitchen told OutKick OutDoors in an exclusive interview that he'd love to try his hand at tournament fishing someday.

In fact, he's already gotten a little taste of what that world looks like.

Earlier this year, Kitchen participated in the Bassmaster Classic Celebrity Pro-Am, where he teamed up with professional angler Tristan McCormick. The two didn't exactly dominate the leaderboard, but Kitchen came away with a few fish, a new friend and an even greater appreciation for the athletes who make their living chasing bass.

"It was amazing. Me and Tristan, we had a great time," Kitchen said. "I didn't know Tristan going into it. I'd just heard his name, but he's a great dude."

McCormick, who grew up near Loretta Lynn's Ranch in Tennessee, was already familiar with motocross thanks to the amateur racing held there. And Kitchen was pleased to discover that he could hold his own on the fishing side of things, too.

"He actually said I wasn't like, you know, sometimes he gets people that go to those events and they say they can fish a little bit and they really don't know what's going on," Kitchen recalled. "But I was proud to at least catch a few fish. We didn't do great, but it was a blast."

More importantly, the experience gave Kitchen a firsthand look at just how demanding professional bass fishing can be.

"It was an eye-opener, too," he admitted. "I've always said, when I'm done racing, I want to give that a shot. I really do. But I have so much more respect for those guys. If I ever wanted to do that, I'd have to really buckle down. You have to put so much time, so much time into it."

And it's not like Kitchen is a newcomer to fishing.

Growing up in Washington state, he developed a love for the outdoors thanks in part to his father. Around age 14 or 15, he discovered an old fly rod in his dad's shop, started practicing casts in the yard and quickly fell in love with fly fishing.

Watch Levi Kitchen's entire interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

These days, Kitchen lives in Florida, where bass fishing has become his primary obsession. But he still makes time to return home to Washington for an annual steelhead fishing trip with his father, friends and family — a tradition that has lasted roughly a decade.

"I still love it," Kitchen said. "When the racing's done down the road, you'll probably find me on a river fly fishing a lot, or on a bass boat. Just maybe not Florida in the summertime."

Fishing also provides a welcome contrast to the intensity of professional motocross.

CHASE ELLIOTT SAYS NASCAR'S GRUELING 10-MONTH SEASON CAN 'EAT YOU UP' WITHOUT AN ESCAPE

Kitchen said he and fellow rider Malcolm Stewart frequently talk about fishing in Florida, and he suspects the sport appeals to motocross athletes because it's such a departure from their day jobs.

"We get to kind of calm down and be a little more present than when you're just wide open on a dirt bike," he explained.

But there's still a competitive element, even when championship points aren't on the line.

"It's another way to be, I guess, kind of competitive with yourself," Kitchen said. "You obviously don't want to go out there and not catch a fish, but sometimes that happens."

And as much as Kitchen enjoys catching fish, he also appreciates the atmosphere surrounding competitive bass fishing.

At the Bassmaster Classic Pro-Am, he found himself surrounded by athletes and celebrities from across the sports world, including NFL Hall of Famer Randy Moss. Kitchen was particularly amused by Moss' impressive collection of fishing boats.

"First, Randy Moss, I'm like, who's this guy with two of the same specced-out, crazy sweet boats?" Kitchen recalled. "And they're like, 'Oh, that's Randy.'"

He also noticed something that set the fishing crowd apart from what he's accustomed to in motocross: Competitors were hanging out together at the hotel bar the night before the tournament.

"You do not see that in dirt bike racing," he said. "They put their game face on when it's time to fish, but just the whole event and weekend is pretty laid-back, which is kind of my style."

Of course, Kitchen isn't preparing to trade his Kawasaki for a bass boat just yet.

Levi Kitchen has big plans for 2027 season

The newly crowned 250 SMX World Champion, who helped end a seven-year championship drought for Pro Circuit Kawasaki, has made it clear that he wants a long career in motocross.

After recovering from a serious crash at Daytona in 2025, Kitchen said he's learned the importance of racing smarter and protecting his longevity in the sport.

"I want to race for a lot more years to come," he said.

And he's certainly not satisfied with one championship. His goals for 2027 include winning both a Supercross and a Pro Motocross title before eventually moving up from the 250 class.

So, no, Levi Kitchen isn't walking away from moto anytime soon.

But when the day finally comes to hang up the helmet, don't be surprised if The Chef trades his dirt bike for a bass boat.



After all, it never hurts to have a backup plan. Especially when that plan involves doing something you already love.

Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

World.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
World.content:
A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses.

The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants.

“The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.”

Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago.

The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation.

“These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.”

“The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization.

Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university.

Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit.

She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.”

“I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.”

She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.”

The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says.

The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances.

“I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News.

The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says.

After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her.

Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on.

She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night.

The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report.

Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report.

Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit.

A spokesperson for the city’s police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department’s involvement in the case.

Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs.

Doe’s lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also “ensure that this doesn’t happen again, and to help reform” policies within the university.

The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case.

“At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it’s not rare. It happens way more than people realize,” Doe said. “There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence.”

World.title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis
World.content:
Emmy-winning actor Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a condition she believed she had for more than five years, leaving her “back at square one” as she continues to experience debilitating medical issues.

Applegate, who revealed the misdiagnosis on the latest episode of her podcast, “MeSsy,” broke down in tears as she recalled a doctor recently telling her: “Congratulations. You don’t have MS.” She said she was “not happy at all” about the news.

“You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better,” Applegate told her co-host, “The Sopranos” actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler. “I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways.”

“I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me,” said Applegate, who spent months in the hospital this year and recently took a break from co-hosting “MeSsy” with Sigler, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis roughly 25 years ago.

00:20 Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS 00:00 00:00

Applegate disclosed that she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2021, calling her medical ordeal “a tough road.” She received a standing ovation at the 2024 Emmy Awards, appearing onstage with a cane. In an interview that year, she said she lived “kind of in hell.”

Multiple sclerosis is a progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information between the brain and the body. The immune system attacks the body’s nerve linings, producing unpredictable symptoms such as pain, fatigue or paralysis.

In the two-part podcast episode released Tuesday, Applegate said the lack of clarity about her medical condition was “unnerving” and “confusing.”

“It’s weird, because I feel like I let everybody down,” she told Sigler. “It’s this weird feeling, because I became this — you and I — the poster children for MS. ... I had a f---ing reason as to why my day sucked every day.”

She said her medical team will work to determine the underlying cause of her symptoms.

“Why did this happen? I had every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” Applegate said.

Applegate is best known for her television roles on Fox’s “Married ... with Children” and Netflix’s “Dead to Me.” She also appeared in both “Anchorman” movies as TV news anchor Veronica Corningstone. She has received eight Emmy nominations, winning in 2003 for her guest appearance on NBC’s “Friends.”

World.title: In-laws plead not guilty to murdering their son-in-law, a NYT executive, at local park
World.content:
The couple accused of killing their son-in-law, New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey, pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, a defense attorney said Monday.

Defense attorney Curtis Briggs argued that his client, Shili Chen, who is married to Shouyong Zhang, did not premeditate the shooting, NBC Bay Area reported. Instead, Briggs told NBC Bay Area that the couple, both 77, acted out of concern after seeing something disturbing while their son-in-law had a supervised visit with his children.

“My client was absolutely concerned for her own life and also concerned for her grandchildren,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area. Zhang is being represented by a public defender.

Alameda County prosecutors say Chen and Zhang watched and waited in a parking lot in Dublin, California, to attack McKinsey, who was embroiled in a bitter divorce and custody battle with their daughter.

Briggs said that McKinsey, 40, had previously threatened Chen’s life three times through a hit man. The couple purchased firearms in March to defend themselves, Briggs said, and were moved to act last month in the parking lot of a popular park.

“They are not cold-blooded killers. They didn’t premeditate anything,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area.

Briggs did not elaborate on what the elderly couple witnessed that drove them to kill their son-in-law.

If convicted, they could both face life in prison without the possibility of parole.

According to local police, 911 calls started coming in around 3 p.m. on Sept. 26 from terrified witnesses, many of whom were with their young children.

Several witnesses told police they saw a black Honda speeding out of the parking lot and later identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, police said in a statement. Officers chased down the car and arrested the couple, according to the police report.

Nearly a decade’s worth of court documents revealed a deeply troubled marriage between McKinsey and his wife, Candice Jang, who has not been charged in connection with his death.

Jonathan McKinsey. via Facebook

McKinsey’s death followed years of violent struggle between Jang and McKinsey, who started dating in 2008 and were married in 2011, according to Jang’s petition for a domestic abuse restraining order. They had three children.

McKinsey had recently filed for divorce and was scheduled to appear in court the same week he died, according to court records.

In separate petitions for restraining orders, McKinsey and Jang each argued that the other was physically and mentally abusive during their marriage. McKinsey and Jang both said they wanted full custody of their children, but McKinsey had an ongoing child abuse case that granted him only supervised visits.

The children were living with Jang and her parents when McKinsey was shot.

He had been previously charged with two misdemeanors — cruelty to a child by endangering health and corporal injury to a child. McKinsey was freed on $50,000 bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program, according to court records. Had he successfully completed the program, the charges would have been dismissed.

According to police reports, Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey with his firearm during interviews with investigators. The husband and wife were each carrying weapons at the time of their arrests.

“Chen and the passenger carried out this shooting in a crowded park parking lot with blatant disregard for public safety where several children were present,” the arresting officer said.

McKinsey allegedly threatened to kill Chen at least three times, NBC Bay Area reported. A bail hearing was set for Nov. 4, followed by a pretrial hearing on Nov. 23.

World.title: Justice Elena Kagan accuses Supreme Court’s conservative majority of undermining democracy
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Liberal Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday sharply criticized the Supreme Court’s conservative majority, saying it undermined democracy in a series of rulings, including several that have prompted a new wave of legislative map-drawing that has increasingly eliminated competitive districts.

Kagan, who has dissented in those cases, also took aim at the majority for striking down campaign finance restrictions and, as she put it, the “evisceration” of the landmark 1965 Voting Rights Act that was enacted to protect minority voters.

“Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions,” she said in remarks at Catholic University’s law school in Washington, D.C.

“I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should,” she added.

Kagan was referring in particular to the 2019 ruling that said federal courts could not intervene to limit extreme partisan gerrymandering. She also mentioned a series of rulings that have gutted the Voting Rights Act, including one this year that led to Republican states eliminating majority Black districts. The court has also consistently struck down campaign finance restrictions, the most recent in June.

Heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, several states have redrawn their congressional maps to maximize the number of seats the majority party can win in that state. Texas kicked things off, at President Donald Trump’s urging, followed by other states, including California.

The 2019 redistricting ruling has been particularly harmful, Kagan said. As a result, “both parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders.”

The lopsided maps deny people “their rights to voting equality” and have the effect of “driving people away from the center, towards the wings, toward the extremes” because candidates only have to worry about winning the primary, she added.

The failure of the court to take action on the issue is “making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” Kagan said.

When states draw legislative districts that almost wipe out the ability of many voters to elect their chosen candidate, it is “very destructive of our democracy,” she added.

As for the increasingly unlimited amounts of money in politics, Kagan said that many voters find it disconcerting.

“I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she said.

During the question-and-answer session with professor Joel Alicea, Kagan was also critical of the Supreme Court’s ruling this year that gave Trump greater control over hitherto independent federal agencies that were set up by Congress to be free from political interference.

She questioned the wisdom of giving the president too much power, saying there is a “danger of one president being able to ride roughshod over all the other institutions of government and over the people.”

But Kagan also defended the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, over claims from the left that it is a rubber stamp for Trump. She cited several rulings in which the president lost, including his attempt to impose sweeping tariffs.

The court is “deeply conservative,” she said, but in certain cases “definitely pushed back on the president.”

World.title: Netflix doesn’t want investors to worry, despite recent shake-ups, layoffs
World.content:
Following a dramatic C-suite reshuffle and its largest round of layoffs in years, Netflix’s top executives reassured investors Tuesday that they have a plan to keep audiences hooked.

The streaming giant announced that its third-quarter revenue grew 12% year over year, to $12.9 billion, while net income rose 48%, to nearly $3.7 billion.

“Our engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years,” co-CEO Greg Peters said on the streamer’s third-quarter earnings call, referring to the company’s performance in the U.S. “But we know that we can do better.”

Revenue increased despite upheaval at Netflix, which last week laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and ousted Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and top film executives Dan Lin and Doug Belgrad.

“We believe we have a responsibility to make hard trade-offs in service of our members, our partners, our employees, our investors and ultimately our long-term growth,” Peters said of the layoffs. “That was the simple thinking behind it and what motivated these recent changes.”

Ted Sarandos, Peter Rice, Bela Bajaria and Dan Lin. Getty; WireImage

Over the last year, Netflix’s stock has dropped significantly, from $124.14 in October 2025 to $68.69 on Tuesday, because of slowing revenue growth.

Netflix remains the biggest subscription streaming video service in the world, with more than 325 million global subscribers. But it has struggled to boost user engagement amid increasing competition from YouTube, despite expanding its push into live sports, video podcasts and gaming.

Co-chief Ted Sarandos tapped former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice to step into Bajaria’s role, telling investors and journalists that he “understands talent relations.”

“In a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life,” Sarandos said. “Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.”

Other major Hollywood studios are also trying to reduce costs and streamline operations.

The Walt Disney Co. has cut hundreds of jobs this year under new CEO Josh D’Amaro, and David Ellison’s Skydance is expected to shrink its workforce across Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. (In February, Netflix officially pulled out of a deal to buy WBD, ceding in a bidding war to Paramount.)

Amid industry consolidation, Netflix reported slower revenue growth in the U.S. and Canada, where sales rose 11% in the third quarter, compared with 17% a year earlier.

Still, in its letter to shareholders, it stressed that its strength lies in its “differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events.” It singled out the performances of recent programming, including “The Last House,” “Death of the Pastor’s Wife” and an NFL game in Australia.

It also touted its upcoming slate of shows and movies, such as “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” a David Fincher-directed, Quentin Tarantino-written sequel to “Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood”; “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” starring Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen; new seasons of its popular shows “The Diplomat” and “Nobody Wants This”; three NFL games on Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day; and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight.

On the earnings call, Sarandos also discussed Netflix’s recent theatrical releases, including its first disclosure of box-office results for the Spanish-language Oscar contender “La bola negra,” and upcoming IMAX releases such as Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.”

“Reminder, we are a streaming-first business. That is our core,” he said. “We start off by looking at the projects we have, asking ourselves how do we best serve movie lovers, many of whom are our members who want to see that movie in a theater, and how do we do it without actually harming the view value to Netflix.”

World.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss merger idea
World.content:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk said Tuesday that the boards of SpaceX and Tesla had separately formed special committees to discuss the idea of a merger, taking a small step toward the possible consolidation of his two biggest companies.

Musk, who is the CEO of both companies, said that the special committees had not reached an agreement and that there was no guarantee they would. He said a merger would require support from both sets of shareholders.

“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said.

Musk spoke about the potential tie-up during a call with Wall Street analysts about SpaceX’s quarterly results, which surpassed estimates; the company’s revenue more than doubled in part from renting out computing capacity to other artificial intelligence firms.

There has been intense speculation in the stock market over whether a combination might happen, and the two companies already overlap in some areas, including semiconductor manufacturing. In January, Tesla announced that it was investing about $2 billion to acquire shares in an AI startup that’s a subsidiary of SpaceX.

Musk said that, because he’s a conflicted party under securities regulations, he is not a member of either special committee or involved in the talks. He said the committees consist of the two boards’ independent directors but did not specify the memberships.

“It’s an odd Kabuki dance, where groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” he said during the earnings calls. He also said that even answering a question about the idea from an analyst felt like “dancing through a minefield.”

Musk, though, endorsed the idea.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies, as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” he said. He mentioned several areas of current or potential future cooperation, including AI software development, chip design and robotics.

Musk has already consolidated some of his other holdings. Last year, he merged his social media company, X, with his AI startup, called at the time xAI. Then, in February, SpaceX acquired xAI, which Musk has since renamed SpaceXSI.

World.title: Cornell responds to Jane Doe letter saying she felt disbelieved
World.content:
The former Cornell student known as Jane Doe has sent a letter to the school saying she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by the university's president, Michael Kotlikoff, after she accused multiple men of sexually assaulting her at a fraternity house in 2024.

In a statement Tuesday, Cornell disputed her account of Kotlikoff's comments.

The letter, obtained by CBS News, was sent earlier this month to Cornell's Faculty Senate as it considers a no-confidence vote in Kotlikoff's administration. In the letter, Jane Doe describes what she calls "a second-hand account" of a conversation between Kotlikoff and the then-president of Cornell's Tri Delta sorority chapter.

"After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff's initial response was along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'" wrote Jane Doe in the letter. "She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story."

Jane Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on Nov. 8, 2024, about three weeks after she said it took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house.

The university said in its statement Tuesday that her description of Kotlikoff's comment in the letter is "incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account."

"The question 'why did it take so long for the assault to be reported' was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024," Cornell said. "He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting."

In her one-page letter, Jane Doe wrote that hearing of the comment "diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."

She added, "I am sharing this account now because, to my knowledge, only a few individuals are aware of the conversation; I do not know if you or other members of the Faculty Senate are among them."

In a statement provided to CBS News on Tuesday regarding the letter, Jane Doe's attorney said, "Jane Doe, through counsel, provided a statement to the Dean of Faculty and Speaker of the Faculty Senate regarding her understanding of comments made by President Kotlikoff in the presence of one of her sorority sisters and one or more faculty members. The letter was sent for informational purposes only. Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it. Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate."

How Cornell and its leadership handled Jane Doe's original report of the alleged assaults is one of the issues raised in the civil lawsuit she filed last month against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and seven of its then-members, and others including her sorority at the time, Delta Delta Delta.

CBS News has reached out to the seven former fraternity members. All have denied wrongdoing. None of them has been charged with a crime.

In a court filing Tuesday, a former president of the Chi Phi fraternity was dropped from her lawsuit. His attorney, Eric Bernstein, told CBS News in a statement that his client wasn't serving as president of the fraternity at the time of the alleged assault.

"We're not validating or commenting on the charges or the allegations themselves but they had the wrong guy here. We're happy with the outcome," Bernstein said in the statement.

World.title: Nigeria confirms an Ebola case in Abuja as a woman arriving from Uganda tests positive
World.content:
Nigeria confirms an Ebola case in Abuja as a woman arriving from Uganda tests positive

toggle caption i Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

LAGOS, Nigeria — Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the Health Ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola.

Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. "We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the latest outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections.

Sponsor Message

Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that "we are facing an extremely serious threat," with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

"This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa," he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country's preparedness for a potential outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers," the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola task force in June following the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,000 people and killed more than 4,300 people.

Sponsor Message

The latest outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa's regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said. Nigeria was one of the countries affected, recording 20 cases before it was declared over in the country after three months.

World.title: Vanessa Kerry is the new WHO envoy for health resilience. What's on her to-do list?
World.content:
Vanessa Kerry is the new WHO envoy for health resilience. What's on her to-do list?

toggle caption i Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images

Resilience is one of those buzzy buzzwords. But what does it mean, exactly? Bouncing back from tragedy? Conquering obstacles? Having the inner strength to follow a dream when the odds are against you?

For Dr. Vanessa Kerry, the definition is pretty straightforward. It boils down to being prepared. In the world of global health, she says, that means "strong systems, primary care and the ability to respond."

Those are the ideas that will guide her in her new job as special envoy for health resilience at the World Health Organization.

Sponsor Message

It's the latest addition to an impressive resume. Kerry was WHO's first special envoy for climate change and health, is director of global and climate health policy in the Department of Environmental Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and is the founder and CEO of Seed Global Health. That nonprofit group has been building resilience in lower-resource countries for over a decade, dispatching coaches and mentors to educate and train local healthcare students and practitioners as well as building financial and material resources.

Kerry's activism reflects seminal moments from her younger years. In grade school, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. At age 14, she traveled to Vietnam with her father, former Senator and Secretary of State John Kerry, and was deeply struck by the poverty she saw.

A high-risk delivery

Then came the crisis in Rwanda.

Between her third and fourth years in medical school, she spent time in a hospital in Rwanda. One day she was asked to "be a helping hand" with a woman's labor and delivery, working with a nurse.

Kerry said, "I'm a student." So that was the team — this medical student from the U.S. and a Rwandan nurse.

Sponsor Message

"The mother was pushing, but the baby was not advancing," Kerry remembers. "The shoulder had gotten stuck, and so we needed to do the maneuvers to help to deliver." She tried to remember everything she could from time spent in a "labor rotation a while back." There was no imaging, no specific training either she or the nurse had had for this type of situation.

"We were lucky," she says, "Because what we remembered worked." Mother and child survived.

Kerry, now 49, recalls: "I remember walking out of that room thinking, that was extremely distressing — more than that, extremely shocking and terrifying.

She could only conclude "this whole system doesn't work."

That harrowing delivery was the germ for Seed Global Health. She knew that many of her colleagues wanted to work to improve global health. But many of the opportunities involved flying in to perform certain procedures, then returning home.

"They made a contribution in that moment, but what then?"

When she returned to Boston from Rwanda to finish her residency at Massachusetts General, she began hatching the idea of working with the Peace Corps to send doctors and nurses to sub-Saharan Africa as medical educators to train health care workers who could then train others — building a country's internal health care system. Seed's collaboration with the Peace Corps lasted from 2012-2018, focusing on the development of country-led efforts at HIV/AIDS epidemic control.

Today, Seed is active in several sub-Saharan African countries for its training efforts. In Uganda, for example, Kerry says that her group has partnered with the Ministry of Health to build up emergency medicine by training 30 emergency medicine physicians. When an Ebola outbreak occurred there earlier this year, she says that these emergency physicians and other specialists were able to train over 3,000 health workers around the country in Ebola case management and infection prevention and control.

Sponsor Message

Seed, she says, has taught her that building resilience "is not a daunting task. If you train health workers, they can monitor and provide healthcare, they can provide surveillance, they can provide prevention."

Building responsive healthcare systems is what her new job is all about, she says. "We've been funding disease by disease and crisis by crisis. We can be thinking about this differently."

Her goal is not merely to jump in when a new outbreak occurs. "If a nation does not have a health system infrastructure in place, they will probably not be prepared to respond to the emergency. Resilience means building a system that will already be in place."

And it also means listening to local voices. "Countries know what their priorities are to care for their population," she says. As the resilience envoy, she wants to make sure there is ample funding so "we more effectively address the biggest burdens of disease."

Diane Cole writes for many publications, including The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post. She is the author of the memoir After Great Pain: A New Life Emerges. Her website is DianeJoyceCole.com

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns
World.content:
DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

toggle caption i Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images

🎧 The DOJ wants California to segregate ballots of those on its list and to delay counting them until investigations are complete. Election law experts doubt the DOJ will succeed, given its past attempts to change state voting processes, Miles Parks tells Up First. He adds that it would be surprising to see a shift just two weeks before the election with ballots already distributed. Research shows that in many cases, when legal permanent residents register to vote, it is due to a misunderstanding of the rules. Experts tell Parks they are concerned that federal law enforcement might use accusations to confiscate ballots during counting, but many local voting officials are preparing by keeping county attorneys on speed dial.

Sponsor Message

Democrats and Republicans are deciding which races to prioritize with Election Day just two weeks away. President Trump is campaigning in key perennial purple states like Georgia, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Florida this week.



🎧 Trump's rally in Kansas and trip to North Carolina aren't where the leader of the Republican Party's attention should be, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and many Republican groups have ceased ad spending in North Carolina, viewing the Senate race as a lost cause. Republicans are prioritizing efforts to save their Senate majority over saving the House majority, while Democrats are capitalizing on opportunities in conservative areas, Fowler says. In Georgia, with a million voters already casting ballots, Fowler says he sees an increase in Black voter turnout in the state and across the South.

Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. They also identified loopholes that allowed users under 18 to bypass age restrictions and block parental oversight of their app activity. The records show that TikTok avoided conducting age surveys, fearing it would have to share results with the Federal Trade Commission.

Life advice

Andee Tagle/NPR

Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.

🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects. Some good medications to have include ibuprofen or naproxen, which can relieve headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation and Acetaminophen, which can lower body temperature.

🤒 Honey acts as an anti-inflammatory and soothes the throat, making it useful for young children who can't take cough medicine. But don't give it to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.

🤒 A thermometer is a must-have for checking your temperature. For children 3 and under, a rectal option is preferred.

🤒 A saline spray or rinse for your nose can help keep the mucous membranes moist and help relieve symptoms by loosening thick mucus during a cold.

For more advice on how to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

toggle caption i Lanna Apisukh for NPR

Pleasant Rowland launched Pleasant Company in 1986 with three dolls — Samantha, Molly and Kirsten — creating an empire known as American Girl. To celebrate its 40th anniversary, author Fiona Davis was asked to write a historical fiction book for adults titled Samantha: The Next Chapter, featuring Samantha Parkington, who has turned 25. The story picks up after Samantha's last book, in which she attended a suffragist rally with her aunt Cornelia. The book is set 15 years later, in 1920, just after the ratification of the 19th Amendment. Samantha learns that her grandmother's inheritance has been stolen, forcing her to transition from socialite to shopgirl overnight. NPR's Samantha Balaban visited the American Girl store in New York with her own Samantha doll to explore the character's evolution over the years, drawing on insights from its staff and Davis. Check out photos from the visit and read more about the history of American Girl dolls.

Sponsor Message

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its menopause treatment guidelines for the first time since 2014. The group now recommends using hormone replacement therapy along with some other treatments to alleviate symptoms. A wedding day can be one of the costliest days in a couple's life. Some are opting to save money by choosing grocery-store cakes over specialty bakers' cakes. Vegemite is such an iconic breakfast spread in Australia that a convicted killer is suing the state of Victoria for the right to eat it in prison. The state has banned Vegemite because it could potentially be used to brew alcohol and throw off dogs.
