See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

PSV survived a second-half onslaught in Porto to secure their first win of the Champions League group stages.

Guus Til scored the only goal when he tapped in from close range after Esmir Bajraktarevic’s shot had come back off the post and was steered across goal by Sven Mijnans.

The Eindhoven club were worth their narrow lead against Francesco Farioli’s side after dominating possession in the first half, but rarely troubled Diogo Costa in the Porto goal.

Til went close with a header early in the second half before putting PSV ahead in the 57th minute.

But the visitors had to defend heroically as Porto poured forward in search of an equaliser, aided by an increasingly fragile Matej Kovar.

The goalkeeper put his defenders in jeopardy with a weak clearance in the 72nd minute, but redeemed himself by saving Victor Froholdt’s shot with his chest before Lutsarel Geertruida blocked the follow-up from Pepê.

A minute later Kovar was left stranded after he rushed out of his penalty area, but Sergiño Dest managed to hack the ball away before Alberto Costa could poke it into the open goal.

At the other end, substitute Denis Man came close to scoring a second for PSV with his first touch when his curling shot beat Costa but failed to sneak inside the post.

The 1-0 win lifts PSV to a provisional 16th place in the Champions League table at the halfway stage of round three, while Porto are still looking for their first point.

Their next match is at home to Belgian side Club Brugge, who will make the short trip to Eindhoven on November 4.

World.title: Churches offer refugees temporary shelter to free up asylum beds
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Council of Churches in the Netherlands is temporarily stepping in to help shelter refugees amid the ongoing asylum crisis.

An overflow of asylum seekers continues to leave many sleeping outside, while those who have already been given residence permits stay in asylum centres awaiting housing.

This caused trouble throughout the summer months, and, with winter approaching, the shortage of beds poses a new danger to the homeless.

The initiative, called Actie Onderdak, was launched by the Council’s 19 member churches and organisations, including protestant, catholic and reformed denominations.

The Council has written to all local councils and parishes asking them to help shelter families currently housed in asylum centres so more beds can be freed up.

The Council requested churches offer space in empty rectories or annexes where possible. The intention is to give families three months in a new location where they can “find peace and get to know their surroundings”.

The plan was developed in coordination with the refugee settlement agency COA, and also endorsed by asylum minister Bart van den Brink.

According to the Council, COA will ensure refugees can move on to a new location after their three-month church stay ends.

World.title: Dutch winter gas storage levels reach minimum limit of 64%
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands has met its target for filling its gas reserves before the onset of winter, but only after reducing its limit to the European Union minimum of 64%.

The Dutch government set a target of 80% capacity by November 1 in 2022, after the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine sent wholesale prices soaring.

Last year it only managed to reach 73.6%, while a surge in prices triggered by the United States’ military action against Iran prompted the state energy company EBN, which is responsible for buying winter supplies, to reduce its orders.

In August the reserves were 45% full, prompting EBN to ask the government to lower its target to 64%, the minimum level agreed between EU member states.

Since then the reserves have been filled to 65.5% and the company hopes to be able to keep topping up supplies for another two weeks.

Last year the level peaked on November 1 and began falling on November 7. At the lowest point, on April 2, the reserves were just 4.5% full.

World.title: Amsterdam hopes 20km/h cycle lane limit will change behaviour
World.content:
Amsterdam city council has introduced an experimental speed limit of 20km/h for cyclists to see if riders can be persuaded to slow down.

Tourists, commuters and shoppers have all complained in recent years of feeling unsafe on the capital’s congested bike paths, but the only speed restriction is a 30 km/h limit for motor vehicles.

A temporary speed limit has been set on a section of Amstelveenseweg, one of the main routes into the city from the south, for four weeks to gauge its effect on cyclists’ behaviour.

But instead of enforcing the limit through fines and cautions, the city council has put up boards showing people how many of their fellow bike users are staying below 20 km/h, in the hope they will nudge people into being more considerate.

Traffic alderman Elise Moeskops told AT5 the idea of the experiment is to see if the signs will encourage a shift in cycling culture.

“If you enforce everything in the city you end up with a very harsh police state, and we don’t have the staff for that,” she said.

Infrastructure problems

“Are people prepared to cycle more slowly if we remind them that that’s an option? The question is what the social norm is on the cycle lane, because we don’t really know.”

But Kees Bakker, spokesman for the cyclists’ union Fietsersbond, was sceptical of the idea. He said better infrastructure was the solution to crowded bike lanes.

“The cycle lane on that road is very narrow and poorly laid out,” he told Dutch News. “There’s a busy pavement alongside it, so pedestrians spill over to the cycle path.

“It doesn’t make much difference if the speed limit is 20 km/h or 50 km/h, because the path is too narrow and there’s no room to overtake.”

Bakker said speed limits were likely to be less effective in bike lanes because not all cyclists travel at the same speed and they need space to overtake.

“Cars mostly drive in file at 30 km/h, but the range of speeds is much wider for cyclists,” he said. “Some of them ride at 15 km/h, others do 25 or even 30. There needs to be room to accommodate everyone, including people who want to coast along side by side at 15 km/h.”

World.title: Dutch destinations: Go back in time in eastern Drenthe
World.content:
Eastern Drenthe is perhaps the most underrated part of the Netherlands. Its rolling scenery, its history and its villages – low thatched farmhouses, tiny brick churches and woodlands – make it a perfect place to spend a few sunny autumn days.

Assen is the provincial capital. It has the region’s main museum and boasts the second-biggest department store in the Netherlands. It is also home to the Dutch TT circuit, offering a wide variety of motorcycle races from April to October. But the real charm of the region is in the countryside.

A weekend is not enough to take in everything, so here is a taster of what eastern Drenthe has to offer.

What to do

Visit the hunebedden

Eastern Drenthe is all about hunebedden, the Neolithic burial chambers built by the Funnel Beaker people over 5,000 years ago. Drenthe is home to 52 of the 54 known hunebedden in the Netherlands, and many are concentrated around Borger, where the national hunebed centre is based.

The biggest hunebed, with the not-so-romantic name D27, is located in the woods next to the visitors’ centre. The grounds are also home to a bizarre collection of zwerfstenen, or boulders, which were brought down to the province from Scandinavia by glaciers. Many of the stones have labels showing exactly where in Sweden or Norway they came from.

In addition, the centre has a café and a sort of Neolithic playground – the Prehistoric Park – where children can check out recreations of ancient homes. During peak season volunteers in costume are on hand to explain about the lives of people who lived in the region and demonstrate ancient crafts. No dogs.

Walk along the Hondsrug

The Hondsrug (literally “dog’s back”) is listed as a Unesco Global Geopark because of its unique history, deriving from the last two ice ages. This 70-kilometre-long glacial ridge made of sand and clay is the only one of its kind in Europe. There are dozens of walking and cycle trails to explore, as well as small museums, such as the De Nabershof working farm near Emmen. You can find out more about the region’s geology at the visitors centre, next to the hunebed centre in Borger.

Stroll around Orvelte

About 20 minutes south of Assen is Orvelte, a Drenthe village untouched by time, which has become a sort of open-air museum. It’s car-free – you park on the outskirts – but there is a horse-drawn “bus” if you have little ones with you who don’t want to walk.

Stroll past the thatched farmhouses, stop off for what we were told is the best apple pie in Drenthe, and check out the little museums – which seem to be based largely on the locals’ hobbies, such as collecting model cars and rare sheep.

There is a good sprinkling of shops, some of which sell tourist tat, but some are upmarket outlets selling wonderful antique pottery and glass, as well as clothes and bric-a-brac. Plenty of options for lunch and morning coffee. If you are into Christmas themes, Orvelte will transform into a Christmas village from December 18 to 20.

Catch up on history at the Drents Museum in Assen

The Drents Museum in the provincial capital Assen hit the headlines in 2025 when criminals broke in overnight and stole a number of priceless gold relics, most of which have since been recovered. There is no Romanian gold on show any longer – the current special exhibition is about Angkor in Cambodia – but the museum is well worth a visit to find out more about the history of the region.

It is heavy on the infotainment, so there’s plenty to keep the kids occupied, but the museum nevertheless has something for everyone. Located in several buildings linked by tunnels and overground walkways, the museum has Neolithic finds, art (a couple of Van Goghs), recreated stijlkamers (period rooms), temporary exhibitions and a fine café for lunch.

Go on a tree walk

The Boomkroonpad – treetop path – takes you from the roots of an oak tree up into the treetops, where you can walk along a very solid metal structure and admire the forest from above. The path is also the starting point for five forest floor walks, ranging from three to 16.5 kilometres, and there are plenty of organised activities for families – deer and mushroom spotting, for example – all year round.

Where to eat

All the attractions we visited had cafés for lunch, mainly selling standard-fare sandwiches and broodjes kroket. Assen has a good selection of cafés and restaurants for dinner. We ate at our hotel, Rikus, which uses local produce and offers three-, four- and five-course menus. Be warned: the portions are big as well as being delicious.

Where to stay

Rikus, a small hotel in the village of Eext, about 20 minutes from Assen and Borger, has an eclectic interior and big bedrooms with views over the countryside. As a couple we paid €331 for bed, breakfast, a three-course dinner and drinks.

There is a hotel and a quaint-looking B&B in Orvelte, and Assen is home to Hotel de Jonge, with a large café terrace in the heart of the old city. Drenthe is popular with Dutch holidaymakers, so, as you would expect, there are plenty of campsites and holiday parks to choose from as well.

Anything else

Unless you are big on cycling or long walks, you really need a car to get around the region. The attractions can get very busy at weekends in the summer months, which may well dent their charm. The Dutch TT Grand Prix takes place on the last Sunday in June.

World.title: Primary school teachers reject four-day week amid staff shortage
World.content:
School leaders in the Netherlands are opting against the idea of a four-day week for primary schools amid a critical shortage of teachers.

A survey conducted by Nu.nl and the Academy & Association of School Leaders (AVS) found that of 308 heads of schools, only three (less than 1%) said they had chosen to reduce required attendance days for pupils as a solution to the crisis.

Primary schools are short of roughly 5,800 teachers nationwide, about 6.3% of all teachers, according to research institute Centerdata.

Despite an increase in teacher numbers since 2024, when the shortage stood at 8.1%, low salaries and long hours remain a problem for enticing people to join the profession. The previous generation of teachers is also retiring, worsening the gap.

Leanne der Steeg, a policy advisor at AVS, told Nu.nl that a four-day school week does not necessarily help the teachers and can harm education.

“A four-day school week also brings ‘hassle’ with it,” she said. “It is not just a matter of sending a class home. Thought must be given to the missed teaching time. Will it be made up at another time, will homework be assigned, and what about children of working parents? And if you free up a teacher for a day by opting for a four-day school week, it requires preparation before they can stand in front of another class.”

World.title: Rail fares to go up by 4.7% next year to help pay for new trains
World.content:
Dutch national train operator NS is set to raise fares by almost 5% on average in 2027, exceeding the rate of inflation for the third year in a row.

The increases are needed “to purchase new, comfortable trains, pay for rising costs and keep investing in good services,” Daan Schut, the management board member responsible for fares, said in a press statement on Tuesday.

NS is offsetting the increase by offering bigger discounts on off-peak fares for passengers who buy in advance. The maximum reduction on so-called PrijsTijd deals will go up from 60% to 80% next year.

The company said it also wanted to discuss reviving the discounted summer subscription rate, which allowed passengers to travel off-peak and at weekends for €49 a month in July and August, rather than the regular fee of €127.50.

The Railrunner fare for children, which allows under-12s to travel across the country all day for a flat rate, is being frozen at €2.50, and the KidsVrij subscription for families, which gives free travel up to the age of 11, will stay unchanged.

The minimum fare for short journeys is going up to €3.10, while the supplement for the high-speed line between Schiphol and Rotterdam is rising by 20 cents to €3.40.

Rail passengers’ organisation Rover criticised the above-inflation rises, pointing to the success of the summer discount as proof that people will travel by train if it is an affordable option.

“Now that NS is finally seeing its passenger numbers growing, passengers are being punished with big ticket increases. By constantly using the maximum room that NS has to raise ticket prices, it is holding back further growth,” a Rover spokesperson said.

Fares have gone up by around 6.5% for each of the last two years, partly to correct the 1.5% rise in 2023, when inflation was 10%. In 2024 prices were frozen thanks to a government cash injection of €120 million.

NS made a profit for the first time in years in 2025, recording a net gain of €380 million, though most of this came from a recalculation of its access charges during the coronavirus pandemic, when fewer trains ran. The charges are the costs the company pays to use the track network.

World.title: Millions to get compensation from takeaway apps over hidden fees
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Food delivery apps Thuisbezorgd and Uber Eats have been forced to stop hiding fees and advertising fake discounts after a complaint by consumer watchdog Consumentenbond.

Millions of customers will also receive a payout voucher in compensation ranging between €5 to €30, the watchdog said.

The companies were putting “small order fees” and other surcharges only at the end of orders, and were advertising misleading discounts for some takeaways.

The Consumentenbond accused Thuisbezorgd in July of hiding charges that often added €2 to €4 to an order. Fake discounts were also show; in one example, Indian snacks priced at €3.75 were later shown as “reduced” from €7.50 to €6.

Both companies told news agency ANP the changes followed “constructive” talks with the Consumentenbond. Uber Eats had already adjusted its charges in June.

World.title: Polish leaders condemn Hegseth’s “scandalous” remarks downplaying role of US allies in Afghanistan
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Leading figures from Poland’s ruling coalition have hit back at US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth over his recent remarks downplaying the contribution of America’s allies during the war in Afghanistan. The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who had declared dead the last of the 44 Polish soldiers who died in Afghanistan. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026 The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over fifty countries. “Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'” The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.” Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026 On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition. At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”. He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks. It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty. To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026 Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name. “Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.” “I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added. Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.” Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.” Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan. Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation. Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”. That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”. The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies "This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026 The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control. The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump. However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given America’s role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory. Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”. World.title: Poland detains Polish-Ukrainian military reservist on suspicion of espionage
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A member of Poland’s military reserve force has been detained for alleged espionage. On Monday afternoon, following media reports of the arrest, a spokesman for the military police confirmed that they had detained a 31-year-old man of Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, who holds the rank of senior private reserve. The suspect, who had at the time been undertaking a course at the Military Medical Academy (WAM) in Łódź, is being held on suspicion of declaring readiness to act for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service against Poland. That crime is punishable by up to eight years in prison. W dniu 16 października 2026 r. żołnierze z Oddziału Żandarmerii Wojskowej w Łodzi, zgodnie z postanowieniem Prokuratora Działu do Spraw Wojskowych Prokuratury Rejonowej Łódź-Polesie w Łodzi, dokonali zatrzymania mężczyzny w wieku 31 lat, obywatelstwa polskiego i ukraińskiego, w… pic.twitter.com/MLpqzfT4iO — Żandarmeria Wojskowa (@Zandarmeria) October 19, 2026 The Polish authorities have not revealed which foreign intelligence service the suspect – who has been placed in detention for three months – is believed to be associated with. Speaking later to reporters, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said that the man had “clearly shown himself to be someone who is conducting reconnaissance of certain types of military installations belonging to the Polish armed forces”. He also revealed that the suspect had recently obtained Polish citizenship. While the authorities have not released further information, Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, reported earlier on Monday that the suspect, whom it named as Vasiliy, had been found in possession of several different phones, documents, and a large amount of money and gold. Poland has recently seen a number of high-profile cases of individuals charged – and in some cases convicted – of spying on behalf of Russia and Belarus. Poland’s security services recently revealed that the number of espionage cases they launched last year was more than double the figure for 2024. Over those two years combined, there were more investigations than in the previous three decades. This month, a former Polish soldier was sentenced to five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. He was tasked with reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa while he travelled through Poland https://t.co/WCmhyHG1Kp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 In July, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force (WOT) with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In December last year, a Russian national was charged with running an espionage and sabotage network in Poland on behalf of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). The agents whom he oversaw were mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians, as have been many others convicted of conducting Russian hybrid activities in Poland. Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała. “Eleven Belarusian citizens and four Russians entered the country on tourist visas, which was inconsistent with the declared purpose of their stay in Poland,” said border guard spokesman Szymon Mościcki. After being detained, they received orders to leave the country within eight days, which is “the shortest possible deadline”, he added, quoted by broadcaster TVP. Piętnastu obywateli Rosji i Białorusi zostało zatrzymanych przez Straż Graniczną. Przyjechali do Polski na wizach turystycznych, choć prawdopodobnie zamierzali wziąć udział w mistrzostwach świata w karate. Otrzymali decyzje nakazujące opuszczenie kraju.https://t.co/czcjQKZ2kw — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 19, 2026 The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała. In early October, Russia’s TASS news agency had reported that some of the country’s junior karatekas, as competitors are known, had planned to compete in the tournament. The World Karate Federation (WKF) allows Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under a neutral banner. However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes. On 15 October, the day after the championships in Bielsko-Biała had started, TASS reported that none of the Russian athletes had been allowed to register by the Polish organisers. Paweł Połtorzecki, president of the Polish Karate Union (PUK), confirmed that, despite PUK warning them not to come, Russian and Belarusian athletes had sought to take part, prompting the organisers to ask the border guard to conduct an inspection. “The first sign was the appearance of a Russian at the refereeing course,” he revealed, quoted by TVP. “That’s when the first detention occurred.” Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily, reports that the Russian karatekas had obtained tourist visas from other countries in the European Schengen area, of which Poland is part. Poland itself does not issue tourist visas to Russians. Poland has been removed as the host of two European junior weightlifting championships after refusing to allow Russian athletes to take part The European Weightlifting Federation says it "does not accept discrimination based on geopolitical circumstances" https://t.co/j7PfiTHZ1M — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing military and humanitarian support while also pressing for tougher international sanctions against Moscow. Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter. In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”. World.title: Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams. Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty. Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026 The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation. The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures. Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies. “The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.” The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation. Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland. World.title: Lithuania says Ukrainian drone that struck car entered its airspace from Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon. Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border. Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU. This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace. What appears to be a drone exploded… — Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026 On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object. President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”. Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace. “I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT. However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”. Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country. In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”. Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”. We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia. We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have… — Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026 Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian. “We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.” The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was. Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming. On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself. It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place. Poland has condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a delegation of European diplomats – including Polish ones – that was visiting the West Bank. It called for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”, saying that the incident is “further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”. The attack has likewise been condemned by France and Belgium, whose nationals were also in the delegation, and the European Union, as well as by the Israeli foreign minister. Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, prompting European condemnation. The violence comes amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the olive harvest. pic.twitter.com/wsP6edL62y — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 18, 2026 On Saturday, the delegation – which included members from France, Belgium and Poland as well as representatives of the Catholic church – visited the mostly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They had come to assess the situation following regular recent attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to harvest olives on their own land. During the visit, the delegation came under attack, with parts of the incident caught on camera. France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, reported that Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, had been “violently assaulted” during the incident. He demanded that Israel arrest the perpetrators and “urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence”. Late on Saturday afternoon, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, issued a statement confirming that the attack had taken place and that the delegation had included an unspecified number of Polish diplomats, who he said had not been harmed. “We express our deep outrage and strongly condemn this incident,” added Wewiór. “Poland consistently opposes violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks on representatives of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.” The spokesman said that Poland now “expects urgent and detailed explanations from the Israeli authorities” and for the perpetrators of the attack to be identified and held accountable. “We also expect effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.” ❗Potwierdzamy, że na Zachodnim Brzegu Jordanu doszło do ataku na konwój, w którym znajdowali się przedstawiciele korpusu dyplomatycznego, w tym polscy dyplomaci. The incident “is further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”, they added, calling for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”. The attack was also “strongly condemned” on Sunday by the European Union’s diplomatic service, which said that it “expects full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians”. The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters. Police forces and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are entering the area accompanied by… — Israel Defense Forces (@IDF) October 17, 2026 The incident involving the diplomatic group came a day after around 80 Israeli settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives, with Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine among those injured. Levine told the Committee to Protect Journalists, an American non-profit organisation, that she had been pushed to the ground by a group of masked settlers, who “were kicking me for I think at least 10 minutes”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said he was “disturbed” by the incident and confirmed that “we’ve asked the Israelis to crack down on that”. .@SecRubio on reporter Heidi Levine being attacked in the West Bank: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing….the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank." pic.twitter.com/Xg10vteeXK — CSPAN (@cspan) October 18, 2026 In August this year, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the IDF had discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. In May, Poland issued a five-year entry ban on Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for his treatment of detained activists, including Polish citizens, from a flotilla seeking to reach Gaza. Last year, Israel criticised Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, after he suggested that Israeli politicians are causing the starvation of mothers and children in Gaza. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges. Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year. #Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨 📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC. 🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej. 🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol — Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026 Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts. Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue. Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee. From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty. Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee. In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight. While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”. The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum. “In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.” Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). World.title: Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government. The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026 Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years. However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison. “Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily. That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus. Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers. Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross. However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support. Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025 In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”. The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability. “This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily. Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022. A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025 They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted. On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”. World.title: How Prague Helped Write the Chemistry of Peptides
World.content:
Prague has a quiet but real place in the history of peptide chemistry.

From the 1950s, chemists at what is now the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry (IOCB) worked out how to build and redesign pituitary peptides, the city hosted the first European Peptide Symposium in 1958, and one of the institute’s analogues was licensed abroad and produced industrially. The same research base now underpins Prague’s new biotech cluster.

A field that started with nine amino acids

In 1953 Vincent du Vigneaud’s group in New York published a short paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society reporting that they had made oxytocin in the laboratory. Oxytocin is a peptide, a chain of just nine amino acids, but nobody had synthesised a peptide hormone before, and two years later the work brought du Vigneaud the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Making even a chain that short was slow and fiddly. Amino acids have more than one reactive group, so a chemist had to block all the groups that should stay out of the reaction, join two units, unblock exactly one end and repeat the whole cycle for the next amino acid. Every step lost some material. What du Vigneaud’s paper showed was that it could be done, and that a peptide whose sequence was known could be rebuilt and, in principle, rebuilt differently.

That same year, Prague got its own institute for the job. The Institute of Organic Chemistry, renamed the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry in 1960, was formally founded in 1953 under František Šorm, who ran it until 1970. Šorm listed peptides and proteins among the handful of subjects the institute would build its research around.

The Prague school of peptide analogues

By 1958 the Prague group was established enough to host the first European Peptide Symposium. It took place in September of that year, and the IOCB chemist Josef Rudinger edited the proceedings, which the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences published in 1960. The symposium has been held regularly since and is now run by the European Peptide Society.

The institute’s peptide chemists spent the next three decades on what is called structure–activity work. The idea is simple to describe and laborious to carry out: take a natural peptide, change one feature, measure how its biological activity shifts and let that result decide the next change. Their material was the family of hormones from the posterior pituitary, the group that oxytocin belongs to, along with its close relative vasopressin. In 1960 they synthesised lysine-vasopressin, a natural form of the hormone found in pigs, and later derived terlipressin from it.

The best-known result came from Milan Zaoral’s team in the early 1960s. Working from vasopressin, they replaced the arginine at position 8 with D-arginine, its mirror-image form, and removed the amino group at the very beginning of the chain. Drawn on paper, the new molecule looks almost identical to the old one. Biologically it behaved very differently: of the two main activities the natural hormone has, the analogue kept one at full strength and lost most of the other. They named it desmopressin.

In the late 1960s the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences licensed desmopressin to the Swedish company Ferring AB, and by the early 1970s it was being made on an industrial scale in both Czechoslovakia and Sweden. For a structure–activity programme, it was about as clear a demonstration as one could ask for that two small, deliberate edits can change what a peptide does.

How synthesis stopped being the bottleneck

While Zaoral’s group was redesigning vasopressin, Bruce Merrifield at the Rockefeller Institute in New York changed the way peptides were made. His 1963 paper described fixing the first amino acid of a chain to a small resin bead. The chain then grew while attached to the bead, and instead of purifying the product after every coupling, the chemist simply washed the excess reagents away.

Solid-phase synthesis, as it became known, was repetitive enough to automate, and Merrifield received the 1984 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. It is still the standard method for producing peptides for research, which is why a sequence that once took a team months can now be ordered from a catalogue.

That availability turned peptides into ordinary laboratory tools. Immunologists use short synthetic sequences to pinpoint which part of a protein an antibody recognises. Biochemists use them as substrates when they measure enzyme activity, receptor researchers use them to study binding, and analytical chemists rely on them as reference materials when they develop methods such as mass spectrometry.

The weak point is the material itself. A coupling step that does not quite finish leaves chains one amino acid short, a protecting group can survive to the end, and some of these by-products are hard to tell apart from the intended peptide. Researchers at Ghent University found this out directly when they tested a set of synthetic peptides bought for their own research with a requested purity of at least 95%. Only about 44% met that figure under their analysis, and in one sample the main compound was not the structure that had been ordered.

Problems like that contribute to a wider issue in experimental science. In a 2016 Nature survey of 1,576 researchers, more than 70% said they had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist’s experiment.

Labs that buy research peptides for this kind of work therefore tend to judge a supplier by its documentation as much as by its catalogue:

Peptides supplied on this basis are laboratory materials, made and documented for experiments, and not intended for use in people or animals.

Prague’s research base today

In September 2023 IOCB Prague, its technology-transfer company i&i Prague, the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institutes of Biotechnology, Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, and the University of Chemistry and Technology, Prague, announced a joint biotechnology cluster called Prague.bio. Its purpose is to bring academic research and business closer together, and in May 2024 Zentiva joined as its first industry partner. The peptide work of the 1950s and 1960s is part of the scientific inheritance the cluster now builds on.

World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prague’s Día de Muertos Festival Returns to Holešovice on November 5th
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will host the fifth annual Día de Muertos festival on November 5, bringing Mexican food, live music, traditional decorations and family activities.

The event, organized in cooperation with Jarritos and Nuevo Progreso, will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Halls 13 and 11 will host a Mexican market and a carnival for children.

Visitors can arrive throughout the day, with the food stalls opening at lunchtime.



The selection will include Mexican and South American specialties, tortillas, grilled dishes and Jarritos soft drinks. A special beer brewed by Falcon brewery for the occasion will also be available.

The food zone will remain open until 10 p.m., giving visitors time to sample different dishes and explore the festival’s other attractions.

One of the main attractions will be a traditional ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, prepared by the Mexican Embassy. Decorated with photographs, flowers, candles and personal objects, the altar will introduce visitors to the traditions behind the holiday.

Día de Muertos is dedicated to remembering deceased family members and loved ones.

In Mexican tradition, the holiday celebrates their continuing place in family life and the belief that their spirits return to visit the living. Its customs differ from Halloween, combining remembrance with food, music, flowers and colorful decorations.

Hall 11 will become the PEDRO Kids’ Zone from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., with a program designed for children and families.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holešovická tržnice (@holesovickatrznice)

Activities will include dance workshops, Mexican music, crafts, stories about the holiday and a game in which children throw balls at illuminated skulls. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet a Xoloitzcuintle, the Mexican hairless dog traditionally associated with guiding souls to the afterlife.

Costumes are welcome, and the organizers have divided the program into six one-hour sessions beginning at 1 p.m., 2 p.m., 3 p.m., 4 p.m., 5 p.m. and 6 p.m.

Admission costs CZK 100 per person for adults and children aged three and older. Tickets are available through GoOut and at the venue, subject to availability. Each ticket covers one hour of activities, after which visitors can explore the rest of the festival.

The program will also feature mariachi musicians, stilt walkers, colorful masks and costumes, and a festival parade. DJs will provide music throughout the day, while a screening of the animated film Coco will offer another introduction to Mexican traditions surrounding death and remembrance.

World.title: PM Magyar reveals how Hungary will fund minimum wage tax cuts in 2027
World.content:
Reducing the personal income tax rate on the minimum wage to 9 percent will cost the budget 250 billion forints (EUR 670m) in 2027, as revenue of roughly the same amount is expected from the wealth tax on billionaires, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in an interview with news site Telex on Tuesday.

Responding to a question, Magyar said there were plans to reduce personal income tax for higher earners as well, but he did not currently see this as a realistic prospect. He added that in Hungary, a great many people are exempt from taxation, with many receiving tax relief or tax-exemption, some for life.

“Someone has to pay taxes, there isn’t really a country, at least in Europe, where there is no personal income tax revenue,” he said. Magyar said the proposal to double family allowances needed to be clarified. There was currently a debate as to whether the increase should also apply to the increased family allowance, he said, adding that he believed it should.

Magyar: Personal income tax cut to cost HUF 250 bn
