World.title: Alice in Wonderland comes to Budapest: Lumina Park opens with 200+ magical light installations!
World.content:
Inspired by Alice in Wonderland, this year’s Lumina Park welcomes visitors from Tuesday on Margaret Island, at the Palatinus Baths in Budapest. Featuring more than 200 light installations, the attraction is open until 7 March 2027.

At the park’s official opening ceremony on Monday evening, Ildikó Borosné Szűts, CEO of Budapest Spas and Hot Springs Plc, recalled that the light park first opened in Budapest in 2022. Since then, it has welcomed visitors with a new theme every season. More than half a million people have visited over the past five years, making it one of the Hungarian capital’s major winter attractions.

Photo: MTI

She explained that one of the main aims behind the project was to balance the seasonal visitor numbers at Palatinus Beach. While the outdoor bathing complex welcomes 6,000–7,000 visitors a day in summer, the figure falls to just 200–300 in winter, making it more difficult to maintain employment for staff throughout the year.

The CEO added that operating the park became particularly challenging at the start of the energy crisis. However, the attraction uses energy-efficient solutions, with its daily energy consumption comparable to that of two pizza ovens.

Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Lumina Park becomes a Budapest winter favourite

At the opening ceremony, Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony highlighted how Lumina Park has gradually become a major tourist attraction over the past five years. Alongside the Sziget Festival, the city’s thermal baths and its Advent Christmas markets, the light park has become part of Budapest’s diverse range of attractions.

Photo: MTI

He recalled that when the initiative was first launched, its concept was not yet entirely clear, but the city trusted Ildikó Borosné Szűts and her team – a decision he said had proved worthwhile.

Karácsony added that this year’s Wonderland theme offers visitors a chance to escape everyday life, while also reminding them that ordinary days can be more beautiful and meaningful.

Photo: MTI Photo: MTI

Don’t miss the first winter weather forecast for Hungary: New winter forecast reveals what could be in store for Hungary this year

What can visitors expect at this year’s Lumina Park?

Inspired by Lewis Carroll’s famous novel, this year’s light trail brings the story’s best-known characters and scenes to life.

Among the highlights are a glowing tunnel leading into Wonderland, the Mad Hatter, the Cheshire Cat, the Queen of Hearts’ castle and a maze. Visitors can also enjoy a musical, interactive animal orchestra.

Photo: MTI

The park offers plenty of additional attractions, including a hand-powered carousel, a giant slide and a film projected onto water mist above the wave pool.

One of this season’s new features is a Santa Claus mini-train, available for an additional fee, according to the park’s promotional material.

Photo: MTI

More than one million light sources

Lumina Park was created through a partnership between Budapest Spas and Hot Springs Plc and its Polish partner, Lumina sp. z o.o.

At the opening ceremony, Jan Szagdaj, CEO of the Polish company, said the team had prepared more than one million light sources, 200 light installations, interactive features and special projections for the park’s fifth season in Budapest.

Photo: MTI

Lumina Park opening hours and visitor information

Visitors can explore the light trail at a leisurely pace in approximately one to one and a half hours.

The park is open from 20 October 2026 to 7 March 2027, every day except Monday, from dusk until 9 PM. During peak periods, opening hours are extended until 10 PM.

For detailed opening hours and further visitor information, check the official Lumina Park website before your visit.

World.title: Budapest to mark 70th anniversary of 1956 revolution with concerts, torchlight procession and historic tram
World.content:
Hungary is preparing a series of commemorative events to mark the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence, with concerts, historical performances and a special vintage tram among the highlights of the celebrations in Budapest on 22 and 23 October.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has invited Hungarians and international visitors alike to join the commemorations, which will honour those who fought for the country’s freedom and independence. In a video shared on Facebook on Tuesday, he outlined the programme planned for the capital, as well as events taking place across Hungary and at Hungarian diplomatic missions abroad.

Torchlight procession and memorial flame on 22 October

The celebrations begin on Thursday, 22 October, with a commemoration at Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) at 3 pm. A traditional torchlight procession will then make its way to Bem Square, where a ceremony featuring student performances and a wreath-laying will pay tribute to the heroes of the revolution.

Later that evening, the commemorations will continue at Nagy Imre Square. The flame of the revolution will be lit at precisely 7.56 PM, a symbolic reference to the year 1956.

State ceremony and concerts on 23 October

The main anniversary programme will take place on Friday, 23 October, with events at several locations across Budapest.

Activities on Kossuth Square, in front of Parliament, will begin in the morning. The official state ceremony is expected to start at 4.30 pm, with Magyar scheduled to deliver a speech during the afternoon commemoration. The Budapest Bár band will perform a concert in the evening.

The Prime Minister will begin the day by visiting Plot 301 at the New Public Cemetery in Rákoskeresztúr, accompanied by ministers, to pay tribute to those who lost their lives in connection with the 1956 events. A flag-raising ceremony is also planned for Kossuth Square, while Parliament’s ceremonial sitting is scheduled to begin at 2 pm.

Families will be able to enjoy a separate programme along the Antall József Embankment during the morning and early afternoon. Performers will include the Súgó Tambura Orchestra from Sükösd. In the evening, the Balázs Elemér Group will give a jazz concert, followed by Márk Járai performing songs associated with Tamás Cseh.

Historic tram and events across Hungary

History will also come to life at various points around the capital through installations and performances recreating scenes from autumn 1956.

One unusual attraction will be a vintage UV tram running on Budapest’s tram line 2 according to its regular timetable. The first vehicles of this type entered service on the same route in April 1956, giving the special service an additional historical connection.

Commemorations will not be limited to Budapest. Cities including Debrecen, Kecskemét, Miskolc, Szeged, Győr, Sopron and Eger will host their own events, with cultural centres, theatres and cinemas welcoming visitors. Hungarian embassies and diplomatic missions around the world will also organise programmes for the anniversary.

If you missed it: A revolution above Budapest: The Citadella’s Untold Story of 1956

Organisers promise a simpler, cheaper approach

Magyar said several state institutions were working together to organise this year’s celebrations, with each contributing according to its responsibilities and available resources. The National Event Management Agency is coordinating the work using its own staff, which the Prime Minister said would make the process cheaper, more transparent and simpler than in previous years.

If the approach proves successful, he added, it could also be used for future state events.

The full programme and regularly updated event information are available at forradalom70.hu and on the anniversary event’s Facebook page.

World.title: Two men pushed around and spat on train ticket inspector in Hungary
World.content:
Two men verbally abused, pushed around and spat at a ticket inspector on a train in eastern Hungary. The Debrecen District Court handed down the rulings on 20 October 2026 after both men admitted their guilt and waived their right to a trial. They were convicted of violence against a person performing a public duty.

Incident began over unpaid tickets

According to the statement, one defendant received two and a half years in a high-security prison, while the other was sentenced to 18 months in prison, suspended for a probationary period of two and a half years. The second defendant has appealed for a more lenient sentence.

The incident took place on 6 May 2025, aboard a train travelling from Debrecen to Záhony. The two men, both from Debrecen, had boarded without tickets and intended to travel to the Apafa area. After the train departed, the ticket inspector checked their tickets. The men said they had none and could not afford to pay, so the inspector instructed them to leave the train at the next stop, Debrecen-Csapókert.

They started insulting and pushing him around

When the train arrived, the inspector told the pair to follow him off the train. As they approached the carriage door, both began shouting insults at him. One man spat in the inspector’s face and angrily pushed him aside by the arm. When the inspector questioned his behaviour, the man turned back and spat on his clothing as well.

The second man also swore at the inspector and spat on his clothes. The abuse continued after both men had left the train, with the pair continuing to insult the employee on the platform until the train departed. The inspector remained on board and subsequently reported the incident to the police via the emergency call line.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

One defendant appeals

The court accepted both men’s admissions of guilt at a preliminary hearing and issued its verdict without a full evidentiary trial, in accordance with the applicable procedural rules. The prosecution and the first defendant, along with his lawyer, accepted the decision. The second defendant and his defence lawyer appealed, seeking a reduction in his sentence.

The case highlights the legal consequences of assaulting railway staff carrying out their duties. Both men were convicted in connection with their treatment of the ticket inspector, although only one has challenged the sentence.

World.title: Israeli President Herzog visits Budapest
World.content:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog met Hungarian President András Baka in Budapest on Tuesday, praising bilateral ties and Hungary’s commitment to protecting Jewish communities ahead of the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog arrived in Budapest on 20 October for a one-day visit, beginning with a meeting with Hungarian President András Baka at Sándor Palace. The two presidents held talks first in private and then in an expanded bilateral format before delivering joint statements to the press.

The visit comes just days before Hungary marks the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. Herzog also highlighted the importance of strengthening ties with Hungary’s new leadership and said he looked forward to meeting Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

Afterwards, he met Magyar, who posted a photo on Facebook:

Herzog draws parallels between Hungarian and Israeli history

In his remarks, Herzog congratulated Baka on taking office and praised Hungary’s historic struggle for freedom and sovereignty.

He recalled how Hungarians rose against tyranny in 1956, saying the revolution demonstrated the courage, determination and faith required to achieve freedom. He added that Israel was familiar with this history, stressing that both nations had learnt that freedom and self-determination could never be taken for granted.

“Freedom and self-determination are values worth protecting and defending, even at significant cost,” Herzog said.

The Israeli president also referred to what he described as the ongoing terrorist threat originating from Iran and the extremism spread through its network of radical allies. Although these groups operate in the Middle East, he argued, their activities threaten the wider world.

Herzog said cooperation between nations committed to freedom was essential in confronting these threats.

Photo: Amos Ben-Gershom / GPO

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Israeli president praises Hungary’s role in bilateral ties

Herzog described Hungary as a friend and ally of Israel, highlighting its role in European politics and its contribution to promoting balanced and constructive relations between Israel and the European Union.

He said the two countries’ bilateral alliance had strengthened considerably over the past year, adding that they were working together to build a secure economic and technological future.

“We can undoubtedly learn a great deal from one another,” he said.

Herzog also welcomed the opportunity to meet Prime Minister Péter Magyar, expressing hope that the two countries could continue pursuing their shared vision of cooperation.

He congratulated Magyar on his election as prime minister, describing his rise to office as an expression of the vitality and dynamism of Hungarian democracy and the Hungarian nation.

Photo: Amos Ben-Gershom / GPO

Herzog welcomes Hungary’s zero-tolerance policy on antisemitism

A significant part of Herzog’s speech focused on the history of Jewish communities in Hungary and the importance of protecting Jewish life. He noted that Jewish communities had flourished in Hungary for centuries, making exceptional contributions to the country’s cultural, scientific, economic and public life.

However, he stressed that this history also included the devastating destruction of Hungarian Jewry during the Holocaust, which he described as a lasting warning to all. Herzog praised Hungary’s declared zero-tolerance policy towards all forms of antisemitism and its efforts to ensure the safety of Jewish communities.

He said the moral lessons drawn from history should serve as a compass for the present, underlining the importance of remembering the past while protecting Jewish life today.

Baka: Hungary remains a safe country for Jewish people

Hungarian President András Baka welcomed Herzog’s visit, saying it aimed to strengthen relations with Hungary’s new leadership and included participation in the Voice of the People conference, an initiative launched by the Israeli president and hosted in Budapest. Baka stressed that Hungary was a safe country for Jewish people and visitors from different backgrounds.

“Hungary condemns all forms of antisemitism in the strongest possible terms,” he said, reaffirming the country’s commitment to protecting Jewish communities and ensuring their security.

He added that Hungary consistently defended these principles at international forums. Baka also described relations between Hungary and Israel as friendly and stable, calling Israel an important economic partner. He said Hungary intended to continue pragmatic cooperation with the country in the coming years.

If you missed it: Israeli ambassador in Budapest says they are delighted to work together with the Magyar government

Presidents recall the shared lessons of 1956

Baka also drew attention to the historical connections between Hungary and Israel, recalling that the Hungarian Revolution and the Suez Crisis took place simultaneously 70 years ago, shaping the international environment of the time. Although the two countries now face different challenges, he said the lessons of history remained relevant.

“Peace, security and stability can never be taken for granted,” Baka said, emphasising the responsibility of current generations to learn from the past and work towards a safer, more stable and more peaceful future.

He concluded by thanking Herzog for his visit and welcoming him to Hungary.

World.title: Hungary could lose EUR billions in compensation if Paks II project is cancelled, expert warns
World.content:
Hungary could face claims worth several billion euros if it terminates its contract with Russia’s Rosatom to build the Paks II nuclear power plant, according to a Hungarian nuclear energy expert. The warning comes as the government considers the future of the project, with a decision expected by the end of the year.

Could the government end the cooperation with Rosatom?

Zsolt Hárfás told InfoRádió that the cancellation of a similar Russian-backed nuclear project in Finland could offer important lessons for Hungary. The proposed Paks II expansion, worth more than EUR 10 billion, is intended to add two new reactor units to Hungary’s existing nuclear power station.

Hárfás said compensation claims could cover design and preparatory work, payments already made, completed work, equipment delivered or still being manufactured, and potential lost profits. The final financial consequences would depend on the terms of any termination and the outcome of subsequent legal proceedings.

Finnish project serves as a warning

In May 2022, Finnish company Fennovoima terminated its contract with Rosatom for the construction of a Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactor. The project had already faced political difficulties, with a Finnish government minister signalling earlier that year that they did not support granting it a construction licence.

According to Rosatom, the International Chamber of Commerce ruled that the contract’s termination was unlawful. The Russian company has said it intends to provide further evidence in support of its compensation claim.

The cancelled Finnish project would have provided an estimated 9.5 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, Hárfás noted. Its termination therefore carried potential consequences beyond the financial dispute, including the loss of planned generating capacity.

The expert believes Hungary should take this experience into account before making a decision on Paks II. Prime Minister Péter Magyar has indicated that ending the agreement with Rosatom is among the possibilities being considered.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Energy security also at stake

Hárfás argued that cancelling Paks II could have long-term implications for Hungary’s electricity supply as well as exposing the country to substantial compensation claims.

Hungary currently relies on electricity imports for a significant part of the year, including supplies from Austria. According to the expert, bringing the two new reactors online could reduce that dependence and potentially allow Hungary to export more electricity to neighbouring countries.

The project has faced political and professional opposition both within Hungary and abroad. Austria, in particular, has consistently opposed the expansion. However, the debate also reflects broader questions about the role of Russian nuclear technology in Europe and the future direction of the continent’s energy policy.

More on Russia: Hungary and Slovakia want EU to ease Russian energy ban rules

What will happen to the Paks II project?

The Hungarian government’s decision, expected by the end of 2026, will determine whether the project proceeds under its existing arrangements or faces a major change of direction.

While Hárfás strongly supports completing Paks II, the scale of any potential compensation claim remains uncertain. The Finnish case is a warning, rather than proof that Hungary would face the same legal outcome. Any financial liability would ultimately depend on the contract, the circumstances of termination and the relevant legal decisions.

World.title: Hungary to cut EUR 4 billion from government spendings next year – Here’s where the money will go instead
World.content:
Hungary’s government plans to cut state spending by HUF 1,465 billion (EUR 4 billion) in 2027 by eliminating wasteful expenditure, reforming public spending and reviewing contracts.

Huge cuts in spending from the government

Hungary’s Finance Minister András Kármán says the measures will help reduce the budget deficit while funding higher wages, pensions, family benefits and public services. Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Finance Minister András Kármán have outlined plans to reduce Hungary’s budget deficit from an expected 7.5% of GDP in 2026 to 4.9% next year.

The government says it has identified significant inefficiencies in the previous administration’s spending and intends to redirect public money towards social support and essential services. Kármán said the planned savings would amount to approximately 1.5% of GDP, while tax changes are expected to generate an additional HUF 665 billion (more than EUR 1.8 billion) in net revenue.

Where will the government save money?

The proposed spending cuts include HUF 246.1 billion (EUR 675 million) from unfavourable concession contracts, HUF 169.5 billion (EUR 465 million) from inefficient economic development subsidies and HUF 135 billion (more than EUR 370 million) linked to the expected abolition of an EU migration-related fine.

Other measures include reducing support for public foundations overseeing universities, cutting government communications and event spending, and reviewing prestige investments and state property expenditure.

The government also plans to reduce spending on public media, introduce more economical central procurement and review funding for politically connected foundations and organisations. Magyar said the government intended to terminate the existing motorway concession contract, although some ongoing projects would continue to generate costs in 2027.

Higher taxes for wealthy individuals and large companies

Hungary’s government expects tax measures to deliver HUF 929 billion (more than EUR 2.5 billion) in additional revenue, partly offset by HUF 264 billion (~EUR 724 million) in household tax reductions. A proposed wealth tax is expected to raise HUF 200 billion (~EUR 548 million) annually. Other revenue measures include higher taxes on large companies, tobacco products and environmentally damaging activities, alongside changes affecting retail, insurance and advertising businesses.

The government argues that these measures will make the tax system fairer and reduce opportunities for large companies to minimise their tax bills. However, Magyar acknowledged that businesses could pass some additional costs on to consumers, making enforcement and consumer protection important.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Families, pensioners and public services to receive more

Despite the planned savings, the government has announced substantial increases in social spending. Family allowance payments are set to double, while the minimum pension will rise fourfold to HUF 120,000 (~EUR 330) per month. A new pensioner SZÉP Card benefit is also planned.

The government intends to spend an additional HUF 510 billion (~EUR 1.4 billion) on healthcare and HUF 734 billion (~EUR 2 billion) more on social provision. A total of HUF 667 billion (~EUR 1.8 billion) is earmarked for sectoral wage increases in 2027, benefiting workers in areas including healthcare, education and social care. The personal income tax rate for minimum-wage earners is also set to fall to 9%.

Stay up-to-date: Government measures could give Hungary’s housing market the boost it needs

Deficit reduction remains a challenge

The government forecasts economic growth of 2.4% in 2027, rising to 3.1% by 2030. It also aims to reduce the budget deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030. However, the plans involve balancing significant new spending commitments against savings and higher tax revenues. The government’s projections will depend on whether the planned cuts materialise, economic growth accelerates and additional tax revenue meets expectations.

While the administration says its approach will restore stability and make public spending more efficient, the final budget legislation will provide further details on how the measures are implemented.

World.title: Dining Guide Top100: Hungary’s best pizzeria has been named – and it’s not in Budapest
World.content:
An iconic restaurant in Encs has retained its title as Hungary’s Best Pizza, while the Dining Guide’s 2026 top 10 includes five Budapest venues and five from elsewhere in the country.

Pizza has become much more than a quick weekday dinner. A well-made dough, patient fermentation and carefully selected ingredients can create an experience worth travelling across the country for. This year, the Dining Guide Top100 Restaurant Guide has highlighted ten pizzerias, with the capital and the countryside sharing the spotlight.

Alongside five Budapest venues, the list features restaurants in Encs, Miskolctapolca, Tata, Székesfehérvár and Nagyrákos. At the top is Anyukám Mondta in Encs, which has once again won the title of Hungary’s Best Pizza in 2026, following its success in 2025.

From classic Neapolitan pizzas to sourdough creations with beautifully puffed, bubbly crusts, there is something for every pizza lover. Here are the ten venues selected by the guide.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Hungary’s top 10 pizzerias in 2026

According to the Dining Guide Top100 Restaurant Guide, the country’s ten standout pizzerias are:

Anyukám Mondta, Encs Circo Pizza Avalon Ristorante, Miskolctapolca Belli di Mamma Fermento Pizzéria Pizza Manufaktúra Zsigmond Terasz & Pince, Tata IGEN, Budapest Ria Pékség és Pizzéria, Székesfehérvár Il Bandito Pizza Kertje, Nagyrákos

1. Anyukám Mondta, Encs

Anyukám Mondta

The passion and experience that brothers Szabolcs and Szilárd Dudás gained in Italy have helped shape one of Hungary’s most celebrated pizzas. Their light, airy dough, made with a high level of hydration, is based on a recipe that originated near Lake Garda.

Early in their careers, the brothers baked and served 300 pizzas every evening at a restaurant in Dró. Later, in Encs, their business evolved from Sarok Café into Pizza Sarok and eventually into the now-iconic Anyukám Mondta. Its pizzas have earned a reputation for their clean flavours and meticulous preparation.

A constant desire to improve, determination, curiosity and the warmth of a specially built oven are all part of the brothers’ approach. They have also built a close relationship with their customers along the way.

The brothers, who have received the Károly Gundel Lifetime Achievement Award, are affectionately known as the “Italians of Encs”. Their pizzas, along with the restaurant’s many other dishes, capture the relaxed spirit of the Mediterranean, combining good humour with consistently high quality.

If you missed it: Hungary’s biggest restaurant awards 2026 announced – here are the Dining Guide winners

2. Circo Pizza

Circo Pizza

Circo is a stylish yet relaxed dining spot where the distinctive dough of Neapolitan pizzas meets exciting toppings and inventive flavour combinations. Natural wines complete the atmosphere, making it a place to enjoy a drink alongside lunch or dinner – or simply to stop by for a pleasant glass of wine.

3. Avalon Ristorante, Miskolctapolca

Avalon Ristorante

Located in the heart of the Bükk Hills, Avalon Ristorante serves authentic, airy Neapolitan pizzas baked in one of the world’s most advanced Morello Forni ovens.

Fresh, local ingredients meet Mediterranean flair, creating a premium dining experience. The restaurant’s elegant yet welcoming, family-friendly atmosphere extends to its pizza offering, making it a destination for those seeking quality food in a distinctive setting.

4. Belli di Mamma

Belli di Mamma

Belli di Mamma gives the atmosphere of a traditional Neapolitan pizzeria a youthful, modern twist. Its long-fermented dough and authentic ingredients produce pizzas that are both refined and full of character, served with genuine hospitality.

5. Fermento Pizzéria

Fermento Pizzéria

Fermento is one of the freshest names on both the Víziváros and wider Budapest pizza scenes. Its team learnt the craft of dough-making from Italian masters, and the menu features Neapolitan classics, calzone, as well as vegan and gluten-free options.

A spirit of constant renewal and a genuine passion for Italian cuisine underpin the offering.

6. Pizza Manufaktúra

Pizza Manufaktúra

Pizza Manufaktúra is a long-standing favourite among Budapest’s pizza lovers. It serves around 20 varieties of pizza, made with airy dough and carefully chosen ingredients, without compromising on quality.

Its informal, playful atmosphere and personal service have helped turn it into a regular haunt for customers. Its pizzas also compete with those served at its sister venue on Víg Street in terms of the balance between crispness and an airy texture.

7. Zsigmond Terasz & Pince, Tata

Zsigmond Terasz

Near Tata Castle, Zsigmond Terasz & Pince pairs impressive views with Neapolitan-inspired pizzas. Its dishes combine local traditions with premium Hungarian and Italian ingredients, topped with carefully selected ingredients.

The terrace adds to the experience, making the venue appealing not only for its food but also for its setting.

8. IGEN, Budapest

IGEN

At IGEN, every bite celebrates the freedom and character of Neapolitan pizza. Expect airy yet flavourful dough, beautifully risen crusts and Mediterranean flavours.

The pizzeria founded by Nóri Vidó respects the strict standards of the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (AVPN), while maintaining a relaxed, informal atmosphere. Here, pizza is both an everyday pleasure and something worth celebrating.

9. Ria Pékség és Pizzéria, Székesfehérvár

Ria Pékség és Pizzéria

Ria Pékség is a place to start the day with sourdough bread and handmade pastries, but its pizzas provide plenty of reasons to return, too.

The thin-crust pizzas are baked in a wood-fired oven, delivering simple yet striking flavours.

10. Il Bandito Pizza Kertje, Nagyrákos

Il Bandito Pizza Kertje

Il Bandito Pizza Kertje is the realisation of a teacher’s dream, brought to life during the summer holidays on the banks of the Zala in Nagyrákos.

In its shady garden, visitors can enjoy sourdough pizzas with beautifully bubbled crusts, including creative regional varieties topped with Hungarian-style ratatouille, túró-style curd cheese with pumpkin seed oil, or porcini mushrooms inspired by the Őrség region.

For hungry walkers exploring the surrounding countryside, it offers a distinctive combination of local flavours, relaxed outdoor dining and handcrafted pizza.

World.title: Journalists Targeted in Row over Croatian Football Fans’ Nazi Slogans
World.content:
The march by Torcida members in Split on October 15. Photo: Torcida Split/Facebook.

Ivan Penava, president of the far-right political party Homeland Movement, which is part of Croatia’s governing coalition, held a press conference on Tuesday to denounce what he called a “political and media witch-hunt” against members of Torcida, a hardcore fan group supporting Hajduk Split football club.

Penava’s remarks came after members of Torcida chanted pro-Nazi and anti-Semitic slogans such as “Auschwitz, Auschwitz,” and “Rise, Adolf” during a street march prior to a Hajduk Split match against the Dutch club Ajax.

Police identified 23 individuals suspected of publicly inciting violence and hatred; several were arrested and six remain in custody.

After the incident was reported, Torcida accused journalists of exaggerating it.

“From a fan fight with Ajax fans, with the selfless help of the media, you have created a first-class national scandal,” the group said.

Torcida published portraits of 12 journalists, presenting them in a format resembling wanted posters, accompanied by the caption: “Croatia has already seen all sorts of wonders, but it hasn’t found enough rope for so many Judases.” The group also posted a photograph of a banner reading “Worm Journalists” on its Facebook page.

The Croatian Journalists’ Association, HND called on the police and the State Attorney’s Office to respond, while the international media freedom organisation SafeJournalists urged the Croatian authorities to provide urgent protection to the threatened journalists and to prosecute those responsible.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who heads the ruling Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, also voiced support.

“We always stand up for journalists. We don’t have to agree with their views, comments or even with what is sometimes an undisguised bias; regardless, we still stand up for them,” Plenkovic said on Monday.

However, Homeland Movement leader Penava, whose party is in coalition with Plenkovic’s HDZ, strongly criticised the Interior Ministry and the media for publishing photographs of suspects who are being sought by the police.

While condemning the pro-Nazi chants during the supporters’ march, Penava claimed that the Interior Ministry “decided to pump up this topic”.

Interior Minister Davor Bozinovic, when asked about Penava’s remarks on Tuesday, said there was nothing unusual about the publication of photographs of wanted suspects.

“When the police are searching for someone and have a photograph, they release it. If they don’t have a photograph, they might release a composite sketch instead,” Bozinovic explained, adding that such procedures were prescribed by the Law on Police Affairs.

“Photographs of all suspects were not released – only those of individuals who are being sought, or who are on the run or in hiding,” Bozinovic said.

World.title: Romanian Parliament Backs New Government After Months of Crisis
World.content:
Romania’s new Prime Minister Luca Niculescu in the Romanian Parliament, 20 October 2026. Photo: EPA/Robert Ghement.

Former journalist and diplomat Luca Niculescu won a parliamentary confidence vote on Tuesday, securing the support needed to form a new government that plans to focus on pressing economic challenges and the implementation of key reforms.

The new cabinet secured 280 votes in favour and 55 against, comfortably exceeding the 233 votes needed for confirmation. It was backed by the main Social Democratic Party (PSD), the Liberal Party (PNL) and several smaller parliamentary groups. However, some lawmakers from nationalist and far-right opposition parties, as well as members of the reformist Union to Save Romania (USR), opposed the government.

Niculescu, 55, will lead a cabinet that includes 11 ministers from the PSD and seven independents.

“Romania has no more time to lose,” Luca Niculescu said ahead of the vote, pledging to focus immediately on budget revisions, energy security and reducing waste in the public sector.

“I am an independent PM, but beyond our different political choices … we share a common responsibility for the future, which we have a duty to build together,” he added.

After more than three decades as a journalist, Luca Niculescu entered public service in 2016 when he was appointed Romania’s ambassador to France. For the past four years, he has served as a state secretary at the Foreign Ministry, coordinating Romania’s accession to the OECD, where he demonstrated his diplomatic skills and ability to negotiate complex reforms.

President Nicusor Dan nominated Niculescu for prime minister on October 5. He represents Dan’s fourth attempt at nominating a prime minister in the five months since liberal leader Ilie Bolojan’s government was removed by a no-confidence motion on May 5.

The first nominee, independent Eugen Tomac, withdrew on June 6 before even facing a parliamentary vote. Three weeks later, parliament rejected the proposed programme and cabinet of liberal politician Adrian Vestea. Siegfried Muresan, a member of the European Parliament, also failed on September 30 to secure sufficient support in a vote.

Romania’s political crisis stems from deep tensions among the parties that previously formed a pro-European governing coalition.

The coalition, formed in June 2025, brought together the centre-left PSD, the centre-right PNL, and two smaller centre-right parties. One of its main objectives was to curb the rise of the far-right party Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR).

The coalition’s mandate included stabilising the economy, which is burdened by the largest budget deficit in the European Union, securing access to 11 billion euros in EU recovery funds and safeguarding Romania’s investment-grade credit rating.

But unpopular austerity measures introduced to cut the budget deficit placed growing strain on the coalition, particularly with the Social Democrats, who withdrew their support.

World.title: Montenegro Adopts Constitutional Changes on Integrity Checks for Ministers
World.content:
Montenegro’s parliament late Monday adopted constitutional amendments requiring integrity checks for prime ministerial candidates and cabinet members before they are nominated, in a move aimed at identifying potential conflicts of interest.

The proposal was backed by the ruling coalition, independent MPs and one MP from the opposition European Alliance (ES). The Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS), Montenegro’s largest opposition party, and the pro-Serb Democratic People’s Party were not present for the vote.

The amendment provides for integrity checks to identify potential conflicts of interest among candidates for prime minister and ministerial posts and allows for steps to be taken to eliminate those risks in accordance with the law.

On Monday, the government accepted a demand by independent MPs, the ES and the United Reform Action party for an additional constitutional amendment requiring additional integrity-check legislation to specify in detail how integrity checks will be conducted.

Momo Koprivica, Deputy Prime Minister for the Political System, Justice and Anti-Corruption, said the aim was to identify potential conflicts of interest and take measures to address them.

“In other words, anyone who wants to run the state cannot do business with the state,” Koprivica said.

He stressed that the proposed rules would not prevent business owners from becoming a minister or prime minister, but would require them to choose between holding public office and continuing to do business with the state.

“You cannot do both,” he said.

The DPS opposed both the government’s original proposal and the revised version, stating it would not support constitutional changes made for the sake of political deals, particularly when the stated objectives could be achieved through legislation.

The DPS said it was ready for serious dialogue on improving integrity checks, but argued that the issue should be regulated by law, with checks conducted before elections and with clear criteria and legal safeguards in place.

It said that conducting checks after voters had expressed their support for electoral lists and candidates could open the door to subsequently challenging their integrity and the political will of voters.

The constitutional amendments are considered an important step towards meeting Montenegro’s obligations under Chapter 23 of its EU accession negotiations, which covers the judiciary and fundamental rights, including the rule of law, the fight against corruption and the accountability of public officials.

Following the provisional closure of three more chapters at an intergovernmental conference on October 12, 21 of the 33 negotiating chapters have been provisionally closed.

European officials have repeatedly stressed the importance of adopting the constitutional amendments as soon as possible to ensure Montenegro remains on track to provisionally close all EU accession negotiating chapters by the end of the year.

World.title: Albanian PM Rama Steps Up Rhetoric Against Student Protesters
World.content:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. Photo: European Commission.

After a week of student-led protests that have seen violent clashes in the streets of Tirana, Prime Minister Edi Rama on Tuesday accused some of the young demonstrators of being ideological extremists – stepping up his rhetoric against his opponents.

“There are students who are extremist in their point of views, students who are bound to politically extremist ideologies,” Rama said at a meeting with secondary school principals from Tirana and Education Minister Mirela Kumbaro.

He insisted that “students who exercise their right to protest are not the problem”, but added: “We are not speaking about the exercising the right to protest, we are speaking about the exercising of violence.”

For seven days, young protesters demanding Rama’s resignation have battled police in the streets with Molotov cocktails, stones and other projectiles. Police have responded with tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets.

Rama has claimed that the protests were incited by foreign intelligence services, alleging Russia and Iran have been seeking to destabilise Albania. He has also accused the Albanian opposition of being involved. He has not presented any concrete evidence for these claims.

At the weekend, Rama described the protest violence as a threat to Albania’s European integration process and his goal of joining the European Union by 2030.

He has strongly backed the State Police’s response to the protests despite accusations that they have used disproportionate force against protesters. Meeting police chiefs on Monday, he a pledged a 2,500-euro bonus for police officers.

“Anyone present at a violent demonstration is a target for the State Police … You are there because you are on [the protesters’] side,” he warned.

He also warned of financial and administrative penalties for protesters, saying that the families of minors would be held liable for damage caused during the protests, while students would lose their scholarships, financial assistance and access to free education.

Opposition figures said that Rama’s rhetoric may only inflame tensions.

“This was a speech in which open threats against anyone daring to protest, even peacefully, were justified through manipulation and lies aimed at portraying the protests – in the kind of language used by [former Albanian dictator] Enver Hoxha – as the work of foreign and domestic enemies,” writer Fatos Lubonja, a former political prisoner under the communist dictatorship, told BIRN.

Asked by BIRN about the legal basis for the warnings issued to protesters and the risk that the prime minister’s statements could escalate violence, the prime minister’s press office said the remarks should be understood in the context of violent acts, rather than the right to protest.

“Prime Minister Edi Rama’s statement must be read in its full context. It does not refer to the exercise of the right to protest, but to acts of violence against police officers, citizens, and public and private property,” the press office said in a written response.

Regarding the warnings directed at the parents of young people protesting in the streets, the prime minister’s office referred to provisions of the Civil Code, saying that “the prime minister’s warnings about financial and administrative consequences for individuals involved in violence do not imply the imposition of collective sanctions or the bypassing of legal procedures”.

World.title: How Serbia’s Ruling Party Turned State Institutions into ‘Vote Machines’
World.content:
Employees at the cadastre service of a small municipality in provincial Serbia were taken aback. Last month, they were asked to put their names on a list pledging their votes to the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

“This has never happened before; everyone is in disbelief, even older colleagues who have been working here since the era of [Slobodan] Milosevic,” said an employee who spoke to BIRN on the condition of anonymity.

Despite their disbelief, everyone in the office added their names to the list.

“We all signed reluctantly, because the next step is that they transfer us as punishment to other towns that are hard to get to,” the employee said.

Employees at the Republic Geodetic Authority, RGZ – the state body responsible for land registries and which has a staff of over 2,000 – are among the most recent to become acquainted with SNS’s long-standing practice of demanding that employees of state institutions and public companies (and sometimes private ones), vote for the party and attend its campaign rallies.

This practice finally reached the RGZ employees ahead of the parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25, but it is a mass, systemic abuse that has been going on for years, observers say.

Since 2014, the OSCE’s election-monitoring arm, the ODIHR, has regularly reported on the pressure faced by voters who work in the public sector. European Commission reports have been noting the same issue since 2017.

A 2022 public opinion survey conducted by the Belgrade-based NGO CRTA, based on a representative sample of 1,075 respondents, found that 14 per cent of Serbia’s population had been pressured to vote for a particular party.

BIRN spoke with eight RGZ employees from across Serbia who reported that they are being pressured to vote for the SNS and to attend party rallies.

They said the pressure started after the new acting director Dalibor Babic was appointed in August this year.

“Ever since the new acting director arrived, they’ve been pushing us for the first time to sign the list. Since the response was very poor, they brought in a party ‘commissar’ to harass people and force them to sign,” said an RGZ employee.

The same person told BIRN that people were forced to attend an SNS campaign rally in Belgrade.

“Ahead of the rally at the [Belgrade] Arena there was a hunt to get us to sign up to go. Turnout was catastrophic even then – not even those who had signed [showed up],” the employee said, referring to an SNS rally held on October 3.

An RGZ employee in another municipality told BIRN that they were asked to go to the SNS rally in Novi Sad, which was supposed to be held in mid-September 2026.

“The week when they announced the rally in Novi Sad, we were told that the new RGZ director had asked people to go there in support of him. In other words, we should go to the SNS rally, but it was really supposed to be our support for the new director,” the employee said. “I just told them I’m not interested in any of it and that they shouldn’t ask me.”

This employee said that they have not suffered any consequences yet.

“So far, nothing. I’ve actually been wondering how many times I’ll be able to tell them no,” the employee said.

The RGZ did not respond to BIRN’s questions.

Under pressure

World.title: US Concessions to Dodik Strengthen Moscow’s Hand in Bosnia
World.content:
Back in October 2025, Milorad Dodik, leader of Republika Srpska’s ruling SNSD party and former president of the Serb-led entity, met Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Minsk, Belarus, and spoke of the “high level of strategic cooperation” between Republika Srpska and Moscow.

The next day, the US Treasury Department removed him from its sanctions list, together with 47 others. The Treasury gave no reasons; the State Department later pointed to “constructive actions taken by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska in recent weeks”. Eleven months on, there is enough on the record to judge the result.

American officials have dealt with Dodik before. In January 1998, Dodik became prime minister of Republika Srpska, presented as the moderate alternative to the hardliners who had run the entity through the 1992-5 war in Bosnia, and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright pledged $5 million in budgetary support. When she visited Brcko in March 2000, Serb protesters chanted “Dodik, traitor” at her motorcade.

That history matters for two reasons. First, Dodik is a pragmatist who has spent three decades adjusting to whoever holds power in Washington, Brussels or Moscow, which is why conditions can move him and an unconditional opening will not. The man Washington once backed against the hardliners became the hardliner it sanctioned.

World.title: Kosovo Risks Losing More EU Funds After Deadlock Delayed Reforms
World.content:
But two years on political instability in Kosovo has delayed ratification of the agreements needed to begin implementation. As a result, Pristina has received only 61.8 million euros in pre-financing. This was just 7 per cent of its total allocation.

Earlier this month, Kosovo’s squabbling parties reached a deal that many hope will put the legislature back on track after three elections in two years and a debilitating row over who should be appointed president.

But much work remains to be done, and much time has been lost in political wrangling, election campaigns and post-poll negotiations.

Kosovo’s Head of Negotiations with the EU, Jeton Zulfaj, states that all the required reforms must be implemented by the end of December, or Kosovo will forfeit more than 90 million euros.

“A total of 131.4 million euros in funding from the European Union’s Growth Plan must be allocated to this package of reforms,” Zulfaj told BIRN.

After three failed attempts, parliament narrowly passed the anti-money laundering law on Friday, one of the key laws in the reform package that would enable Kosovo to join the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). Kosovo’s non-membership of SEPA had been costing its citizens some 55 million euros per year.

However, 16 other laws still need to be adopted by December.

“Securing the votes, especially for some of these laws, remains a challenge,” Zulfaj admitted.

Kujtim Dobruna, director of ECIKS, an NGO focused on sustainable economic development, investment promotion and public-private sector growth in Kosovo, said that losing EU funds simply due to failure to meet the criteria was irresponsible.

“For a small economy like Kosovo, more than 100 million euros is a significant amount, especially when we still face basic infrastructure problems that should have been resolved long ago,” he told BIRN. “Kosovo cannot afford this.”

Following a June deadline, Kosovo submitted its first formal disbursement request in July. In its request, Kosovo claimed progress in anti-corruption, women’s and youth employment, judicial accountability and early childhood education enrolment. But it did not explain the exact extent to which these criteria had been fulfilled.

Kosovo has requested 142.6 million euros, including 66.3 million euros for direct disbursement to the Kosovo Treasury and 76.3 million euros through the Western Balkans Investment Framework, WBIF. Of the total requested, 35.3 million euros was in loans and 40.9 million in non-repayable support.

The European Commission confirmed that the request is under assessment, with the amounts expected to be clarified by the end of October.

“Kosovo risks losing additional funds if it fails to meet a reform milestone by the end of the grace period. For 23 of the 64 milestones, originally due in 2025, that period expired at the end of June 2026,” the European Commission told BIRN.

The Commission is assessing whether Kosovo has met each requirement. “Each milestone effectively has its own price tag, and payments are released based on the level of implementation,” it noted.

In practice, the Commission enjoys broad discretion over how the funds are used and could redirect them to other priorities.

According to the Commission, implementation of the Growth Plan in the region has been highly uneven. While some countries have advanced reforms and secured EU funding, others, including Kosovo and Serbia, are making slower progress.

The €140 million already withdrawn from Kosovo and Bosnia and Herzegovina has remained in the region after being transferred to the European Innovation Council Compartment for the Western Balkans.

The next reporting deadline comes in January 2027, when the grace periods for steps originally due in 2025 expire.

According to the Commission, slow progress in implementing reforms puts Kosovo, Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina at risk of losing hundreds of millions of euros in total. All three countries have seen significant delays in adopting their reform agendas and accessing initial funding, risking permanent cuts to their allocations.

Time running short for complex reforms

World.title: Serbians Linked to Protest Movement Allegedly Hit by Spyware Attacks
World.content:
There is high likelihood that the rector of the University of Belgrade, Vladan Djokic, and a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime, Rade Bajic, were targeted by spyware earlier this year, digital rights investigators from the NGO SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab said on Monday.

Both Djokic and Bajic have been supporters of the student-led movement that has been organising anti-government protests for almost two years. Bajic also investigated official corruption in a failed project in Belgrade linked to the Affinity Partners investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab said that they concluded that Djokic was hacked with Pegasus spyware, created by Israeli NSO Group.

“The infection leveraged a zero-click exploit. No action, such as a click or opening a file was necessary for infection. Our investigation into this case is ongoing,” The Citizen Lab said regarding Djokic’s case.

The Citizen Lab is a research unit affiliated with the University of Toronto that investigates “novel threats to democracy, human rights, and global security in the digital ecosystem.”

In August 2026, Bajic received an Apple Threat Notification. “These notifications are high-confidence indicators of targeting with mercenary spyware such as Pegasus,” The Citizen Lab said

SHARE Foundation said that “surveillance of judicial staff and university officials directly threatens the independence of institutions and their ability to work free from pressure”.

“In the justice system, it can undermine the independence of courts and prosecutors and discourage action in the public interest. At universities, it erodes academic autonomy and freedom of expression,” the organisation said. “When the institutions meant to protect the public interest become targets of surveillance, it is not just individuals who pay the price, but society as a whole.”

It added that these trends are especially concerning ahead of the October 25 parliamentary elections, “when protecting freedom of expression, political activity, and privacy is critical”.

Djokic has been a prominent supporter of the student-led movement and has often been targeted for criticism by pro-government tabloids and officials for months. In March this year, officers from the Anti-Corruption Department of the Criminal Police Directorate also raided the Rectorate at Belgrade University as part of a probe into a student’s unexplained death, a move some said was intended to put pressure on Djokic.

As well as probing official corruption allegations related to the Kushner project in Belgrade, Bajic spoke publicly about political interference in the controversial scheme on the site of the old Yugoslav Army headquarters.

In connection with the project, Serbian Minister of Culture Nikola Selakovic was charged with illegally removing the cultural heritage status of the headquarters in order to pave the way for its demolition and redevelopment. His trial is ongoing.

Last month, citing findings from SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab, the Student Blockade protest movement announced that 14 people – members of the student movement, opposition politicians and activists – had been targeted with advanced spyware.

Lawyers representing one of the targeted student activists, Jelena Kontic, filed a criminal complaint on October 6 with the Prosecutor’s Office for High-Tech Crime over the installation of Pegasus spyware on her phone, allegedly by Serbian security forces.

The latest allegations come six days before the parliamentary elections in Serbia, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party facing a strong challenge from the opposition Student List, which grew out of the protest movement.

World.title: Women serve across Estonian Defense Forces as country's demographics shift
World.content:
Women can hold their own across the Estonian Defense Forces, officials say, as demographic shifts make their role in the country's wartime reserve increasingly important.

While conscription and national defense obligations in Estonia currently still apply only to men, Anu Rannaveski, director general of the Defense Resources Agency (KRA), said women in the EDF are by no means limited to support roles.

"Women currently serve as conscripts in units across the board, including those with greater mental and physical demands, such as Special Operations Forces (ESTSOF) and the Engineer Battalion, as well as throughout military intelligence," Rannaveski said.

Around 50 women volunteer for conscription each year, a figure that has remained steady over the 13 years women have been allowed to serve. In some years, half of the women who complete conscription have gone on to pursue military careers.

"They can handle any unit," she emphasized, noting that around 250 women serve across the EDF on active duty.

But demographic changes in Estonia could make their participation increasingly important. Around 8,000 young men currently reach conscription age each year, but in recent years, annual births have fallen to just 4,000 to 5,000 boys.

The country needs about 4,100 conscripts a year to maintain its wartime reserve.

"From 2035 onward, filling conscript ranks without women will become quite difficult," Rannaveski acknowledged.

Women can request specific unit

The KRA chief said women are held to the same standards as men in service. "Sometimes on marches, women will even carry the gear of weaker men," she added.

They do, however, receive one accommodation: the agency generally tries to place women volunteering for service in the unit they choose.

"We try to accommodate their preferences when it comes to choosing a unit for conscription," Rannaveski said. "With the exception of units with their own selection process, such as ESTSOF and Cyber Command, where placement is based on candidates' overall ranking."

Rannaveski said young men in Estonia are liable for conscription between the ages of 18 and 27, while national defense obligations continue to apply to all men through age 61.

The EDF's next conscription intake is scheduled for February.

World.title: Cafe service coming to Elron's new Tallinn-Tartu trains
World.content:
New Škoda electric trains on Elron's Tallinn-Tartu route will offer onboard cafe service, letting passengers buy food and drinks during their journey.

The catering contract was awarded to Maitseelamused OÜ, a prepared-foods company owned by Estonian chef Joel Ostrat.

The onboard cafes will offer hot and cold drinks, sandwiches, desserts, salads and snacks, with plans to expand the menu.

"I want to bring restaurant-quality food and solutions to fast, modern trains," Ostrat said, including offerings passengers might not expect to find onboard.

While Elron has not previously offered food or drinks on board its trains, Edelaraudtee, which operated passenger trains in Estonia until 2013, offered its first-class passengers complimentary hot drinks and a menu including sandwiches.

Katri Kruuse, Elron's long-distance service manager, said the new Škoda trains will take the current operator's long-distance service to a new level.

"Our goal is to make the journey more enjoyable by keeping the products and services passengers need within easy reach throughout the trip," Kruuse said.

Preparations for the cafe service, she added, are in their final stages.

Estonian state-owned passenger rail operator Elron served 7.66 million passengers in 2025.

World.title: International tender launched for Tallinn film studio complex
World.content:
Tallinnfilm Studios has announced an international public procurement tender for the design and construction of a film studio complex planned for Paljassaare.

Tallinnfilm Studios director Joonas Tartu said the goal is to create an environment for filmmakers where Estonian and international film professionals can collaborate under the best possible conditions.

The approximately 6,000-square-meter complex will include three state-of-the-art film studios and the necessary support and auxiliary facilities. The film studios are scheduled for completion in 2028.

"Nearly 100 experts in their respective fields have participated in developing the concept for the complex to ensure that the future studio environment fully meets the requirements of modern film production. Modern studios and well-designed support infrastructure will help create an internationally competitive filmmaking environment, attract more film productions to Estonia and lay the groundwork for the growth and development of the local film industry," Tartu explained.

Tallinnfilm Studios construction manager Neeme Nõmme said the aim of the comprehensive procurement process is to find a partner capable of combining high construction quality, functionality and cost-effectiveness while understanding the project's broader cultural significance.

"Construction companies have until December 15 to familiarize themselves with the Tallinnfilm Studios project and submit their bids," he added.

"We expect professionalism, responsibility and high ethical standards from the construction companies participating in the tender. We want to create a complex that both its builders and all of Estonia can be proud of. Our goal is to build a film studio complex that meets international quality standards and will serve Estonia's film industry for decades," Nõmme said.

World.title: Study: Wetlands flora needs support to bounce back after restoration
World.content:
Restoring natural water levels alone may not be enough to rehabilitate severely degraded wetlands, according to a new study . Restoration efforts must also actively encourage vegetation recovery, writes Ilona Tamm, a junior research fellow at the University of Tartu.

Many wetlands around the world have been restored, but far less is known about whether these areas actually begin functioning as wetlands again. Monitoring often lasts only a short time and many projects lack sufficiently clear objectives against which to assess the success of restoration efforts.

When a peatland is drained, oxygen enters the peat, causing the organic matter stored there to decompose more rapidly and release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Raising the water level slows this process and helps prevent further peat loss, but a wet area is not necessarily a restored wetland. For that to happen, conditions must develop that allow vegetation characteristic of wetlands to grow again.

In our recently published study, my colleagues from the University of Tartu and the University of California, Berkeley, and I therefore examined two wetlands with long histories of drainage, tracking changes in water levels, vegetation and carbon dioxide and methane fluxes over four years following restoration. One of the wetlands, Ess-soo, is located on a former peat extraction site in southern Estonia, while the other, Hill Slough, lies in California's Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta.

Both sites were restored in 2021 after decades of drainage and land use. Four years later, the results were surprisingly similar: restoring water levels had not led to significant vegetation growth.

Two very different wetlands, one similar concern

Vegetation generally struggles to recover at former peat extraction sites. Peat extraction removes much of the original vegetation and the seeds and other material needed for plants to spread. The remaining bare peat surface is acidic, nutrient-poor and dry. As a result, even a former peat extraction site that has been abandoned for decades can remain largely devoid of vegetation.

Ess-soo was originally a natural raised bog, but peat extraction in the second half of the 20th century fundamentally transformed the area. Restoration work began in 2021 at the 58-hectare former peat extraction site, which had been abandoned for nearly 30 years. The site was divided into several sections, with different restoration methods applied to each.

Our study focused on an 8.3-hectare section where drainage ditches were blocked and shallow pools were created to raise the water level and encourage the natural recovery of peatland vegetation. The aim was to keep the water level close to the ground surface and create conditions suitable for the return of vegetation characteristic of transitional mires.

Following restoration, a problem emerged at Ess-soo: conditions in different parts of the same site were either too dry or too wet. Lower-lying sections of the peatland remained permanently submerged, causing vegetation to decline, while water levels in higher areas fell too far below the surface.

During the dry summer of 2024, the water level remained too far below the surface across much of the study area for more than a month. Four years after restoration, vegetation still covered only about 30 percent of the drier ground. Sphagnum mosses, which are particularly important for the formation of new peat, were not found in the study area either before or after restoration.

At Hill Slough, the problem was different, but the outcome was similar. Located in a Mediterranean climate, the wetland underwent extensive diking and drainage beginning in the mid-19th century to make way for farming and livestock grazing. In 2021, the natural water regime was restored across the 100-hectare study area by opening the levees. The aim was to reintroduce tidal flows and improve habitats for wildlife characteristic of wetlands.

However, at Hill Slough, which had been cut off from its natural water regime for more than a century, the original wetland vegetation had undergone substantial changes. When the area was once again exposed to daily tidal fluctuations, leaving much of it frequently submerged, the vegetation that had been present before restoration rapidly declined.

Water levels fluctuated by more than a meter over the course of a day, while shifting soft sediments and unstable ground likely made it even harder for plants to establish themselves. As a result, Hill Slough became almost entirely a mudflat, with only a few plants managing to establish themselves along the higher edges of the site.

Lack of vegetation impacts climate benefits

Very slow vegetation growth means that wetland ecosystems recover only gradually, directly affecting the carbon cycle. Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis. When vegetation is sparse, carbon uptake also remains low.

At the same time, restoring water to a wetland has an important effect of its own. Under wet conditions, less oxygen can penetrate the peat, slowing its decomposition and potentially reducing carbon dioxide emissions. However, oxygen-poor conditions can also increase methane production. Therefore, assessing the climate impact of a restored wetland requires considering both carbon dioxide and methane.

Both study sites remained net sources of carbon throughout the monitoring period, meaning they released more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere than they absorbed. At Ess-soo, net carbon dioxide emissions during the drought year of 2024 were approximately 158 grams of carbon per square meter per year, compared with around 42 grams in the wetter year of 2025. Meanwhile, methane emissions increased from approximately six grams to nine grams. The lower carbon dioxide emissions were consistent with cooler, wetter conditions that may have slowed peat decomposition.

Emissions at Hill Slough were generally higher. Over the four-year period, net carbon dioxide emissions declined from approximately 334 grams to 270 grams of carbon per square meter per year. Methane emissions, meanwhile, increased after the first year and subsequently remained high, reaching approximately 22 grams.

The differences between the two sites are likely related to climate, vegetation and water regimes. For example, Estonia's cooler climate limits microbial activity and the decomposition of organic matter during winter. In other words, restoring water levels may have reduced some organic matter decomposition, but sparse vegetation meant that neither site had yet reached a point where carbon uptake by plants could offset emissions.

Slow recovery not inevitable

Such carbon fluxes are not unusual in restored wetlands with sparse vegetation. Carbon dioxide emissions at Hill Slough were similar to those measured at other restored wetlands in California's delta where vegetation had not returned. By contrast, strong carbon dioxide uptake has been recorded at restored wetlands with similar conditions but well-established vegetation.

Ess-soo's carbon balance was similar to that of partially vegetated former peat extraction sites undergoing restoration, while net carbon dioxide uptake has also been achieved at peatlands with more extensive vegetation. However, even well-established vegetation does not automatically mean that a wetland will become a net carbon sink every year.

The slow recovery of Ess-soo and Hill Slough does not mean that such outcomes should be accepted as inevitable. Vegetation in tidal wetlands typically becomes established within three to five years and, in the best cases, within just one year. There are also examples of former peat extraction sites, where recovery is generally slower, achieving full vegetation cover in approximately five years.

Rapid recovery often requires more than simply restoring water levels. Depending on the site, restoration efforts can include improving water management, preparing the soil, adjusting ground elevation and actively encouraging vegetation recovery, for example through planting or transplanting sphagnum mosses. No such active vegetation restoration measures were used in the sections of Ess-soo and Hill Slough examined in this study.

If monitoring shows that vegetation is not recovering or water levels are not behaving as planned, restoration measures should be adjusted rather than simply waiting. This requires setting clear, measurable objectives from the outset and monitoring results over an extended period. Sharing both successes and challenges is equally important, as comparisons between different sites can help improve the planning of future restoration projects.

This is precisely what the comparison between Ess-soo and Hill Slough demonstrates: similar obstacles can arise in very different wetlands. These findings do not diminish the need for wetland restoration. Rather, they show that successful restoration involves more than simply bringing back water — ecosystem recovery must be monitored and, when necessary, actively guided.

The study was published in the journal Restoration Ecology.

World.title: Ad agency Tank breaks apolitical streak to handle Reform Party's 2027 campaign
World.content:
According to agency founder and creative director Joel Volkov, the deciding factor was the Reform Party's values, which can stand up to far-right populist politics.

Kontuur Leo Burnett has previously handled most of the Reform Party's election campaigns, but the party decided to seek a new partner earlier this year.

Reform Party Secretary-General Kristo Enn Vaga told ERR that Tank was chosen for its fresh ideas and enthusiasm. Although the agency has no previous experience in political communications, Vaga believes it can bring new energy both to the party's campaign and to Estonia's broader political communications and public relations landscape.

Tank creative director Joel Volkov said the agency had ruled out working with other political parties but made an exception for the Reform Party.

"Tank has never produced political advertising in its 31 years of operation. When the Reform Party approached us in early spring 2026, we took some time to think before turning them down outright. This time, we decided to help," Volkov told ERR.

Volkov acknowledged that the Reform Party has struggled politically, with politicians making mistakes in difficult situations, going back on their word and communicating poorly. He said the party's declining approval ratings reflected those problems.

Nevertheless, Volkov believes the Reform Party retains considerable political value because of its liberal, pro-business worldview, which he considers essential to Estonia's future prosperity.

"We believe that these are precisely the kinds of values that can stand up to the rise of far-right populist politics without inciting hatred. Such politics are also spreading rapidly in Estonia, encouraged by foreign agents," Volkov said.

Joel Volkov. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

According to Volkov, the Reform Party's main challenge is not name recognition, which remains high, but rebuilding public trust.

He argued that restoring trust requires politicians to acknowledge their weaknesses and mistakes rather than praise their own achievements. The process, he said, will take time, honesty and a willingness to demonstrate that the party understands voters' concerns.

Volkov described the Reform Party's new "pep talk" campaign as a creative response to that challenge, saying it could be one of Estonia's first election campaigns in which politicians focus on listening rather than dominating the conversation.

A clear enough campaign slogan?

Vaga said the party's campaign slogan, "A Clear Course for the Future," ("Kindel suund on tulevik") was developed in cooperation with Tank and carries a deeper political message.

He explained that certainty has traditionally been central to the Reform Party's messaging, particularly when it has held government responsibility. Given Estonia's challenging security environment, he said reassuring the public that the country is protected remains especially important.

The slogan's emphasis on the future is also intended to distinguish the Reform Party from political opponents that Vaga believes are focused on dismantling existing institutions and returning to the past.

Vaga said the Reform Party wants Estonia to continue developing as a country with expanding freedoms and a growing economy, arguing that building a more prosperous future for subsequent generations has been a central party objective for decades.

Prime Minister and Reform Party leader Kristen Michal made a similar argument on Vikerraadio Tuesday. He accused EKRE, the Center Party and Isamaa of wanting to move backward rather than forward in both their values and approach to technology.

Asked whether voters would understand the slogan's multiple meanings, Vaga acknowledged that not everyone would consider its deeper political message. However, he said the slogan would make sense to voters when presented alongside the Reform Party's name.

Kristo Enn Vaga. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Both Vaga and Michal also dismissed suggestions that the absence of Hanno Pevkur and Jürgen Ligi from campaign videos released over the weekend was deliberate.

Michal said the two politicians were likely traveling or otherwise unavailable when the videos were filmed. Vaga added that Pevkur had not yet confirmed whether he would run in the Riigikogu elections.

Election promises to be gradually unveiled starting in November

Looking ahead, Vaga said the Reform Party's campaign will include video and television ads, as well as outdoor advertising. The party will also begin announcing its election promises and revealing which electoral districts its candidates will contest.

While Vaga did not disclose any specific campaign promises, he said national defense and economic growth would remain key priorities. The party is also developing proposals on family policy, parental benefits, long-term energy planning and improving pensioners' living standards, including continued pension indexation.

According to Vaga, the Reform Party's election platform will be nearly 100 pages long, containing both specific proposals and broader commitments. The party plans to begin publishing it chapter by chapter in November.

Vaga also confirmed that the party will make changes to its lead candidates in several electoral districts, as some politicians who ran in the previous election will not be standing again.

He noted that Kaja Kallas, who headed the party's list in Harju and Rapla counties in the last election as Reform Party chair, now holds a senior position in Europe and is no longer active in domestic politics.

The late Siim Kallas will also be absent from the ballot.

Vaga said further details about the party's candidates and their electoral districts would be announced in November.

The Riigikogu elections are scheduled for March 2027.
