Doubao had released its Smart Assistant Execution Protocol on Sept. 14, giving developers one month to decide whether to let the assistant operate their apps.

Apps owned by ByteDance’s rival technology companies Tencent and Alibaba make up nearly 60% of the list, including WeChat from the former and digital payment system Alipay from the latter, according to domestic media outlet Cailian Press. Others include those from e-commerce giant Meituan, ride-hailing platform Didi, lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, e-commerce platform Pinduoduo, China’s three state-run telecommunications carriers, several banks, and rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi. The listed apps can still be installed and used manually.

Absent from the list are e-commerce giant JD.com and most apps from internet service company Baidu, with the exception of Baidu Maps. A Baidu employee told domestic media outlet Caijing magazine that the phone’s shipment volume remains too small to pose a meaningful concern for the company.

Nubia bills the NaviX Ultra as “the world’s first AI-powered smartphone,” bringing agentic AI to consumers. The company, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, said that within seconds of the smartphone’s Sept. 16 launch, it generated 100 million yuan ($15 million) in sales. The phone’s price starts at 5,999 yuan.

Nubia released a prototype of the current AI phone, the M153, for 3,499 yuan in December last year. Though it quickly sold out, users soon reported that whenever the assistant attempted to operate WeChat, they were automatically logged out of the app. Doubao’s developers later disabled the assistant’s ability to operate the super app.

On the same day Doubao published the list of restricted apps, Nubia announced a software update — including improved localized data search, call-recording summaries, and call screening functions — and offered users six months of free Doubao membership, worth roughly 400 yuan.

As of Monday, none of the included app developers have commented publicly on the news.

Liu Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University’s Institute for National Strategic Studies, told Cailian Press that China has no regulations relating to how AI agents operate third-party applications.

Given the lack of oversight, Liu said, it is understandable that developers would deny such access over data security and user privacy concerns. He added that their resistance may also reflect a desire to protect their own AI ecosystems, particularly given Doubao’s already vast user base.

In its post, Doubao’s developers stated that other apps can opt out of its GUI technology at any time, and its list of cooperating companies would be updated every Wednesday.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.title: Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.content:
SHANGHAI – Popular language-learning app Duolingo has released a Shanghainese course featuring lessons on modern culture and life in old Shanghai as well as offline activities in the city.

The course, launched Thursday, features roughly 50 lessons drawn from everyday life in Shanghai, from ordering street food and taking public transit to exchanging greetings and navigating the city’s landmarks. To access the Shanghainese course, users must first set Chinese as their display language.

Founded in the U.S. in 2011, Duolingo offers courses in over 40 languages. The launch of the company’s Shanghainese course marks its second Chinese dialect offering, following Cantonese released in 2022. China is the company’s fastest-growing and second-largest market.

The course revolves around aspects of modern life in Shanghai like workplace dynamics and coffee culture, while also featuring old Shanghai themes, such as life in the city’s longtang lane houses and local phrases for traditional games, Tan Xiuting, a senior course designer of Duolingo, told Sixth Tone at the launch event in Shanghai on Friday.

Lessons also extend beyond the screen, with offline check-in spots around Shanghai, as well as themed activities on buses and in subway stations. Duolingo has also partnered with local shops; for example, if a user orders a coffee in Shanghainese at a partner café, they will receive a gift.

Wang Chen, an official with Duolingo, said that the course underscores the company’s “long-term commitment” to the Chinese market and its linguistic diversity.

“We want to make dialects cool and help local language and culture stay alive in contemporary life through products that are digital, engaging, and easy to access,” Wang said.

Shanghainese, or the Hu dialect, is a Wu Chinese variety spoken by roughly 10 million people, primarily in Shanghai and the surrounding Yangtze River Delta region. Difficult for native Mandarin speakers to understand, it features more tones and numerous English and French loanwords due to the city’s opening as a treaty port in the mid-19th century. It also preserves many classical Chinese words and structures.

The dialect has declined in recent decades, as national policies have pushed Mandarin use in schools, workplaces, and the media. In the last decade, Shanghai has reintroduced Shanghainese in some kindergartens and on public transportation, and has held speech competitions to inspire younger generations to learn it. TV programs, films, music, and standup comedy shows in Shanghainese have also emerged in recent years.

Zhou Yuwen, a 30-year-old branding manager born and raised in Shanghai, told Sixth Tone that her generation was expected to speak Mandarin both inside and outside the classroom, but over time, Shanghainese-speaking environments decreased.

“I can understand Shanghainese, but when I try to speak it, it comes out so ‘Yangjingbang’ that I feel too embarrassed to keep going,” she said, referencing the colloquial name for the pidgin English used between European and local merchants in Shanghai in the 19th century.

Zhou said she felt “excited” by the release of Duolingo’s Shanghainese course, and shared news of the course’s launch on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, hoping to encourage others to learn. “It’s a pity that someone like me, who was born, grew up, and worked my whole life in Shanghai, can’t speak proper Shanghainese,” she said. “I absolutely love the dialect, and I hope to see it not just preserved, but truly flourish.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.title: In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.content:
“I’m pregnant. After much consideration and thorough discussions with the company and my bandmates, I have decided to temporarily leave the group to focus on rest and recovery,” reads a statement signed by Mity, one of five members of the new girl group BABYQUEEN, alongside a selfie of her wearing pink pajamas in bed.

At first glance, nothing seems out of the ordinary, except that she and the entire BABYQUEEN pop group are AI-generated.

The announcement, published Tuesday on the group’s official Xiaohongshu account, also known as RedNote, has drawn criticism for turning women’s reproductive health into entertainment, as well as jokes and incredulity about the situation’s perceived absurdity.

AI girl group accounts have proliferated on Chinese social media in recent months, with virtual idols often maintaining social media accounts where they share glimpses of their daily lives and even secure and promote brand endorsements.

BABYQUEEN, styled as a South Korean girl group, launched its Xiaohongshu account on Sept. 7. As of Friday, the account, whose IP address is located in China’s northeastern Liaoning province, has roughly 1,000 followers.

Mity’s pregnancy was initially announced on the group’s account the day before, reading, “To prioritize her health during pregnancy and prepare for childbirth, she will temporarily suspend all group and individual variety show appearances and stage performances after thorough discussions with the team.” It also urged followers not to “over-speculate about her private life.”

Since it went viral on social media, the topic has attracted more than 6 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Friday.

Many users have expressed astonishment. “AI group members can get pregnant now? I don’t understand the virtual world anymore,” one highly upvoted comment reads. Others joked that the group’s creators might be running short on tokens, implying they had to let one member go because they lacked the computing power.

Users also accused the band’s makers of using the story for views while showing little respect for women. “Using ‘pregnant and preparing for childbirth’ as a marketing hook and a sensationalized narrative trivializes real women’s reproductive experiences by turning them into entertainment,” one comment reads.

The day of the announcement, the account also released a teaser post for a new song performed by the group’s four remaining members.

In a since-deleted Tuesday post on the BABYQUEEN account, the group’s creators cited pressures of running the group as the reason for the pregnancy announcement.

“We’re just a few girls who like K-Pop, and we’re still students,” they wrote, adding that they had “not earned a single cent” from the endeavor. They also said they had experienced personal attacks and online harassment.

On the group’s official parent account, BABYPVSSY Entertainment, the creators said Mity might next “explore two possible career paths: acting or becoming a maternity and infant content creator.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.title: The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.content:
In 2016, two groups of Chinese livestreamers began feuding on Kuaishou, a short-video platform popular in China’s countryside and lower-tier cities. Their leaders, Brother Hu and Captain Shamate, were both grassroots streamers from Northeast China, or Dongbei. Video after video, they traded insults, accusations, and challenges. These gang-style exchanges were loud, theatrical, and unmistakably regional, full of Northeastern Chinese dialects, bravado, and the kind of chaos that early Chinese livestreaming platforms thrived on.

The feud was widely believed to be staged, a scripted collaboration designed for dramatic effect. But that did little to diminish its appeal. Audiences couldn’t stop watching, and clips of the confrontations soon took on a life of their own. Over time, they spawned an influential body of memes that spread across various media, even video games, one of which has now become an unlikely hit on Steam.

The phenomenon emerged against the backdrop of Dongbei’s changing cultural identity. Once the heartland of China’s heavy industry, the region is often referred to as the country’s Rust Belt after decades of industrial decline. Locals have turned that history into both tragedy and comedy. TV dramas such as “The Long Season” have tapped into nostalgia for the region’s industrial heyday, helping make the “Dongbei Renaissance” a cultural buzzword. Northeasterners have long played an outsized role in Chinese comedy. On television, Zhao Benshan’s sketches made the Northeastern accent familiar to audiences nationwide; on Kuaishou, Northeastern dialects and slang became a rich source of humor and memes.

It was in this context that the feud between Brother Hu and Captain Shamate gained traction. Fans recorded and reposted clips to streaming site Bilibili, where they were remixed, quoted, and jokingly treated as “classics.” The saga became known as “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.”

Seven years later, those memes were turned into a video game. A Summer in Northeast China (DongBeiZhiXia), released for free on Steam on Jan. 9, 2023, was developed and published by Zhuangbuchun Studio, led by Zhuangbuchun, a Bilibili content creator with over 2 million followers. Up till today, the game has since accumulated more than 12,000 positive reviews on Steam, earning an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating despite being available only in Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Its success shows just how far a regional internet joke can travel when platform dynamics, an existing fan community, and a developer’s instincts align at the right moment.

A Summer in Northeast China is a “gal game,” a genre typically centered on interactions with female characters. Set years after the original Kuaishou incidents, the game follows Xiaoliang, who must recover her memories with the help of a cast of female companions, each loosely inspired by figures from the “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” phenomenon. The game’s most conspicuous adaptation is its gender-swapping: the male roles at the center of the original memes are reimagined as women, retaining their names, signature visual traits, and personalities while being reshaped to fit the conventions of the gal game and ACGN (anime, comics, games, and novels) aesthetics.

In effect, the game translates its source material across cultural registers. “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” ran on masculine confrontation, local bravado, and the rough-edged authenticity of Kuaishou livestreaming. A Summer in Northeast China recasts that material through the softer, character-driven lens of the gal game, while keeping enough recognizable references to reward those who remember the source. Events from the original memes return as callbacks for longtime fans, while the first-person linear narrative gives newcomers an accessible way into Xiaoliang’s story.

The game also draws on subcultures Zhuangbuchun knows well, including shamate — a Chinese youth subculture known for its flamboyant hairstyles and fashion — and otaku — intense fandom of anime, manga, games, and related media, originating in Japan — while its use of Northeastern dialect keeps it rooted in Dongbei. Together, these influences reflect the game’s broader approach: combining distinctly Northeastern humor and internet culture with the appeal of manga and anime.

Zhuangbuchun made the game the way many Chinese indie developers do: on a limited budget and in public. The project was self-funded, with a crowdfunding campaign on domestic creator-sponsorship platform Afdian covering part of the cost. He handled much of the design and direction himself, outsourced some work, and recruited voice actors for the female cast.

But developing the game in public was not simply a funding strategy. It also became central to how Zhuangbuchun built an audience around the project. Nearly a year before the game’s launch, in April 2022, he posted a video announcing his gender-swapped take on “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” The video received over 1.5 million views, 71,000 likes, 23,000 saves, and 11,000 reposts.

From there, Zhuangbuchun kept followers closely involved in development. He posted early character designs, solicited feedback on voice acting, and explained delays. When viewers complained about an accent or suggested a different look, he listened and sometimes changed the game accordingly. In that sense, the project was not simply marketed to its eventual players. It was partly shaped by them.

Zhuangbuchun also visited Shenyang, the capital of the northeastern Liaoning province, several times to document where the original Kuaishou events took place. On one return trip after the game’s release, he even ran into some of its fans. These travel vlogs reinforced the sense that the game was being made by someone invested not only in the memes but also in the places and culture from which they emerged.

The steady updates kept the project visible on Bilibili and positioned Zhuangbuchun as part of the internet culture that turned the original Kuaishou videos into “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” His existing followers helped attract attention, while the project’s local roots kept audiences engaged. The original Kuaishou streamers added another layer to this relationship, posting reaction videos and engaging with Zhuangbuchun’s posts, further blurring the line between the game and the people who inspired it.

A Summer in Northeast China is neither the first game to adapt internet memes nor the first to blend Chinese regional culture with global subcultural aesthetics. What makes it unusual is the particular combination: a free gal game with a gender-swapped cast, a distinctly Northeastern setting, a developer who was already a prominent Bilibili creator, and source material rooted in the unruly world of early Kuaishou livestreaming.

For indie developers working with limited resources, A Summer in Northeast China offers a distinctive example of how online culture can move across platforms and media. The same platforms that provided the game with its source material also supplied an audience, feedback, publicity, and a community willing to participate in its development. Rather than simply adapting an existing meme, Zhuangbuchun used the participatory culture surrounding it to carry the material far beyond its origins.

That process creates tensions between local authenticity and internet marketability, and between the crude energy of the original memes and the game’s polished presentation. Yet, A Summer in Northeast China never loses sight of its regional origins. Zhuangbuchun, who has told me he loves Dongbei despite not being from the region, is part of that story: an outsider drawn into its culture who now helps reshape it for new audiences. The game has traveled from Kuaishou to Bilibili to Steam, changing along the way. But for all the distance it has traveled, it has never really left Northeast China.

Zhu Siheng, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Rochester, and Han Yisong, a postdoctoral researcher at the City University of Hong Kong, also made contributions to this research.

(Header image: Promotional art for the video game “A Summer in Northeast China” on Steam.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019126/Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.title: Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019126/Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.content:
Users in China who “sold their faces,” or licensed their likenesses, for use in AI short dramas and livestreams months ago report receiving few or no requests for their use, and consequently almost no related income.

Domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily reported Monday that many users on multiple domestic face-licensing platforms, such as NCAIGC, Mirafans, and ActID, which promise steady income and payment after use of a person’s likeness in their licensing agreements, have not received remuneration.

Face-licensing platforms first emerged around May this year, fueled by the growth of AI-generated content, particularly ultrashort dramas. At a September press conference held by the State Council Information Office, it was announced that more than 90% of the 430,000 ultrashort dramas released in China in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated.

The platforms attract users by advertising a low barrier to entry and high returns, with claims such as “earn nearly 2,500 yuan ($370) in three days with face selling” going viral on social media, state broadcaster CCTV reported Tuesday.

Face licensing lets individuals license their digital likenesses — otherwise protected from use by others under China’s Personal Information Protection Law — to a platform for use in AI ultrashort dramas and ads, among other content.

According to CCTV, registration on face-licensing platforms usually requires users to undergo real-name authentication, upload photos of themselves, and set a desired price for each use of their likeness. Some platforms also require users to specify which roles and scenarios they allow companies to use their likenesses for, such as villains, death scenes, or romance.

Buyers can select single-use or single-project authorization, and the licensor must accept within 24 hours, after which authorization documents are generated and materials released. Platforms take about a 30% cut.

Regular users can earn about 100 yuan per short video that uses their likeness, with some platforms setting a 500-yuan minimum, while professional actors may reportedly receive up to 10,000 yuan.

Wang Jinlin, a model based in the southern city of Guilin, licensed her face on ActID in May. If a buyer selects her portrait for commercial use, she says they’ll typically offer a one-time payment of 500 to 1,000 yuan. But so far, no studio has asked to use her likeness, she told Sixth Tone.

“There are probably few companies making AI live-action short videos right now — there’s no complete pipeline yet,” Wang said. She sees joining the platform as a way to protect her portrait: storing her portrait data should flag unauthorized use, and require any creator to apply for authorization through the platform before using her likeness.

That many report never receiving payments after licensing their faces could be because demand for non-celebrity likenesses is low. The head of AI production at a film and television company, surnamed Zheng, told CCTV that companies mainly seek celebrity and short-drama influencer likenesses, leaving little opportunity for regular people.

Liu Xiao, founder of ActID, told Southern Metropolis Daily that the platform ultimately provides users with an entry point to be seen and selected by buyers, rather than a contract that guarantees monetization.

Criminals may also steal others’ likenesses for AI use rather than go through official channels like face-licensing platforms. On Oct. 8, Beijing’s market regulator warned that lawbreakers tend to scrape selfies, videos, and voices from social platforms and use AI to generate avatars and clone voices from this material for commercial and livestream use.

“Many celebrities cannot fully guarantee their portrait and voice rights, let alone facial licensing in the AI field,” Zheng said. “It’s hard for ordinary people to define how large the gray area (of legal portrait use) is.”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An authorization page on face-licensing platform NCAIGC, Aug. 26, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019112/A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.title: A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019112/A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.content:
HEBEI, North China — It began with a “crazy” idea: use yoga to lift the village out of poverty. And it worked.

In 2016, yoga put Yugouliang on the map. Tucked away in the northern Hebei province, about 300 kilometers from Beijing, the village began attracting experts, journalists, and advertisers to watch its mostly elderly population perform stretches, headstands, and the splits beside crop fields, chicken coops, and sheep pens.

New revenue streams followed: livestream sales, online classes, yoga festivals, TV appearances, and even a movie. By 2020, the annual per capita net income for households under the national poverty alleviation program had reached 12,335 yuan ($1,840), up from 2,800 yuan in 2015, taking the village above the poverty line.

Today, a large stone marker proclaiming Yugouliang a “National Fitness Yoga Demonstration Village” still stands at the village entrance, but the national attention has long faded.

As the officials who drove the trend departed and the locals aged, the streets fell quiet, and the young people who had returned to help with social media marketing and sales left once again for better opportunities in major cities.

Yet 10 years on from that viral fame, yoga remains a force in many households here, either as a source of income or simply as a memory of how it opened a door to another world.

Stretching the imagination

When Jin Xiuying, then Yugouliang’s director of women’s affairs, was first tasked with going door to door to promote yoga in March 2016, she didn’t even know how to write the word in Chinese.

Naturally, she had a hard time convincing villagers. She recalls typical responses like, “Are you crazy? Farm work is exhausting enough. Who has time to exercise?” Others were confused and thought she was offering free fish, as the phrase sounds similar to “yoga” in Mandarin.

“Do me a favor, have a try,” she urged them. “The new official wants us to do it.”

She was referring to Lu Wenzhen, then 50, who had recently been appointed the village’s resident first secretary as part of a national program that dispatched officials from major cities to help develop impoverished rural areas. He’d previously been the Party secretary of a vocational college in Shijiazhuang, the Hebei capital.

Lu arrived that February, taking a seven-hour car ride to a village so remote that he couldn’t locate it on his map app.

Its 100 or so residents — mostly the middle-aged wives and elderly parents of migrant workers — survived by farming crops, raising cattle and sheep, or renting out their land. More than half survived on incomes of less than 2,952 yuan a year, below the official poverty line, while chronic illnesses like bronchitis, arthritis, and rheumatism were common due to years of physical labor and the cold climate.

In early 2016, the village still had no internet access, and playing mahjong or card games were among the few forms of entertainment. While visiting people’s homes, Lu observed that many elderly women would sit cross-legged for long periods on their kang, a traditional heated brick platform.

It reminded Lu of the lotus position in yoga — and that’s when he struck on the idea that this 5,000-year-old Eastern exercise could be the village’s ticket out of poverty. The locals could learn through movements they already knew: sitting on a kang, pulling weeds from the fields, and pushing a stone mill to make tofu.

The only issue was that Lu had never practiced yoga. So he watched instructional videos online, then taught others what he’d learned on an open field outside the village committee office.

He started with breathing exercises, getting villagers to stand with their legs bent, extend their arms in a circle in front of their chests, and make long “woo woo” sounds. Then they would crawl on all fours to strengthen their shoulders and backs and improve their balance. Yoga poses came later.

Lu bought 50 pairs of white gloves to protect his students’ hands during floor exercises, as well as 100 red foam yoga mats. Soon, nearly 70 villagers were showing up to his twice-daily training sessions, mostly women aged over 65.

At first, Jin received complaints from villagers about soreness, and she was still convinced that “Lu was just trying something out and wouldn’t stay long.” But after three months, the symptoms from her herniated disc began to ease, potentially saving her tens of thousands of yuan in medical costs, and others were reporting that they also felt healthier. So she persisted.

In March 2017, a producer from Hebei TV called to invite the village’s “yoga grannies” to perform in its studio. A month later, the state broadcaster CCTV broadcast a clip of Yugouliang residents in various poses.

The unprecedented attention inspired the locals to train harder to master tougher positions, such as the one-legged tree pose, the Sirsasana handstand, and lateral splits. More men began joining Lu’s sessions, and even the village’s superstitious hawks stopped suggesting that female yoga practitioners would bring about poor harvests by “pointing their backsides at heaven.”

Rising fortunes

In the summer of 2017, Jin’s daughter returned from university for the holiday and helped register an account on the Kuaishou short-video platform to promote “China’s yoga village.” In just over a year, it gained more than 300,000 followers.

Then came livestreaming. Most evenings, villagers would gather beside a concrete road to film themselves practicing yoga under the streetlights. They sold local products — potato noodles, red beans, soybeans, oat flour, and quinoa — and prerecorded yoga courses, which brought in thousands of yuan on a good day.

The income was divided according to how often each villager took part. Frequent participants were making more than 1,000 yuan a month, five times the rural pension at the time.

The group practiced year-round. In winter, they filmed in an abandoned single-story house after blocking holes in the walls and windows with old clothes and installing two coal-fired stoves to stay warm.

Wu Qilian, 83, who then practiced yoga with her husband, said that her grandson quit as a gig worker in Beijing to return home and run a social media account for the family. Livestreaming helped them earn several thousand yuan a year in additional income.

Yoga competitions and festivals were organized to attract visitors, while the village women continued to perform on TV shows across the country, wearing their signature blue headscarves and red athletic outfits.

“If you couldn’t do a headstand, if you weren’t good enough, they wouldn’t take you out to perform,” Li Xiufang told Sixth Tone. The 69-year-old returned to the village from Beijing after retiring at 55 and found “everyone was doing yoga, so I just joined in.”

Netizens dubbed Yugouliang “China’s No. 1 Yoga Village,” while the national sports authority designated it as a “National Fitness Yoga Demonstration Village.”

In 2022, the Chinese media giant Tencent released the movie “Welcome to Yoga Village” via its streaming service. A dramatized account of Lu’s poverty-alleviation efforts, it features several locals in minor speaking roles.

“Look at this. I’m a movie star,” said Zhang Xiying, 72, who had a few lines of dialogue. Pointing to a wall of photos in her home dedicated to her on-screen appearances, she added, “If I didn’t do yoga, who would invite an old woman like me anywhere?”

The village also secured more than 2.69 million yuan in government funding to build a small quinoa processing plant, creating 16 jobs. Many locals had switched to growing the grain because of its popularity among fitness enthusiasts.

On Feb. 29, 2020, Yugouliang was officially declared out of poverty.

Twist of fate

The boom times didn’t last long. Compared with other crops, quinoa requires deeper and more intensive tilling, so the aging villagers soon stopped growing it. Lu’s attempts to introduce a new variety of potato also failed when negotiations to secure a wholesale buyer broke down.

Livestream sales, which led to competition as well as resentment from families not sharing in the revenue, saw a sharp drop-off. After only a year back home, Wu’s grandson returned to Beijing to look for work.

Meanwhile, several members of the yoga group died, including Wu’s husband, or moved away to live with their children. Many of those remaining in the village are either too old to achieve difficult positions or have debilitating health issues.

Jin stepped down as the village’s director of women’s affairs in 2021. Residents say her successor promised to pay for yoga participation, but the money never materialized, so they stopped attending.

Liu Runtao, 58, took the role this year and has been struggling to put the team back together. She’d never practiced yoga before returning to the village in recent years. Now, when she posts notices about training sessions, usually only her relatives show up.

In villages like Yugouliang, organizing events and upgrading infrastructure often depend on approval and funding from town or county authorities. However, as officials change, so do their offices’ priorities.

Lu told Sixth Tone that he would sometimes win a higher official’s backing for a project only to see them transferred out before anything was finalized, taking things back to square one. Even when the village was at its most popular, funding to update its tourism facilities was slow to come.

Lu stepped down as resident first secretary in 2023 and returned to the vocational college in Shijiazhuang. Now 60, he still returns for major events and helps promote Yugouliang, but he feels it’s now someone else’s responsibility to keep the “yoga village” narrative alive.

Winding down

On one sunny July afternoon, a group of villagers sat chatting at a bus stop. Services pass through here just twice a day. Apart from the occasional truck carrying agricultural supplies, the main road is largely silent.

Liu had arranged a yoga training session, but just nine elderly women showed up. Most residents can no longer achieve the poses that made them famous. Only the septuagenarian Zhang can still balance with both feet off the ground.

The new resident first secretary, Li Jidong, who worked for the same Shijiazhuang college as Lu, watched from the sidelines. He has little interest in yoga, apparently seeing it more as a liability. “What if someone has a brain hemorrhage while doing it?” he said, after interrupting the session to suggest the elderly women attempt a safer activity.

Li believes that Yugouliang’s remote location and climate make Lu’s vision of building a tourism industry here difficult to realize.

“I don’t have that kind of ability. No single institution or person can solve a problem this big on their own,” he said. Li has only been in the job for two years but admits that he already wants to leave.

During a recent yoga event, Li asked people to help with livestream sales of local farm products, but the results were disappointing.

The village Party secretary, Zhang Pengcheng, who took over from his father in 2021, said he has also tried encouraging residents to make short videos and livestream, but many struggle even to use smartphones, let alone speak standard Mandarin with viewers online.

Yet he sees the remaining yoga team as the “embers” to spark a tourism boom. In 2025, he organized a gala in which the team performed on ice beside a bonfire. A livestream of the event drew about 100,000 viewers.

But for now, the priority is improving infrastructure. In July last year, the township government and local businesses funded the opening of a guesthouse with room for up to 86 guests. It has yet to turn a profit. When Sixth Tone visited, its doors and windows were shuttered.

The village has also built a canteen for pensioners, with dishes starting at just 2 yuan. It was also temporarily closed in July because of a staff shortage.

Before stepping down, Jin earned a yoga instructor qualification in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, and has since relocated to Zhangbei Town, about 60 kilometers from Yugouliang. She offers free classes to locals and teaches online six days a week.

Of the few residents still practicing yoga in Yugouliang, Zhang Xiying, despite her age, remains the most able and enthusiastic — though not for the village’s benefit, but for her own family’s.

“Exercise keeps me healthy,” she said, after wrapping up a practice session. “And I need to take good care of my old man.”

Additional reporting: Wu Huiyuan; editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Villagers practice yoga together on a summer afternoon in Yugouliang, Hebei province, July 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections
World.content:
DONALD TRUMP. US President Donald Trump gestures after his speech during the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, USA, September 9, 2026.

US President Donald Trump's record-low popularity, voter concerns over affordability and a fierce immigration debate are shaping the November 3 US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump’s record-low popularity, voter frustration over the cost of living and a fierce immigration fight are shaping the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Democrats gain the power to challenge his administration.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of each chamber.

The outcome will hinge on a relatively small number of competitive races, but the campaigns are being shaped nationally by Trump himself and voter concerns over affordability and immigration.

Here is a look at the three issues defining the election:

Donald Trump

The president has put himself front and center in the closing stretch of the campaign cycle despite his record-low popularity, with upcoming rallies in Florida, Iowa, Michigan and Texas. Trump’s approval rating has fallen to an all-time low of 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Yet he has repeatedly urged voters to pretend he’s on the ballot, an effort that could motivate Democrats and independents to rally against his party despite the message being aimed at increasing turnout among Trump’s base.

Democrats have said Trump has broken his campaign promises to lower costs and end wars. They have vowed to tackle an affordability agenda to reduce Americans’ cost of living and hold the administration accountable for alleged corruption if voters give them control of either chamber.

Affordability

Voters have consistently ranked the cost of living as the top issue this election cycle. Half of registered voters surveyed in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll cited the cost of living as the most important factor in how they will vote. In the same poll, voters highlighted health care, gasoline, food and housing as the top household bills lawmakers should focus on.

Republicans’ top legislative achievement was a tax cut extension that slashed roughly $1 trillion in spending for Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and other health programs. Democrats last year forced a government shutdown over a failed effort to extend expiring health subsidies that benefited 24 million Americans.

Gas prices have spiked since the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February. The national average price of gas is $4.28 — $1.20 higher than it was a year ago, according to AAA. The average cost of diesel is $6.32 — a $2.70 increase from a year earlier.

Grocery costs are up 1.8% over the past year, according to US Bureau of Labor Statistics data on consumer prices. Federal Housing Finance Agency data show home prices rose 2.1% over the past year. Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill earlier this year. It became law without Trump’s signature.

Immigration

Preliminary data from the Department of Homeland Security showed a 95% drop in migrants apprehended at the southwest border compared to former president Joe Biden’s administration. The agency said there have been no Border Patrol releases the entire fiscal year for the first time ever.

But fatal encounters with federal immigration agents have occurred in Maine, Minnesota and Texas. The backlash to the deaths of two US citizens in Minnesota pulled many Democrats in competitive primaries to the left this year, with some candidates calling for the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and others saying Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished.

Democrats and Republicans sparred over immigration funding this year in a stalemate that forced Republicans to unilaterally pass a $70 billion bill to fund ICE and the Border Patrol for the remainder of Trump’s presidency. Republicans counter Democrats’ criticism by saying Democrats support open borders.

Federal immigration officials also raided the Washington home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota this month, drawing widespread condemnation from Democrats. A person familiar with the case against Omar told Reuters one potential aim of the investigation could be to strip her of US citizenship and deport her.

Other issues

Artificial intelligence and data centers, cryptocurrency, abortion and Israel could also influence voters in individual races. In Ohio’s Senate race, for example, Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown has labeled Republican Senator Jon Husted the face of data centers, and the crypto super PAC Defend American Jobs has spent more than $46 million to reelect Husted over Brown, a former US senator who chaired the chamber’s Banking Committee.

In Maine’s Senate race, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson is hoping voters don’t forget that Republican Senator Susan Collins helped confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which later overturned the federal right to abortion. Collins is on the election ballot for the first time since the high court made abortion a state issue rather than a federal right.

In Michigan, Republican nominee Mike Rogers has indicated he would accept help from a pro-Israel super PAC that spent more than $30 million backing Democratic US Representative Haley Stevens in her unsuccessful primary against Abdul El-Sayed, who now faces Rogers in the general election. The group has already spent more than $280,000 on mailers against El-Sayed.

Earlier this week, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection. – Rappler.com

World.title: France to deploy troops, admits to failures over weekend unrest
World.content:
PROTEST. Residents gather during a protest following a fire at the town hall in Limoges, France, October 18, 2026. Reuters

Targeted curfews are implemented to restore calm, with the government admitting to intelligence failures and static police deployments during the unrest

PARIS, France – France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, October 20, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend’s violence.

“The deployment next Saturday (October 24) will be massive,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities on October 17.

In a sometimes rowdy debate, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the military would be deployed alongside police, while the government pledged to overhaul tactics after widespread criticism that city centers had been left vulnerable.

Targeted curfews help restore calm

Framing the crisis as a choice “between violence and the Republic,” Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating public anger over high living costs and declining public services.

The turmoil shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls.

Protests in other European countries, including Italy and Albania, have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes.

A night of relative calm in France followed targeted curfews imposed in several areas affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localized curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said.

Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state’s response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not canceling planned police leave.

Nunez apologized for the mistakes. “I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility,” he said.

Suspect arrested for Limoges town hall destruction

Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence.

Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group.

Sylvain Maillard, a Renaissance deputy for Paris, told Reuters some apps had become “a walkie-talkie system for rioters and looters.”

Underscoring the broad impact of the crisis, French borrowing costs rose further on Tuesday as investors fretted about the prospect of more unrest, with the yield on benchmark 10-year government bonds touching its highest level in 24 years.

Supermarket chain Carrefour said it had lost tens of millions of euros through theft and damage, warning that it faced an “unprecedented situation” because of the disorder.

France’s main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday, pledging to maintain pressure on Macron’s government over what it says is a deteriorating and underfunded education system. “We carry on,” it said on social media.

Separately, groups identifying themselves as “Gilets Jaunes” (Yellow Vests) called for protest actions over rising fuel costs.

The yellow vest movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprang up in 2018 during Macron’s first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Traffic blockades continued for months until the government made costly concessions it can ill afford now.

Italy faces new form of unrest, minister says

Northern Italian cities, including the financial capital Milan, were also hit by riots last weekend.

Though not on the scale seen in France, the unrest nonetheless jolted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government, which was expected to introduce new security measures at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday.

Defense Minister Guido Crosetto described the disturbances as a form of “hybrid warfare” conducted through social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and other online networks.

“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras,” Crosetto wrote on X. “The West has yet to realize this or take any meaningful action in response.”

In Milan’s central Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, sportswear retailer On and a Levi’s store that were targeted during the unrest had reopened on Tuesday but remained boarded up. Luxury stores had restored merchandise to window displays after temporarily removing it for security reasons.

In Albania, protesters were expected to take to the streets of Tirana for a seventh consecutive day against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama. – Rappler.com

World.title: Parts of Northern Luzon to be rainy as Super Typhoon Rosal speeds up
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 21, 2026, 4 am.

Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is located 990 kilometers east of Northern Luzon at 4 am on Wednesday, October 21

MANILA, Philippines – At least three provinces in Northern Luzon are expected to have moderate to heavy rain on Wednesday, October 21, as Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) accelerated before dawn.

As of 4 am on Wednesday, Rosal was already 990 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, moving west northwest at 30 kilometers per hour from the previous 25 km/h.

The super typhoon had intensified further on Tuesday evening, October 20, with its maximum sustained winds reaching 215 km/h from 195 km/h. Its gustiness also went up to 265 km/h from 240 km/h.

Rosal remains unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will still have an impact due to its size and intensity. It will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday, October 22, and Friday afternoon, October 23.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) released an updated rainfall outlook at 5 am on Wednesday, showing that the following provinces are expected to see significant rain:

Wednesday, October 21

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

Thursday, October 22

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Batanes

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

Friday, October 23

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes

On Wednesday, aside from the provinces mentioned above, Rosal may trigger moderate to at times heavy rain in Batanes, Isabela, and Catanduanes, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms in the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Bicol, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Ilocos Sur, Quezon, and Eastern Visayas.

PAGASA also advised more areas to brace for strong winds from the super typhoon. Here are the areas covered by Signal No. 1 as of 5 am on Wednesday:

Batanes

Babuyan Islands

mainland Cagayan

eastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, Delfin Albano, Santo Tomas, Tumauini, San Pablo, Ilagan City, San Mariano, Dinapigue)

northern and central parts of Apayao (Calanasan, Luna, Santa Marcela, Flora, Pudtol, Kabugao)

northeastern part of Ilocos Norte (Pagudpud, Adams)

northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

The highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal due to Rosal is Signal No. 2 or 3.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Wednesday, October 21

Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Bicol, Romblon, Eastern Visayas, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani

Thursday, October 22

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Northern Mindanao, Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Friday, October 23

most of Luzon and Visayas, Camiguin, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Travel is becoming increasingly dangerous in more seaboards in Luzon on Wednesday, with the highest waves up to 8 meters or around 26 feet high.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Seaboards of Batanes; northern and eastern seaboards of Cagayan including Babuyan Islands – waves up to 8 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Cagayan; seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 6 meters high

Eastern seaboard of northern Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes – waves up to 5 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, and Northern Samar; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Eastern seaboards of northern Quezon and Eastern Samar; remaining seaboard of Northern Samar; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 4 meters high

Eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands, Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group, and Davao Oriental; remaining seaboards of Catanduanes and Ilocos Norte – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboards of Ilocos Sur, La Union, Surigao del Sur, and Surigao del Norte; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining eastern seaboards of Quezon; northwestern seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Eastern seaboard of Davao Occidental – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

PAGASA said Rosal can still strengthen further as it moves over the Philippine Sea on Wednesday morning, but it is likely to gradually weaken afterwards. It could weaken into a typhoon on Thursday and into a severe tropical storm by Sunday, October 25.

Rosal’s latest forecast track shows it is projected to maintain its west northwest direction on Wednesday, before heading northwest until Friday morning and recurving northeast by Sunday.

It may leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24.

Rosal, which entered PAR on Tuesday, is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Padayon Cebu: A new space to chat how to make the province more livable
World.content:
Rappler and civil society groups launch a workspace in the Rappler app to push for a better quality of life in Cebu

CEBU, Philippines – “Whether making decisions in the community, [or] writing stories that create meaningful impact, all these efforts are more meaningful when the people on the ground are involved and given a platform to speak up,” Luis Calopez, a Cebuano mover said in Rappler’s Padayon Cebu chat room on Friday, October 16.

The young mover is now among more than a hundred Cebuanos who joined the new Padayon Cebu chat room on Muni, a community-building platform found on Rappler’s free app.

In the chat room, attendees of the Move Cebu: Sugbo Alang Sa Sugbuanon forum, Cebu civil society groups, experts, and community leaders have begun conversations on how Cebu can best find solutions to problems its residents face daily — from constant flooding to traffic, to solid waste management.

“It’s really a place where we want facts to thrive,” Rappler’s head of community Pia Ranada said during the launch of the Padayon Cebu chat room at the public forum held on Wednesday, October 14.

UNITING FOR A BETTER CEBU. The just-launched Padayon Cebu chat room is used as a repository of insights and questions during the Move Cebu public forum on how to improve quality of life in Cebu. Photo by Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

Ranada explained that amid the ongoing challenges that newsrooms face and the pitfalls of profit-driven algorithms on social media, there needs to be a platform where Cebuanos could freely interact with experts, civil society groups, and journalists to discuss local issues, collaborate on solutions, and keep the province moving forward. (READ: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity)

Padayon Cebu is envisioned to be a “working space” for Cebu citizens who want a place to share their concerns, mobilize for change, and demand for policies and action. Unlike the usual social media platforms, Muni won’t drown out facts and advocacies with micro-targeting and profit-driven feeds.

“For instance, you’re a student who wants to organize a run to make Cebu more walkable, you can share your press release or invite, your sign-up form on the Padayon Cebu chat room,” Ranada said.

Apart from sharing information, the community head emphasized that chat room members could directly ask Rappler’s journalists questions and even offer suggestions on coverage they’re doing in the province.

“It’s a great way for you to stay connected and get verified information about Cebu, and more than that, mobilize your communities to act on problems that you really care about and want to solve,” Ranada said.

Joining the Cebu conversation

Jun Muntuerto, lawyer and convenor of the Cebu Citizens Initiative (CCI), said on the Padayon Cebu chat room on Thursday that the province needs to act now and prepare for harder times due to ongoing international conflicts, trade tensions, and other events affecting the regions.

“Our public life is increasingly drawn toward partisan disputes and preparations for the 2028 elections. Public accountability matters, but Cebu also needs sustained attention to livelihoods, prices, jobs, public services, and emergency readiness,” Muntuerto stressed.

The same sentiments were echoed during Rappler’s huddle with partners and local community leaders on Friday afternoon, October 16. There, the groups identified key issues that affected the province and committed themselves to collaborating and implementing solutions.

“We commit to creative communication campaigns, making space for fisherfolks and also monitoring and evaluation, to constantly document and pursue research studies,” CCI member Kenneth Kabingue said.

“We recommend continuing educational and capacity-building efforts with local communities and working together with government units to tackle the environmental crisis from all facets and entry points where we can,” Vhon Michael Tobes of Zero Hour PH said.

If you’d like to join the conversation on what you can do to help make Cebu more livable, join the Padayon Cebu chat room here. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] GCash ends debut flat at P6.60 as early gains fade
World.content:
Even with the Philippine president gracing its listing bell, GCash finished its much-anticipated market debut right where it started at P6.60. While heavy turnover and an intraday bounce to P6.76 proved that trading interest was real, persistent selling pressure and a secondary-heavy share sale show that political fanfare cannot bypass cold market arithmetic.

Not even the presence of the Philippine president could keep GCash shares above their offer price on their first day of trading.

But writing off the country’s most anticipated market debut after a single session would be premature. One day on the boards cannot determine whether a marquee fintech listing can deliver lasting value.

With President “Bongbong” Ferdinand Marcos Jr. attending the listing bell ceremony on Tuesday, October 20, GCash parent Mynt entered the Philippine Stock Exchange amid lofty expectations that its arrival would energize a sluggish bourse.

In early trading, the stock climbed to an intraday peak of P6.76—roughly 2.42% above its P6.60 offer price. Yet that initial surge quickly met heavy resistance. By the closing bell, the shares had surrendered their modest advance, finishing flat right at P6.60.

It was hardly a quiet debut. Online brokerage DragonFi reported that approximately 1.3 billion shares changed hands. Multiplying that reported volume by the day’s P6.60 to P6.76 trading band yields a calculated turnover between P8.58 billion and P8.79 billion.

That represents massive churn for a stock that ultimately ended exactly where its IPO subscribers started. The offering certainly commanded market attention, but buyers were unwilling to sustain an opening-day premium.

The retreat from P6.76 indicates that sellers became increasingly assertive as the day unfolded. In market parlance, selling pressure overwhelmed buying appetite. Technically, every matched trade requires both a buyer and a seller, but when sellers grow eager enough to accept progressively lower bids, prices naturally slip.

Quick profit-taking explains a good portion of that slide. Retail and institutional subscribers allocated shares at P6.60 had an immediate window to lock in gross gains above that level, even if brokerage commissions and transaction taxes chipped away at their net proceeds.

Conversely, buyers who chased the morning pop near P6.76 ended the day nursing an unrealized loss of roughly 2.37%. Depending on entry price, the very same session felt either like a harmless draw or an immediate disappointment. Everyday familiarity with an app does not alter the arithmetic of trading.

The president’s presence lent the occasion undeniable significance beyond corporate balance sheets. It tethered the listing to Malacañang’s broader push to deepen domestic capital markets and encourage financial inclusion.

For millions of Filipinos who routinely use GCash to send money and settle household bills, owning shares offered a tangible bridge between everyday transactions and corporate ownership.

Yet political theater cannot override market valuation. A ceremonial podium appearance may shine a bright spotlight on the trading floor, but durable demand requires underlying earnings momentum and sustained investor conviction. Retail investors deserve that clear distinction, especially when brand affection makes equity risk seem deceptively simple.

The structure of the offering also demands careful scrutiny. The roughly P60.9-billion transaction delivered only about P10.6 billion in gross primary proceeds to Mynt’s treasury.

A staggering P50.3 billion—approximately 83% of the total—represented secondary shares sold by existing shareholders. Providing liquidity to early venture backers is a standard, legitimate function of an exchange. (READ: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday)

But everyday investors must remember that the vast majority of public capital did not go toward building new servers or expanding product lines; it flowed directly to early owners taking cash off the table.

Can GCASH regain upward momentum in the coming sessions? It is entirely possible. Global funds and domestic institutions that received smaller allocations than requested during bookbuilding could step into the secondary market to build full positions.

Other institutional accounts may simply be waiting for opening-week volatility to subside before deploying capital. Potential demand, however, only matters when buyers actually commit funds at higher price levels.

Vantage Point’s near-term projections remain within reach. Our initial baseline scenario projected the stock settling between P7.00 and P7.70 by October 27, anchored around a P7.40 midpoint. From Tuesday’s P6.60 close, reaching P7.00 requires a 6.1% advance; hitting P7.40 demands 12.1%; and testing P7.70 entails a 16.7% gain. These figures represent analytical benchmarks rather than guaranteed returns.

Tuesday’s flat finish undeniably tempers our early optimism. An intraday high of P6.76 fell short of the lower bound of our weekly target band. Oversubscribed order books and cornerstone commitments failed to spark a runaway opening pop. While our baseline thesis survives its first trial, the market tape offers little justification to elevate our expectations.

The enduring investment case rests squarely on operating performance. In the first half of 2026, Mynt’s net profit grew by just 7.3% to P10.82 billion, while core EBITDA dropped 4% and margins narrowed to 27.3%.

Sharp gains in deposit interest from a P68.6-billion cash balance cushioned the bottom line, but discerning investors must separate operating franchise earnings from passive interest earned on bank balances.

At P6.60, Mynt’s roughly P441.5-billion equity valuation already requires meaningful execution. Our conditional year-end scenario of P7.30 to P8.20 remains grounded on that assumption. The coming days will measure trading conviction; subsequent earnings reports will reveal whether that conviction has real teeth. GCash has captured the market’s undivided attention. It must now earn its premium. – Rappler.com

World.title: New urban poor commissioner has lavish lifestyle. Palace still defends her.
World.content:
Groups such as Akbayan Youth says the position requires someone who has credentials and pro-people qualities, since the work entails dealing with informal settlers

The Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor (PCUP) just had a new commissioner, 27-year-old Zofia Canlas, and social media is not having it.

Canlas is a biology graduate from the De La Salle University in Manila in 2024, according to her LinkedIn profile, but that’s not what stood out to people on the internet. What did were her photos posted on Instagram while touring Italy, Spain, France, Greece, and the United States.

Her Instagram and Facebook accounts suddenly became unavailable as of Tuesday, October 20.

Screenshot from Zofia Canlas’ Instagram account

When her Facebook was still accessible, it showed photos of Canlas wearing a dress made by her sister, Ampcor Eunice Canlas, a fashion designer, in 2024. The dress was dedicated to their father, Jomar Canlas, who was described as a journalist and someone who “works now in The House of the President in Malacañang as ASEC (assistant secretary).”

“From meeting Lana Del Rey @honeymoon then straight to your Oath-taking as a Commissioner (heart emoji) Told yah October is your month my lil Cancer babe!!!

“Congratulations to our very 1st commissioner in our family, Comm. Canlas! Very proud Capricorn Ate here forever (heart emoji),” Ampcor commented on her sister’s oath-taking post.

Del Rey’s recent performance was at the music festival at the Formula 1 Singapore Airlines Singapore Grand Prix 2026 last October 11.

Groups such as Akbayan Youth slammed her appointment. Critics said the position requires someone who has credentials and pro-people qualities, since the work entails dealing with informal settlers.

In a briefing on Tuesday, Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said that Canlas was not new in the PCUP.

Canlas has served as the commission’s chief of staff since July 2025.

Before that, she was the first nominee of the Batang Quiapo Party-list during the 2025 midterm elections. Her sister was the sixth nominee.

On October 13 and October 14, Canlas was present as a commissioner in PCUP events.

So what makes this Gen Z, who just graduated two years ago, qualified? Aside from her previous work, no other qualification was cited by the Palace spokesperson during the briefing.

“Ang Pangulo naman po, ito ang laging binabanggit at sinasabi: Anuman ang estado mo sa buhay, mayaman ka, mahirap ka, kung ikaw ay may kakayanan na magtrabaho, magsilbi para sa bayan, iyan po ang numero uno para sa Pangulo — ang totoo at dedikado, may dedikasyon na makapagsilbi sa bayan,” Castro told reporters.

(The President always says this: Whatever your status in life is, whether you are rich or poor, if you have the ability to work and serve the people, that is the most important thing for him — the person who is true and dedicated, the one who has dedication to serve the country.)

Play Video

Formed in 1986, the PCUP serves as a “direct link of the urban poor to the government in policy formulation and program implementation addressed to their needs.”

Its mandate includes conducting consultation with and preparation of informal settler families if they will be affected by development projects, accrediting urban poor groups, and monitoring demolition and eviction.

The PCUP has a chairperson and four commissioners.

For Castro, if one is impartial, it will be easy for them to fulfill their mandate.

“Ang pakikipag-negotiate para sa ating mga kababayan na nasa laylayan ng lipunan, hindi po kailangan [na maging] lawyer. Kailangan lang na may dedikasyon at may puso sa kaniyang trabaho,” Castro explained.

(One does not need to be a lawyer to negotiate with the poorest Filipinos. It only needs dedication and heart for the work.)

Asked whether the Palace is worried about appointing someone who appears to have a lavish lifestyle, Castro just said that Canlas must be given a chance to serve.

“Hindi natin mahuhusgahan ang isang taong hindi pa ninyo nakikita kung paano magtrabaho. Tingnan po muna natin. Kapag nakita ninyong nagkamali at saka po tayo pumuna,” she said.

(We cannot judge a person if we have not seen them working. Let’s check her work first. If we see her committing mistakes, that’s the time we pass criticism.)

Canlas’ new position has a salary of around P2 million per year, or around P173,000 per month, according to the 2027 budget documents. – Rappler.com

World.title: Police attempt to nab journalists at DAR protest: What we know so far
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Quezon City police attempted to nab at least two journalists while others were hurt while they covered a protest in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform’s Central Office on Monday, October 19.

This year’s protest was part of the annual Peasant Month Kampuhan staged by farmers from different regions and progressive groups to amplify their call against land-grabbing, militarization, and the absence of genuine land reform.

Media under attack

At around 12:34 pm, Tudla Productions correspondent Robie Matias, a campus journalist from the Far Eastern University, was hurt after police moved to disperse the camp. Matias accused the police of deliberately stepping on him, the College Editors Guild of the Philippines (CEGP) said in a statement.

Over an hour later, police snatched and destroyed bamboo sticks that were supposed to be used for the farmers’ camp. According to peasant-based network Tanggol Magsasaka, a human rights watchdog, at least 23 peasant advocates were hurt.

At around 5 pm, violence again erupted in front of DAR. Police dragged Bulatlat reporter Aaron Ernest Cruz even as he repeatedly identified himself as a member of the media and showed them his ID.

In circulating videos on social media, at least five cops were seen yanking Cruz away from the protest, causing his shirt to be torn apart. His bag went missing, and police repeatedly elbowed him.

Cruz said that prior to the incident, a commotion started between protesters and authorities. He was backing off when a patrolman grabbed him and his camera, and hit him with a riot shield.

“I immediately showed my press ID and shouting ‘Taga-media ako (I’m from the media).’ The police continuously pulled me in an estimated 20 meters to 40 meters. A paralegal pulled me over away from the police, and that’s the reason why I managed to escape. I already got my medico-legal stating that I [sustained] an injury in my right eyebrow due to their assault,” said Cruz, who also sustained scratches.

“I condemn the police brutality that happened to me and to all media workers that have been harassed, assaulted, and, much worse killed, at the hand of state forces. We deal with these problems when we are just doing our job. The government and its state forces should be accountable for their long-list of records of harassing journalists,” he added in his statement.

Groups condemn attack on media

The CEGP joined Bulatlat in calling on the Commission on Human Rights to investigate the incidents and hold the police accountable for their actions.

The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines also issued a statement, criticizing the PNP. The NUJP questioned the value of the PNP’s revised media relations policy, and reminded the PNP of its commitment under the United Nations Plan of Action on the Safety of Journalists and the Issue of Impunity.

It was not the first time that media got hurt by police during a protest coverage. During the September 21, 2025 riots that followed an anti-corruption protest, police grabbed and hit photojournalist Zedrich Xylak Madrid while he was taking photos in Mendiola.

The Alyansa ng Kabataang Mamamahayag of the PUP where Cruz was a campus journalist also joined in condemning the incident.

QC Mayor Belmonte orders probe

On Tuesday, October 20, Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte ordered an investigation into the confrontation.

“Pinaiimbestigahan na ni Mayor Joy Belmonte ang pangyayari. Gaya ng lagi, ang paniniwala ng Lungsod: Dapat panagutin ang sinuman na mapatutunayang gumamit ng kapangyarihan para manakit, manakot, o humadlang sa mapayapang pagpapahayag. Binigyang-diin ng alkalde ang atas na maximum tolerance dapat ang ipinapatupad ng QCPD,” the city government said in a statement.

(Mayor Joy Belmonte has ordered an investigation into the incident. As a matter of practice, the City believes: Those who are proven to have used their power to hurt, intimidate, or obstruct the peaceful assembly should be held accountable. The mayor also stressed the order of maximum tolerance that should be implemented by the QCPD.)

The city government also said that it has allowed the farmers to continue their “peaceful and orderly” mobilization until noon of Wednesday, October 21.

“ Ang kanilang mga hinaing ay dapat pakinggan at tugunan sa pamamagitan ng dayalogo (Their grievances should be heard and addressed through dialogue),” the city government added.

The city government also met with DAR, the police, and representatives from the farmers’ groups on Tuesday on how to maintain order and ensure safety and cleanliness in the area during protests. – Rappler.com

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.
