World.title: Sabah lose to Borussia Dortmund by a narrow margin – UEFA Champions League (VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. The UEFA Champions League league-phase match between Azerbaijan’s Sabah FC and Germany’s Borussia Dortmund, held in Baku, has come to an end.

The match, played at the Baku Olympic Stadium, ended in a 2–1 victory for the German side.

Serhou Guirassy scored for Borussia Dortmund in the 10th and 53rd minutes, while Aiden McCarthy netted Sabah’s only goal in the 39th minute.

As a result, the Owls suffered their second defeat in the league phase.

In their opening match, Sabah lost 4–0 to English club Manchester United. In their second fixture, they defeated Czech side Slavia Prague 2–0.

Sabah will face Norwegian club Viking in the next round.

World.title: PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry
World.content:
The PNG Chiefs have unveiled the club's inaugural logo ahead of its debut NRL season in 2028.

The club says the striking logo, designed by a team of graphic artists in Papua New Guinea, depicts what makes the Chiefs "strong and what makes us unique".

A supporters' jersey was also unveiled on Wednesday.

The new logo and jersey were described as a defining moment for the new club as it prepares to enter the NRL, based in a nation which is obsessed with rugby league.

PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said the unveiling of the logo marked "one of the most significant milestones in the journey of the PNG Chiefs".

"This is the first time that our club has its true, complete identity — a logo and jersey that our players, partners and fans can hold to as their own," McPherson said.

"The logo of the PNG Chiefs tells a story about Papua New Guinea — our people, what makes us strong and what makes us unique.

"The jersey of the PNG Chiefs is more than what players wear when they take to the field; it is a symbol of belonging, unity and the opportunity to represent millions of Papua New Guineans on the national stage.

"We know the responsibility that comes with establishing this club and we are incredibly proud to show our club to the world today.

"We strive for the PNG Chiefs to be something our country is proud of in every way — not because of the success that we will achieve on the field, but for the opportunities and legacy we will create for our country."

Elements of the PNG Chiefs logo

As per the PNG Chiefs media release

The feather headpiece: Inspired by Papua New Guinea's ceremonial plumes, the five feathers represent strength, beauty, chiefly status and national pride, with the Southern Cross connecting the club to the nation's flag.

The cassowary bone: Inspired by warrior traditions, the cassowary bone symbolises chiefly status, courage, power and the fighting spirit of the team.

The face: The chief's face represents the shape of Papua New Guinea, with ceremonial red paint showing a nation united through one warrior, one team and one purpose.

The kina shells: Representing traditional wealth, trade and prestige across Papua New Guinea's coastal, island and highland communities, the kina symbolises the value, legacy and future the club is building for the nation.

World.title: Snooker player in tears, hugged by presenter, after emotional and raw interview
World.content:
Former world number one snooker player Mark Allen has given an emotional and tearful interview, which involved a hug from the presenter and the admission that he may give up the game.

Allen, 40, took a break from playing after losing a dramatic semifinal in April's World Snooker Championship in April.

The Northern Irishman is understood to have taken time away from the game to deal with private matters, and it has cast doubt over the 40-year-old's future in the sport.

Loading Instagram content

Allen returned to the table for the first time since the world championship semi, where he missed a match-ball black that would have sent him to the decider, with a 4-2 defeat in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open to good friend Jordan Brown.

After the defeat, Allen did an interview with TNT Sports presenter Rachel Casey, where he admitted he was strongly considering throwing away the game he loved.

"I'm in a bad place at the minute, so even just to go out there and try was tough," Allen said.

"I think if I weren't playing Jordan, I wouldn't have come back.

"I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates — I thought that was a better way to sign out."

Asked if he was genuinely considering retirement, the winner of 12 ranking tournaments said it was a real possibility.

"I've been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don't see a future with snooker in it, if I'm honest," he said.

"It's sad to say, because it's all I've loved to do since I was 12, but the last few months has been really difficult, and it's put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute, I'm just trying to survive."

In a touching moment, the interview was paused as Casey gave a clearly distraught Allen a comforting hug.

Allen also gave an interview with BBC Sport NI, where he said he was not prepared to retire now, but he had contemplated it "for a while".

Allen is a former world number one with 12 ranking titles in his career since turning professional in 2005.

He has won his home Northern Ireland Open twice, as well as two of the three Triple Crown events — Masters (2018) and the UK Championship (2022).

Loading Instagram content

Brown, who advances to the final 32 in Belfast with his win, described the match against his friend Allen as " the hardest match I've ever had to deal with".

"I don't even know what to say, I'm lost for words," he told Casey on TNT Sports.

"I've missed him, I love him. Just a great guy, through and through."

World.title: Black beats brown as marketing changes the makeup of Australian cattle herd
World.content:
It may seem like a fickle fashion trend, but as far as the Australian cattle industry is concerned, brown is out and black is in.

Just ask Stephen and Jodi Peake, who, after six decades of breeding Hereford cattle in north-west New South Wales, are selling off their entire herd.

The two have spent years perfecting their stock and genetics, broken weight-gain records with their steers and even once sold a prize bull for more than $60,000.

Stephen and Jodi Peake from the Bowen Pastoral Company based in Gunnedah and Barraba. (ABC New England: Juno Robertson)

But as the Peakes near retirement, they have decided to focus on two of their other breeds: Angus and Wagyu.

"Angus are a worldwide popular breed. They tick a lot of boxes for the end consumer as well as the producer," Mr Peake said.

"Every breed has their day in the sun."

Angus were a minority breed 30 years ago. (Supplied: Stephen and Jodi Peake)

An Angus boom

Hereford cattle were first brought to Australia 200 years ago and have historically dominated its beef industry.

In 1990, farm survey data from the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences showed the breed was the country's most popular, making up just over a quarter of the national herd.

By comparison, Angus cattle were just over 4 per cent.

Fast forward 35 years and the black cattle breed has surged in popularity through savvy marketing, fast-food branding and export markets.

Charles Boog says that, based on available information, Angus beef has become dominant. (Supplied: Charles Boog)

According to a recent Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA) survey, Angus led national herd growth between 2023 and 2025, gaining 1.76 million head.

Market analyst Charles Boog said it was difficult to accurately study long-term breed preferences in Australia because there is no mandate to record cattle breeds at saleyards.

But looking at a "patchwork of information", one thing is clear: Angus has taken the lead.

"As one indicator of current breeding demand, [trade publication] Beef Central recorded 11,328 Angus bulls sold at auction in 2025 compared with 1,780 Herefords," he said.

More money, more marketing

Brad Hine from peak body Angus Australia said the breed's success was partly a marketing story.

The Angus name strengthened in 1995 when the association established guidelines for a verified label.

Beef exports to Japan also grew significantly through the 90s, with the foreign market offering a premium for black cattle.

"Verified Angus Beef" must contain a minimum of 75 per cent Angus-breed content with no dairy characteristics. (Supplied: Stephen and Jodi Peake)

McDonald's premium-branded Angus products, marketed globally from 2009 until June this year, also helped establish the breed as a known commodity.

Dr Hine said sale data from AuctionsPlus showed farmers now made more money per head on Angus cattle.

The nation's Angus herd grew by an estimated 1.76 million head between 2023-2025. (Supplied: Stephen and Jodi Peake)

A mixed cattle future

Herefords Australia chief executive Hamish Chandler said despite a historical departure from the breed, the association's membership numbers have stabilised over the past five years.

He said he was confident the breed would play a critical role into the future, as genetic research improved.

"Over the last two to three years, the number of Hereford cows in the national breeding herd has increased by around 26 per cent," he said.

Hamish Chandler says there is still a role for Herefords. (ABC New England: Juno Robertson)

Agriculture consultant Alastair Rayner said Australia's cattle breed mix would likely stabilise around where it is today, with a possible "increase in tropically infused cattle" in the future.

The MLA survey pointed to a similar trend, with Santa Gertrudis and Droughtmasters the second and third fastest growing herds, respectively.

Both are crossbreeds with European and Indian origins.

Crossbreeds like the Droughtmaster are gaining in popularity. (Supplied: Droughtmaster Australia)

Mr Rayner said unlike in the past, "there's never going to be just one breed" dominating the industry, as different environments call for different types of cattle.

"Rather than choosing a breed and trying to make everything fit, work out what you need and find the breed that best fits you," he said.

World.title: Lawyer tells court Brendan Nugent has rare neurological condition
World.content:
The man accused of driving his vehicle into federal MP Helen Haines outside her electorate office has faced court in Wangaratta, his lawyer saying he suffers from a rare neurological condition.

Brendan Nugent, 43, was flanked by security guards as he was brought into a small courtroom, which was packed with news reporters, shortly after 10am.

The Tarrawingee man is facing charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Mr Nugent was charged last night over the attack on Ms Haines, with witnesses alleging his Toyota LandCruiser repeatedly rammed into the 65-year-old Indi MP.

A police van enters the court precinct in Wangaratta ahead of Brendan Nugent's apperance. (ABC News: Oliver Gordon)

Documents released by the Wangaratta Magistrates Court showed police had laid the extra charges of cultivating cannabis and possessing cannabis.

Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said at a press conference this morning that the investigation was "far from complete" and that police were not ruling out "further serious charges".

Ms Haines remains in a critical but stable condition in hospital and has had one of her legs amputated.

Helen Haines live updates: Get the latest about the attack on the Victorian MP in our blog.

Wearing a grey jumper and black pants, Mr Nugent sat in the court dock flanked by security guards, metres away from police and people in the public gallery.

His lawyer told Magistrate Vaughan his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody.

"My client suffers from idiopathic transverse myelitis. It's a neurological disorder and he's been suffering from concussion," the lawyer said.

The lawyer said Mr Nugent was not currently medicated and it was unclear if he had seen a doctor since his arrest.

The case will next return to the Wangaratta court on February 4 for a committal mention hearing. (ABC News: James Oaten)

There were no concerns about Mr Nugent withdrawing from drugs, the lawyer said.

Idiopathic transverse myelitis is a spinal cord condition, with symptoms that can cause paralysis, numbness and tingling, and sharp pain.

Police not ruling out more charges over MP attack Victoria Police and AFP commissioners say they have not ruled out laying further charges against Brendan Nugent over his alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines.

Further details of the alleged offending were not aired in court.

Magistrate Vaughan said police would complete a brief of evidence by December 24, which will be provided to the defence.

The case will next return to the Wangaratta court on February 4 for a committal mention hearing.

Mr Nugent, who was not required to speak in court or enter a plea, stood when the magistrate addressed him at the end of the hearing.

"I have asked that a medical professional see you immediately," Magistrate Vaughan said.

No application for bail was made.

World.title: One in four people with severe depression may have a dysregulated body clock
World.content:
Sam Hockey's mental health journey stretches across more than two decades.

A diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder and insomnia at age eight, after being trapped in a house fire,and then being "horribly bullied" in high school had a significant impact on his mental health.

"I overslept as a way of escapism but then I would also not wake up rested," he said.

"I had intense low energy, and when it came to school, my cognitive function wasn't great, then didn't have the mental or emotional capacity to really combat the bullying."

Sam Hockey is using his lived experience to help researchers better understand circadian depression. (Supplied: Sam Hockey)

In hindsight, Mr Hockey said these sleep symptoms were the first signs he had circadian depression, a proposed new subtype of the mood disorder from experts at the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre.

A new Australian study, published today in The British Journal of Psychiatry, suggests about one in four people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, like Mr Hockey, have this subtype.

Researchers say the subtype is linked to the body's internal clock and people with it often report being a "night owl" or waking up feeling very tired.

Lead researcher Emiliana Tonini from the Brain and Mind Centre said the findings had implications for early intervention and treatment.

"Depression is not a uniform illness and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," she said.

What is circadian depression?

According to the World Health Organization, about 322 million people globally have depression, a mood disorder which causes persistent sadness, emptiness or loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities.

In this new study, Dr Tonini and her team looked at clinical and genetic data from 11,380 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression who took part in a long-running national depression study.

They found 2,604 people in this group met the criteria for circadian depression as they self-reported three or more of the following:

Waking up very tired

Being a "night owl"

Experiencing a seasonal pattern of illness

Sleeping later

Sleeping more when depressed

Experiencing "social jet lag" where sleep timings vary greatly between work days and free days

Patients with circadian depression also reported "more severe mental health symptoms" than those with non-circadian depression, Dr Tonini said.

This included an earlier age of onset, more severe symptoms like mania, suicidality, weight gain during mental health episodes and more complex mental health trajectories.

The research also suggests people with circadian depression may have a different genetic profile to those with non-circadian depression, including a higher genetic risk for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Ian Hickie (left) and Emiliana Tonini suggest circadian depression is linked to the body’s 24-hour internal clock. (Supplied: University of Sydney)

Philip Mitchell, scientia professor of psychiatry at the University of New South Wales who did not contribute to the research, said more research was needed before circadian depression could be classified as its own subtype.

"At the moment it's not reaching the bar where this could enter clinical practice, but I think this is very thought-provoking for the field," he said.

Professor Mitchell said there was overlap between the features of circadian depression and a recognised subtype called atypical depression, which indicated the need for a clearer distinction between the two.

And he added that more international research was needed to support the Australian findings.

How is sleep and depression connected?

The study suggests circadian depression is linked to the body's 24-hour internal clock which regulates the sleep-wake cycle.

Brain and Mind Centre co-director and clinical psychiatrist Ian Hickie said this internal clock underpinned "your mood, your metabolism, your concentration, your sleep-wake cycle and many other key factors as well".

Professor Hickie said light exposure, movement and eating patterns were important to help regulate the body's 24-hour internal clock, or circadian rhythm.

"It isn't just sleep, it's not just about sleeping better," he said.

Most of the people identified by researchers as having circadian depression were women. (Getty Images: Gravity Images)

Shanthakumar Wilson Rajaratnam, professor of sleep and circadian medicine at Monash University who did not contribute to the study, said a dysregulated circadian system could impact a range of different body systems, including cardiovascular function.

Criteria used to define circadian depression, such as being a "night owl" or waking up very tired, might not solely be driven by circadian dysfunction, he said.

Professor Rajaratnam said symptoms that might explain circadian dysfunction could also be explained by disturbed sleep.

"Symptoms and sleep complaints have a high degree of comorbidity and overlap with depression and mood disturbances," he said.

What does this mean for treatment?

According to this study, patients with circadian depression may be less responsive to traditional antidepressants.

However, Dr Tonini said this finding came from self-reported data, which meant more research was needed to test the efficacy of traditional antidepressants in this proposed subgroup.

She said targeted treatments —such as melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants, light therapy and behavioural changes —may improve outcomes for patients with circadian depression.

Circadian depression is not currently listed as a standalone diagnosis in the US's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders which is used as a handbook for diagnosis globally. (Unsplash: christopher lemercier)

More than two decades after his first mental health diagnosis, things have greatly improved for Mr Hockey.

As a youth lived-experience researcher with the Brain and Mind Centre, he was one of the co-authors on the new study.

He said that understanding more about his 24-hour internal clock earlier in life would have saved "a lot of grief, a lot of trouble, a lot of money, and hardship".

But learning about circadian patterns and making behavioural changes, such as putting his bedside light on a timer, had helped him regulate his body clock.

Professor Mitchell and Professor Rajaratnam agreed that there was enough evidence in this study to warrant asking patients with depression about their circadian patterns.

But this was in addition to, not instead of, traditional treatment options.

"It's important to address the sleep and circadian complaints in patients that are presenting with psychiatric disorders, including depression, as well as treating the depression symptoms," Professor Rajaratnam said.

World.title: Councillor who told woman it was a 'pity' she wasn't bashed won't resign
World.content:
A Mid North Coast councillor is refusing to resign after an investigation found he made a violent comment to a woman online.

Noel Selby said he would not be stepping down but would consider attending a men's behavioural-change program after his peers unanimously called for his resignation.

A decision on how to discipline the Kempsey Shire councillor was reached after more than an hour of confidential discussion about an independent investigator's report which found that Cr Selby posted a comment to a woman raising domestic violence concerns saying it was a "pity he hadn't bashed you".

Cr Selby declined to comment after the proceedings but shared a written statement and told the ABC he would not resign.

"I stand by my original statement that my FB page was hacked!" it read.

"I am against all acts of domestic violence."

Cr Noel Selby (centre) and Kempsey Shire Council CEO Andrew Meddle (right). (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

Cr Selby said in his statement that he had "never abused any woman in my 75 years" and had worked with several local community groups, including the Country Women's Association and Rotary.

"My reason for wanting to be on council in the first place was to try and make Kempsey Shire a better place for everybody to live in," he said.

"That's what I intend to do in the future, because that's what I was voted in for."

Community 'rightfully outraged'

This week's meeting came after the Kemspey Shire Council engaged business management consultancy group Centium to investigate complaints made about a post that appeared to come from Cr Selby's personal Facebook account.

Kempsey Mayor Kinne Ring told the ABC after the meeting that the investigator's recommendation of a censure — a formal reprimand from council condemning the behaviour — did not go far enough.

"We can't make Cr Selby resign, but we can request that he resign," she said.

"Ultimately, council decided to not only censure him but also request that he resign and that we recommend he engage in a men's behavioural-change program.

"We could have just censured him, but we don't think that really matched the severity of what Cr Selby had done and we really considered this a serious matter."

Mayor Kinne Ring condemns Cr Noel Selby's behaviour. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

Cr Ring said the community was "rightfully outraged" by Cr Selby's comment, noting the prevalence of domestic violence in the region.

She said the matter had cost council more than $40,000 in lost time and resources.

"As a woman, as a 31-year-old female with sisters, with nieces, with my own mother, I don't condone violence against women or violence in any form," Cr Ring said.

" It's been a really challenging investigation for me, to not be able to make my feelings clear. "

Cr Ring acknowledged community concerns that the council had not taken a firm enough position when the allegation was first raised, but said the right outcome had been reached and procedures followed.

The matter will now be referred to the Office of Local Government for further consideration, which could lead to Cr Selby's disqualification as a councillor.

Deputy Mayor Arthur Bain said councillors had taken the strongest stance possible under current legislation, after being "inundated with concerns".

Arthur Bain says councillors have unanimously supported the motion. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

"I hope we're sending a very, very clear message to the community we don't condone violence, or threats or intimidation, particularly to women," he said.

June Wilson, the executive officer of domestic violence service Kempsey Families, said while she welcomed the council's decision, she did not believe Cr Selby had taken accountability for his actions.

"We do need to know that sort of behaviour can't be tolerated by anyone, particularly in a position of privilege and a fair degree of power," Ms Wilson said.

June Wilson says she doesn't believe Cr Noel Selby has taken accountability for his actions. (Supplied: June Wilson)

" I think the message is very clear, but I still have concerns about the outcomes. "

Ms Wilson said men's behavioural-change programs involved "deeply reflective" and "profound" personal work and often intensive case management to understand the impact of words and behaviour.

"If someone is not willing to hold themselves to account, men's behaviour change is a complete waste of time," she said.

"The appropriate thing to do would be to acknowledge that you've made an error, however that happened, and just step out of the limelight and retire or resign."

World.title: Police not ruling out further serious charges over Helen Haines attack
World.content:
Further serious charges may be laid against a Victorian man over his alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines on Monday.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Ms Haines, 65, remains in hospital in a critical but stable condition.

Victoria Police and the Australian Federal Police (AFP) told a press conference this morning they have not ruled out laying further charges, including attempted murder.

Helen Haines live updates: Get the latest about the attack on the Victorian MP in our blog.

"While I say this investigation is far from complete, we are not ruling out further serious charges," Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said.

"I want to further add that we have deployed a number of staff into Wangaratta to give assurance to members of the public.

"We do believe this was a deliberate but isolated act."

Chief Commissioner Bush said there were no "intelligence holdings" against Mr Nugent and police had no information to suggest he was an "immediate threat".

Helen Haines remains in a critical but stable condition in hospital. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Details of Mr Nugent's previous brushes with the law have emerged since he was arrested on Monday.

He was charged with breaching an interim personal safety intervention order in July 2022 at Tarrawingee, where he lives.

The case went to the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court.

Court records show the charges were dismissed in December, 2022 and the matter was finalised.

Brendan Nugent is facing three charges over the alleged attack on Helen Haines. (X)

Mr Nugent appears to be a long-time resident in Ms Haines's electorate.

In a statement yesterday, Mr Nugent's family said they were long-time friends of Ms Haines.

"Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable," father Rod Nugent and Rod's partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.

"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."

ABC Verify revealed that Mr Nugent posted to social media regularly for more than a decade about the environment and politics.

A neighbour told the ABC that they had called the police on him numerous times, and sources have confirmed that he has undergone a mental health assessment following the alleged attack.

Chief Commissioner Bush said police would investigate whether the 43-year-old was involved in the sovereign citizen movement or whether the attack was personal.

"His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," he said.

"That's obviously something we're exploring.

"We haven't had any direct evidence of that … But we're not ruling it out."

Two police officers were killed in nearby Porepunkah in August last year by self-proclaimed "sovereign citizen" Dezi Freeman.

Chief Commissioner Bush said Ms Haines had been a huge support to local officers and the community during that time.

"She gave wonderful support to local police, and I know that my colleagues there absolutely appreciate what she did and continues to do for them," he said.

Local officers swiftly attended the scene at Wangaratta on Monday, Chief Commissioner Bush said.

"Our officers in Wangaratta arrived on that traumatic scene within seconds, in fact I think it was 8 seconds," he said.

"Their actions prevented further serious harm to Helen."

Ms Haines lost a leg following the incident and surgeons at Melbourne's Alfred Hospital are still fighting to save her other leg.

People were seen sobbing outside a church in Wangaratta after a vigil for Helen Haines on Tuesday. (ABC News: Nate Woodall)

Unlawful behaviour towards MPs increasing

AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said authorities had been seeing an increase in unlawful behaviour towards parliamentarians, with "almost one individual every week" charged for targeting Commonwealth officials.

"I hope that this terrible event — that will forever change the life of the member for Indi and her family — gives our country time to pause and reflect on the growing threats and unlawful behaviour against those who hold a Commonwealth office in Australia," she said.

Victoria Police said it would leverage its state command and coordination centre to ensure it was across further political threats.

"Especially leading up to the election, against any politicians in this state, to make sure there is a centralised place of reporting, a place where we can proactively search for any threats and ensure that we act quickly and we act proactively," Chief Commissioner Bush said.

World.title: Only a handful of wigmakers exist in Australia — meet one of them
World.content:
With a needle and strands of human hair, professional wigmaker Rebecca Bank can transform a dancer into a nefarious villain or an elegant aristocrat.

As West Australian Ballet's head of wigs and makeup, she is one of a small handful of people in the state who make wigs for shows for a living.

"It is a very niche job, so a lot of the time people don't really know what I do in a day," Ms Bank said.

"There's not an awful lot of us around."

Wigmaker Rebecca Bank describes her job as "very niche". (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

With hair, moustaches and goatees, she transforms, ages and defines dancers on the stage.

"It is often very in the background, but can be a very important part to get the era right and the feel of the show right — especially in live theatre with quick changes," Ms Bank said.

"If you do it well, people don't know there's a wig on."

Wigs are handcrafted for the WA Ballet and can take weeks to complete. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

The process involves speaking with the designer, taking a mould from the dancer's head, padding that with cork and netting it before the knotting process begins.

It can take weeks to complete a wig.

Some of the many wigs crafted for the WA Ballet. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

"We have to sit in quite a specific position to see the very small mesh to get the hair in," Ms Bank said.

"It can be quite challenging on the body to sit for eight hours straight knotting."

Expensive headpieces

Most of the wigs are made from human hair, which makes the price of each headpiece about $5,000.

Unlike those creating wigs for film, Ms Bank has the added challenge to quickly swap the wigs on dancers within less than two minutes off-stage.

Wigmakers use a variety of tools to make their creations. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

"The main thing for us is the dancers do have to feel confident when they're on stage, so they can't feel like the wig is loose in any way."

"Security for them is such an important thing."

Growing up with a love of ballet and theatre, she was drawn to the craft and studied in Germany.

Ms Bank says there were far fewer opportunities to learn the skills in Australia, but she hopes that will start to change with the help of a course launched in WA this year.

Learning the craft

Since February, a class of 18 young creatives looking to enter the theatre, film and TV industries have been learning the basics of wig making, costume, special effects and makeup at Perth's North Metropolitan TAFE.

From constructing 18th century wigs and yak-hair made moustaches to synthetic pieces, the students learn a variety of techniques.

Students at Perth's North Metropolitan TAFE learn a variety of wig making and costume techniques. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Hair and wig lecturer Delia Stanley said the course was important to allow young wigmakers to continue to work in WA.

"Now we've got the [Perth] film studios, we've got lots more opportunities in WA," Ms Stanley said.

"Rather than getting people from over east, I think it's a great thing that people are getting trained in our own state and that you know they're going to have those opportunities now."

Rebecca Bank puts the finishing touches to a wig as she fits it to a dancer. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

The passionate wigmaker and period hair stylist is delighted by the pieces the students have made.

"It's such a joy to be able to pass those skills on to other people as well and know that there's this new generation coming through," Ms Stanley said.

World.title: ‘Checkmate’: Russia is winning the war as Ukraine runs out of friends
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Checkmate’: Russia is winning the war as Ukraine runs out of friends Catherine Belton October 21, 2026 — 11:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Kremlin is counting the Trump administration’s latest turn against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as a major triumph and, coupled with political upheaval in Europe, a sign that Western support for Ukraine is finally crumbling. In the 10 days since Vladimir Putin last spoke by telephone with the American president, Donald Trump has announced a sanctions waiver for Russian diesel supplies to the global market, throttled Ukraine’s access to vital battlefield satellite systems, put sweeping new sanctions against Russian on hold, as well as moved even more firmly to Russia’s side by calling for Zelensky’s ouster and holding up supplies of critical interceptor missiles. Vladimir Putin is counting on Donald Trump’s latest turn against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Fairfax Media On Monday, Trump blasted the Ukrainian president again, saying it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine”. The stakes seem higher than ever. Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is set to travel to Oslo this week to meet Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is expected participate via video link.



“The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path,” Store said. Zelensky said on Sunday that if Washington aligned with Russia, Ukraine would not survive. “If the United States will support Putin – it’s unbelievable, it’s a tragedy,” he told NBC News’ Meet the Press on Sunday. “If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand.” Loading While the European leaders and Zelensky might hope to use the Oslo meeting to steer the Trump administration to a tougher stance against Moscow, Kremlin officials have been crowing that victory over Ukraine is on the horizon, and that Trump’s recent moves are steps toward an ever closer alignment between Washington and Moscow.



Trump’s recent ratcheting up of pressure on Zelensky could mean the US president is again seeking to strong-arm the Ukrainian leader into a deal on terms favourable to Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Witkoff is expected to brief Putin following the Oslo talks. Related Article Opinion

Aviation Starlink’s growing influence has one big point of failure Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation Earlier, Peskov said Ukraine’s recent resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries – in defiance of Trump’s demands – showed Zelensky’s administration in its death throes. “Some final signs of agony are being observed,” Peskov said. “The Kyiv regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events.”



“Checkmate,” Kremlin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted triumphantly. In Moscow, members of the Russian elite said that Putin, a former KGB officer, once again managed to turn the US president. Putin has decades of experience charming and manipulating foreign leaders, and has demonstrated a consistent ability to flatter Trump and pull him on side, analysts and officials said. This time, they said, the Russian leader preyed on Trump’s fears over low approval ratings and sky-high energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections, offering a deal on Russian diesel fuel that will supply just a fraction of America’s daily consumption and have no impact on prices. On Friday, the average US diesel price continued to climb to $US6.33 per gallon, an increase of about 5 cents per gallon from the previous week.



“Russia’s leaders have achieved a certain political victory,” said a Russian academic close to senior Russian diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy. “All this happened after their telephone call. Probably Putin was able to convince Trump.” Putin, the academic added, “probably conducted this conversation very professionally and prepared his arguments well”. Local residents remove debris from a heavily damaged house as smoke rises from a destroyed warehouse, in the background, after Russian drone attacks on the outskirt of Kyiv, Ukraine. AP Mikhail Khodorkovsky, once Russia’s richest man and now an opposition leader in exile, said recent events followed a pattern in Putin’s relations with Trump. “I am absolutely convinced that they believe that they managed to take advantage, as they always do; they are opportunists,” Khodorkovsky said. “In this case, they believe they have waited for the moment of Trump’s additional weakness and [taken] advantage of it.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Total war’: The human face of the assault on Ukraine “For Putin, everything that is happening today are signs of the West’s weakness.” Dmitriev, the special envoy, and other Russian officials hailed the diesel deal and Trump’s waiving of tough sanctions that were to be imposed under a bill adopted in honour of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a firm GOP supporter of Ukraine, as steps toward broader Russia-US economic cooperation. Historically, Russia and the US have never been big economic partners, with Russia exporting little of interest to the US market. “There is a whole range of economic and investment projects being discussed with the American side that will be implemented,” Dmitriev told a Russian energy forum last week. “Our list of projects being discussed with the American side also includes various projects in the Arctic, energy projects, LNG [liquefied natural gas] projects and other areas.”



“More and more Americans, including within the administration, understand that sanctions harm the United States itself,” he added. In July – after years of Putin refusing to drop his maximalist demands in Ukraine – Trump finally seemed to side with Zelensky, telling reporters he was doing “an amazing job” and even backing Ukraine’s deep strikes on Russian oil refineries. Ukraine is expendable on strategic grounds, in Trump’s view, and it was standing in the way of a perfectly good campaign talking point. Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for Europe. “It’s an escalation, but it’s also an escalation that can help lead to an end” of the war, Trump said. But as the US conflict with Iran dragged on, keeping upward pressure on global oil prices, and as the midterm elections drew ever nearer, the Trump administration suddenly turned again.



After an August 31 meeting with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a Group of 20 (G20) event in Asheville, North Carolina, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries as the reason for surging fuel prices – rather than the war in Iran. It was then easy for Putin to recruit Trump into sharing that viewpoint, some observers said. Loading “The simplest explanation is that Trump was simply interested in having a talking point for the midterms on diesel, that he has a deal to lower it,” said Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for Europe during George W. Bush’s administration. “I think it is just Trump lashing out because he’s feeling cornered and unhappy with the midterms, and Zelensky stood in his way,” Fried said, especially after Zelensky publicly derided Trump as “weak” after he announced the diesel deal.



“Trump then extended his frustration to add pressure and try to force a settlement based on a great power deal with Putin, who is skilled at playing his more gullible interlocutors,” he said. That Trump and Putin share a view that strongmen should dominate a world divided into spheres of influence made it even easier for Putin, Fried added. Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump share a view that strongmen should dominate a world. AP “Trump appears to have been attracted to this view for decades,” he said. “And therefore, Ukraine is expendable on strategic grounds, in Trump’s view, and it was standing in the way of a perfectly good campaign talking point.” Trump’s latest swing toward Putin was hardly surprising, said a former senior US intelligence official.



“It almost doesn’t matter what he says, because Trump just seems like he’s very eager. He’s a very receptive audience,” the former intelligence official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. “If you look at the longer-term trends, he has clearly a preference for Putin over Zelensky, and that transcends any kind of temporary relaxation of the tensions that he has with Zelensky.” “He likes strong authoritarian leaders,” the official said. “And deep down, there is this underlying belief on his part that Ukraine cannot win this war, that Russia is bigger, Russia is stronger, Russia is going to crush Ukraine if that’s what it takes.” Related Article US midterms Long lines, late nights, adulation: What it’s really like inside Trump’s midterm election rallies Signs point to Trump seeking to strong-arm Ukraine into a deal by December, when Trump has invited Putin to join him at the G20 leaders’ summit in Miami, said Andrew Weiss, a Russian expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.



“The only way I can explain it is that it’s connected to the milestones leading up to the meeting of the G20 in December,” Weiss said. “I feel like what’s going on here is not really about diesel or refinery long-range strikes. It’s really about Trump thinking that he can push the Ukrainians into some sort of political settlement.” The Russians have “tried to use the administration as a battering ram to get the Ukrainians to surrender Donbas,” Weiss said, referring to the swatch of eastern Ukraine coveted by Putin. “But then that only opens up a subsequent conversation about constraints on Ukrainian military capabilities” he added, or other underlying Russian demands. “The administration has repeatedly misdiagnosed what the Russians want, and the Russians don’t make that easy because they don’t say exactly what they want.” Washington Post Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Cheaper rent, brightest minds: Why Melbourne is about to become Australia’s boom city
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAustralian economy Opinion Cheaper rent, brightest minds: Why Melbourne is about to become Australia’s boom city Aruna Sathanapally Grattan Institute CEO October 21, 2026 — 11:44am

October 21, 2026 — 11:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Another day, another bleak assessment of the state of Victoria, and its capital, Melbourne. Since the pandemic, it has been hard to avoid them. Even walking around the city centre has been a reminder of vibrancy lost. For the city hardest hit by the pandemic, the road back is a long one. Melbourne is building again towards a new cultural and economic boom. Wayne Taylor This is clearest in the state’s finances. All budgets (save Western Australia’s) are under pressure. But Victoria has gone from a relatively rich state to a relatively poor state, ahead of only Tasmania and South Australia. And with healthcare spending on the rise, infrastructure investment still at record levels, and the threat of a difficult bushfire season ahead, budget pressures aren’t likely to ease any time soon. But that is not the full story of Melbourne’s fortunes: the city could be on the cusp of an economic renewal.



Melbourne has long held a strong position in the battle of Australian cities when it comes to quality of life. It has consistently ranked as Australia’s most liveable city, and during much of the 2010s as the most liveable in the world. This year it was voted Time Out’s best city worldwide. Culture, sports, food, trams, and green spaces have made Melbourne marvellous. But right now, the real ace Melbourne has up its sleeve is its housing market. The view of Melbourne’s CBD along the Yarra. Joe Armao The steep – and damaging – climb in the cost of housing seen across Australia since the pandemic has not hit every city evenly. Today, median rents in Melbourne are the second lowest among capitals cities, after only Hobart. In fact, median rents for houses are the lowest of all capital cities. This makes a material difference to the cost of living for Melburnians. And it is particularly important for young people, and those in the early stages of their careers. In Melbourne, median rents for newly advertised dwellings are around 40 per cent of the median full-time wages of those aged 25-34. This is the lowest of any capital city. In Sydney, median rent chews up half of the equivalent median wage.



Not only does your wage go further in Melbourne, but affordable housing – particularly homes for rent – is a vital support to a healthy labour market. It supports mobility and allows people to take a chance and try new things. If you are a young professional looking to build your career, say in a national firm, there are very good reasons to take a job in the Melbourne office. Liveability and affordability in the one place. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent If you are an employer in Melbourne, the wage pressures you face at each salary review are not as acute as Sydney, Brisbane or Perth. If you are creative, or a freelancer, you will have a better shot building your base out of Melbourne. And the more skilled, creative or otherwise entrepreneurial people move to Melbourne, the more the city benefits from “agglomeration”, reaching a critical mass where networks form and exciting things happen. This has happened in cities down on their luck before: Montreal in the late 1990s, setting the stage for the creative boom in the early 2000s. Austin, Texas, is another recent example. It’s hard to disentangle how much of weaker house price growth in Melbourne is down to supply growth, a weaker economy or reforms to land taxes. But when it comes to slower growth in rents relative to incomes, the picture is clearer: in Melbourne there has been a steadier supply of housing to meet demands of population growth and smaller households.



Of course, even in Melbourne, housing costs are still punishingly high in many of the city’s most desirable areas. But Victoria’s land use planning reforms are changing that. These reforms are more substantial than those in NSW, and well ahead of Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth where restrictive low-density zones still cover most residential land. The Grattan Institute estimated last year that Victoria’s reforms will increase zoned capacity equivalent to 70 per cent of the existing housing stock, compared with 40 per cent for NSW. This arises predominantly from the state’s new “Townhouse Code”, but also the much-publicised Activity Centre Program; both examples of measures to boost gentle and medium density in the places people most want to live, and close to jobs. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly None of this is cause for complacency: the Victorian government needs to stay the course on reforms to allow more homes in the places Melburnians want to live. Construction productivity desperately needs a shot in the arm. Nor is it only about housing – you also need good transport networks, effective measures to bust congestion, and planning that makes the most of existing infrastructure rather than enabling more sprawl. Institutions like top-tier universities and globally leading firms also play a key role in agglomeration of knowledge workers and innovators, particularly through attracting the world’s best and brightest here. Melbourne’s story is still being written. And a commitment to remaining the most affordable city to rent in Australia will make it even more marvellous.



Dr Aruna Sathanapally is chief executive of the Grattan Institute. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Power protests light fuse on $2 billion data centre implosion, as NextDC shares plummet
World.content:
PoliticsFederalInvestigations Power protests light fuse on $2 billion data centre implosion, as NextDC shares plummet Clay Lucas October 21, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. What began as a community protest in Melbourne’s inner west over enormous electricity poles being installed on narrow residential streets has now rocked the nation’s highest-profile data centre developer, as it scrambles to find a new way to supply energy to its flagship centre. On Wednesday, ASX-listed NextDC told investors it would slash its expected profits and construction spending as it dealt with delays in supplying energy to its M3 centre in West Footscray, triggering a share price plummet. NextDC’s M3 data centre in West Footscray. Joe Armao NextDC came out of a two-day trading halt on Wednesday warning investors that the final stages of the politically contentious development would also not be approved until after next month’s state election. The delays are the result of a community blockade in September, revealed by this masthead, against electricity distributor Jemena’s rollout of 15-metre tall 66,000-volt residential power poles. The protests prompted Jemena to halt construction until at least February.



The delays have left NextDC saying it now lacks the extra grid capacity needed to power its expanding data halls at West Footscray. The market reaction against the data centre developer was sharp: NextDC shares collapsed to $5.46 on Wednesday, down more than 40 per cent from their Monday closing price of $9.57. The crash wiped billions off the company’s valuation, driving its stock to its lowest point since 2019 – a far cry from its peak of $17.22 a year ago. Jemena power lines in a Yarraville residential street, with the NextDC data centre in the background (left). Joe Armao NextDC on Wednesday also revealed it was putting the brakes on its wider construction pipeline, in a move which could alarm state and federal governments as data centre construction is one of the few bright spots in the sluggish Australian economy. NextDC slashed its construction budget for the coming financial year from up to $5.75 billion to between $4.5 billion and $5 billion, pausing developments without client contract commitments. Previously, the company had built new data centres without having tenants contracted to go into them.



NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said the company had paused expectations from its West Footscray project, and would halt speculative expansion projects and land buys not already locked in by paying clients. “With [West Footscray] revenue deferred, we have paused projects not backed by customer contracts and put that capital behind the capacity our customers have already contracted,” he said. Yarraville resident Milco Bogoevski was among those who led the community protest to stop Jemena installing its enormous power poles in his residential street. He said while he was sympathetic to data centre operators – “No one here wants to see industry fail; we want industry to succeed” – what had happened was the direct result of power companies and business not listening to the community.



“These power lines, this material, it was going to be in our street, we were going to have to deal with it for decades after they left – power operators like Jemena, and [businesses like NextDC], they’re going to need to engage more with the community.” Bogoevski said the community opposition to the enormous West Footscray data centre and the impact of other data centres in Melbourne’s inner west could help swing seats in the November 28 election. A sign in Sanderson Street, Yarraville, on Tuesday. Jason South “The state government is responsible for power – it comes down to them. There is a good chance that an issue like this could flip this seat away from Labor; we’ve got a couple of issues like this that Labor hasn’t paid attention to,” he said. NextDC’s market shock represents the clearest evidence yet that Victoria’s rapid push to attract power-hungry artificial intelligence infrastructure has run into severe grid constraints and suburban backlash.



The M3 facility in West Footscray is designed to eventually span 10 hectares in an industrial pocket adjacent to residential homes. The site already occupies five hectares and was undergoing a $750 million expansion. However, feeding the expanding site required Jemena to replace standard wooden electricity poles with 15-metre concrete poles carrying 66,000 volts along residential streets in West Footscray and neighbouring Yarraville. A typical residential power pole carries about 400 volts. A Maribyrnong City Council spokeswoman noted that some poles in the rollout rise as high as 22 metres, which is equivalent to seven storeys.



The rollout ground to a halt in Yarraville last month following direct action by residents, who blockaded contractor trucks with parked cars, ignored door-knocks and filled excavation pits to stop high-voltage lines reaching the NextDC site. Jemena bowed to pressure and paused work to consult further, leaving the high-capacity route unfinished. Related Article Data centres Labor facing internal revolt over data centre spree NextDC said a state a planning permit decision for its next stages of its West Footscray project had also been delayed. With the Victorian government entering caretaker mode on November 3 ahead of the election, a planning decision for the site is now not expected until 2027. The mounting political and community friction creates a growing challenge for the election. As premier, Jacinta Allan and her then-economic development minister Danny Pearson aggressively courted hyperscale data operators, using fast-tracked planning schemes to bypass municipal councils and grant approvals in as little as 28 days.



Data centres consume about 2 per cent of national grid power, but the Australian Energy Market Operator has forecast that share could rise to 9 per cent by 2035 as AI adoption accelerates. To address growing concerns, Premier Ben Carroll last month introduced new rules requiring data centre developers to supply their own renewable energy, use recycled water, and maintain a minimum 150-metre buffer from homes. Community pushback is now hitting projects nationwide. Developer Green Square was recently forced to pull a proposed project in Western Australia, Goodman Group shelved a $1.2 billion facility in the Sydney suburb of Lane Cove, and private developer Firmus was forced to abandon a planned $44 billion stock market float. World.title: I protected politicians and presidents. It used to be easier to tell who the bad guy was
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Opinion I protected politicians and presidents. It used to be easier to tell who the bad guy was Rob Albert Former police close personal protection officer October 21, 2026 — 11:30am

October 21, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of my first jobs when I joined the NSW Police Protection Operations Unit was to provide a security escort to then prime minister John Howard through the Sydney CBD. A young man spotted the “C1” number plates and the little Australian flag fluttering as the PM’s white saloon car rolled by. So he ran up to the window, stuck up his middle finger, shouted a few expletives and stood down. A very minor incident, but I point it out because Australians have always had the larrikin tendency to feel they have the right not only to tell their mates what they think of them and where to go but also their elected representatives – in this case Australia’s 25th prime minister in 2005. Rob Albert has protected everyone from politicians to presidents, with some royalty thrown in. Marija Ercegovac Fast-forward two decades and things are radically different. I am deeply saddened by the attack on Helen Haines and wish her a full recovery, although I wonder if it’s possible to fully recover from an attack such as this – physically or psychologically.



But what about politically? Things are different. People are polarised. There’s anger at a level beyond a middle finger at a consulate car window. Many are stressed personally, financially and, regrettably, sometimes those with strong emotional connections to an ideology react violently towards those who don’t agree with them. Rob Albert protecting William and Kate on a royal visit to Sydney. Keeping our politicians safe has never been harder for police. At Counter Terrorism Command we always figured an attack could come at any time, from anywhere and from anyone. The result of a spontaneous decision or a finely tuned, pre-planned event. What’s changed is that anything is a weapon now. We used to think of weapons as firearms we had a register for, but now a Toyota Land Cruiser or any vehicle can inflict as much if not more damage than a gun. And in a rural area on a suburban street where politicians like Haines would have prided themselves on informal links to the communities they served, well, the basic security measures are fewer and further between.



I’ve provided close personal protection over the years to presidents, kings and queens, prime ministers, premiers, as well as various members of the military or spy agencies from Australia and abroad. Related Article Updated

Haines attack Suspect in Haines attack clashed with neighbours as his health unravelled Many of those people I admired and respected, and would willingly have risked my life to protect them in the office they held. I also looked after people for whom I had, let’s just say, less respect for and with whom I strongly disagreed politically, but I still would have risked my life to protect them. That was the job I signed up for. The question I ask myself and I ask the nation is how have we become a country where an everyday person would seek to attack, maim or kill another person they disagree with when I was willing to lay down my life for someone I disliked? When I escorted that car carrying Howard through Sydney in 2005, sure, people were divided on many topics. People disagreed. But the right and the left didn’t seem as deeply entrenched and diametrically opposed as they are now and any attack we anticipated came more from organised terror or crime groups rather than “Joe Citizen” who’d been blowing up on social media.



The indoctrination or radicalisation of people, whether it be through educational institutions, clubs, online through the dark web or through social media platforms has generated a subculture of people who are unable to live peacefully with others who might disagree with them or think differently. Their response to this conditioning is too often violent or hostile, heightening the threat and risk to high office holders. Rob Albert protecting William and Kate in Sydney. It used to be easier to tell who the bad guy was. Crime wore a balaclava and carried a gun, it didn’t dress in civvies in broad daylight while driving down the main street of Wangaratta. What’s the solution? It would be impossible and impractical to provide protection for every politician. Budget restraints, manpower, intelligence, surveillance … there is too much to do at too big a cost.



Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing My view from the news chair: the worst of the mob is coming for us Hugh Riminton Journalist and author Haines. Bondi. Whatever else is happening or about to happen in Australia, how do we stop it from happening or, worse still, becoming a common occurrence? It must start from the top, so my first appeal is to those leaders I would have “taken a bullet for”. Everyone I talk to has one common complaint – people no longer feel heard. People no longer feel cared about. People no longer feel safe, and it’s driving many of them to more radical solutions, radical politics and radical actions. So don’t play politics like a game because its consequences flow on to us. Bipartisan approaches may be required on some occasions. Rise above political point scoring and come together on the big issues for the sake of the country, the sake of its people, and the sake of Helen Haines. If all we see is you disagreeing, all we will do is disagree.



My second appeal is to the people of Australia. Maintain the larrikin! Debate. Disagree. But violence is never an option. Its consequences are catastrophic and rather than changing what you want it to change, history shows it usually has the opposite effect. Rob Albert is a former NSW Police close personal protection officer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Elon Musk’s $5 trillion monster: Tesla and SpaceX exploring the biggest merger in history
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions Elon Musk’s $5 trillion monster: Tesla and SpaceX exploring the biggest merger in history Richard Clough and Ed Ludlow Updated October 21, 2026 — 11:26am ,first published October 21, 2026 — 9:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, a preliminary step toward what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time. Musk has in the past tantalised shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive officer of both companies, said on SpaceX’s earnings webcast. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” Elon Musk says that a merger isn’t certain and would require shareholder support. AP Photo/Matt Rourke Musk said he isn’t participating in the committee discussions because he is a conflicted party, and that the committees have yet to agree on terms.



A blockbuster deal would unite Tesla’s electric vehicle, energy and robotics businesses with SpaceX’s rocket launch and satellite internet operations. Underpinning it all are the companies’ shared ambitions in artificial intelligence — or what some in the industry are now calling superintelligence — fuelling investments in areas such as data centres and driverless cars. SpaceX shares surged 8.1 per cent in post-market trading after reporting robust quarterly results, while Tesla climbed 1.8 per cent. Tesla is scheduled to release its third-quarter results on Thursday morning (AEDT). Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The scope of a potential merger is staggering, with both SpaceX and Tesla among the largest companies in the world and holding dominant positions in their respective industries. SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, has a market value of about $US2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly $US1.5 trillion. SpaceX and Tesla already have numerous business ties, overlapping investor bases and even some shared personnel. The rocket maker has purchased more than $US100 million worth of Tesla Cybertrucks, while xAI is a major customer of Tesla’s utility-scale batteries.



A combination has been widely expected since SpaceX rode a wave of investor enthusiasm to a record initial public offering this year, giving the company both currency and an implicit green light from shareholders to make a play for Tesla, making Musk the world’s first trillionaire. Bloomberg News reported in January that SpaceX had weighed a Tesla merger before ultimately deciding to acquire xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence startup. Musk cautioned that a merger isn’t certain and would require shareholder support. He said Tesla would need approval from 50 per cent of all shareholders, rather than simply a majority of those voting. “I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said. SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, has a market value of about $US2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly $US1.5 trillion. Bloomberg “Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty. I think that would be overstating it.”



SpaceX earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said it was tracking an annual revenue run rate of up to $US1 trillion. SpaceX’s revenue climbed 161 per cent to $US14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $US7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-centre capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Reflection AI rather than from its own models. Related Article Opinion

Future technology Why Elon Musk’s new Roadster will fly off the shelves Michelle Cazzulino Writer “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity and superintelligence,” Musk said on the call. He ended his portion of prepared remarks with a seemingly off-script remark: “In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of ’27 is somewhere between $US500 billion and a trillion.” The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous — capital expenses nearly tripled.

World.title: Is it a bus? Is it a Metro? Brisbane will investigate small Metro vehicles
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandBrisbane Metro Is it a bus? Is it a Metro? Brisbane will investigate small Metro vehicles Felicity Caldwell October 21, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Brisbane will investigate buying mini Metro vehicles to speed up services across the city as new data shows peak-hour speeds on major roads are slower than they were six years ago. The vehicles would be smaller than the current Brisbane Metro, which the council said was designed for busways. The council has not committed to the power source of the potential new buses, instead saying: “smaller vehicles powered by several possible fuel sources suitable for high-frequency operational requirements, including battery electric buses and other sustainable energy solutions, could bring bus rapid transit services closer to thousands more residents”. A Brisbane Metro vehicle. Courtney Kruk Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said building new busways and tunnels through established suburbs could cost billions and take years to deliver, causing significant disruption.



“We know we can use our existing road corridors in smarter, more efficient ways to get more people on public transport,” he said. Related Article Public Transport Back to diesel: LNP dumps Queensland’s electric bus program The council has not yet revealed more details, including whether a tender will be released, a delivery date, or how smaller Metros would differ from existing buses. A Metro can carry 150 people, or up to 170 in “event mode”, standard buses have a capacity of 79 people and bendy buses can hold more than 110. Labor opposition leader Jared Cassidy said Brisbane needed a public transport shake-up, not a new type of bus.



“Brisbane’s bus network is not working. We need more services connecting more people to more places,” he said. The RACQ floated the idea of “Metro Glider” services – smaller, more agile electric buses modelled after the Metro – last year. In October 2025, RACQ general manager advocacy Joshua Cooney said Metro Glider buses could act as suburban connectors, channelling passengers onto main, high-frequency routes, servicing key corridors leading into the city that larger Metros could not access. A leaked document obtained by this masthead in May showed the proposed expansion of the Brisbane Metro, including 22 new stations and stops to the north, south, east and airport, was unlikely to be finished before the 2032 Olympic Games. It suggested the council would instead partner with the state government to give buses priority on Old Cleveland Road and Gympie Road, with a staged rollout of future corridors from late 2032.



However, Schrinner argued without federal funding there would be no expansion of the Metro. Related Article Traffic On these Brisbane roads, riding a scooter would be faster than driving The $36 million expansion business case is due to be finished by August next year, and will look at how existing corridors could be used as well as future options, such as the proposed Gympie Road tunnel. Exactly two years ago, the first Metro rolled out, almost nine years after then-lord mayor Graham Quirk announced his Metro plan. Meanwhile, more than 70 per cent of south-east Queensland’s road sections were slower in 2025 during peak hour than in 2019, according to the RACQ’s annual travel speeds report.



On the Gateway Motorway between Nudgee and Pine River Bridge, motorists lost an average of 15.34 minutes each trip during the afternoon peak, the equivalent of more than 2.5 days a year extra spent in traffic. On Gympie Road, drivers averaged 25.2km/h in the afternoon peak between Kedron and Beams Road at Carseldine, adding almost nine minutes to the trip. The Centenary Motorway between Ipswich Motorway and Fig Tree Pocket Road averaged 32.8km/h during the morning commute, adding nearly eight minutes.
