World.title: ‘Checkmate’: Russia is winning the war as Ukraine runs out of friends
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Checkmate’: Russia is winning the war as Ukraine runs out of friends Catherine Belton October 21, 2026 — 11:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Kremlin is counting the Trump administration’s latest turn against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as a major triumph and, coupled with political upheaval in Europe, a sign that Western support for Ukraine is finally crumbling. In the 10 days since Vladimir Putin last spoke by telephone with the American president, Donald Trump has announced a sanctions waiver for Russian diesel supplies to the global market, throttled Ukraine’s access to vital battlefield satellite systems, put sweeping new sanctions against Russian on hold, as well as moved even more firmly to Russia’s side by calling for Zelensky’s ouster and holding up supplies of critical interceptor missiles. Vladimir Putin is counting on Donald Trump’s latest turn against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Fairfax Media On Monday, Trump blasted the Ukrainian president again, saying it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine”. The stakes seem higher than ever. Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is set to travel to Oslo this week to meet Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is expected participate via video link.



“The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path,” Store said. Zelensky said on Sunday that if Washington aligned with Russia, Ukraine would not survive. “If the United States will support Putin – it’s unbelievable, it’s a tragedy,” he told NBC News’ Meet the Press on Sunday. “If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand.” Loading While the European leaders and Zelensky might hope to use the Oslo meeting to steer the Trump administration to a tougher stance against Moscow, Kremlin officials have been crowing that victory over Ukraine is on the horizon, and that Trump’s recent moves are steps toward an ever closer alignment between Washington and Moscow.



Trump’s recent ratcheting up of pressure on Zelensky could mean the US president is again seeking to strong-arm the Ukrainian leader into a deal on terms favourable to Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Witkoff is expected to brief Putin following the Oslo talks. Related Article Opinion

Aviation Starlink’s growing influence has one big point of failure Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation Earlier, Peskov said Ukraine’s recent resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries – in defiance of Trump’s demands – showed Zelensky’s administration in its death throes. “Some final signs of agony are being observed,” Peskov said. “The Kyiv regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events.”



“Checkmate,” Kremlin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted triumphantly. In Moscow, members of the Russian elite said that Putin, a former KGB officer, once again managed to turn the US president. Putin has decades of experience charming and manipulating foreign leaders, and has demonstrated a consistent ability to flatter Trump and pull him on side, analysts and officials said. This time, they said, the Russian leader preyed on Trump’s fears over low approval ratings and sky-high energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections, offering a deal on Russian diesel fuel that will supply just a fraction of America’s daily consumption and have no impact on prices. On Friday, the average US diesel price continued to climb to $US6.33 per gallon, an increase of about 5 cents per gallon from the previous week.



“Russia’s leaders have achieved a certain political victory,” said a Russian academic close to senior Russian diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy. “All this happened after their telephone call. Probably Putin was able to convince Trump.” Putin, the academic added, “probably conducted this conversation very professionally and prepared his arguments well”. Local residents remove debris from a heavily damaged house as smoke rises from a destroyed warehouse, in the background, after Russian drone attacks on the outskirt of Kyiv, Ukraine. AP Mikhail Khodorkovsky, once Russia’s richest man and now an opposition leader in exile, said recent events followed a pattern in Putin’s relations with Trump. “I am absolutely convinced that they believe that they managed to take advantage, as they always do; they are opportunists,” Khodorkovsky said. “In this case, they believe they have waited for the moment of Trump’s additional weakness and [taken] advantage of it.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Total war’: The human face of the assault on Ukraine “For Putin, everything that is happening today are signs of the West’s weakness.” Dmitriev, the special envoy, and other Russian officials hailed the diesel deal and Trump’s waiving of tough sanctions that were to be imposed under a bill adopted in honour of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a firm GOP supporter of Ukraine, as steps toward broader Russia-US economic cooperation. Historically, Russia and the US have never been big economic partners, with Russia exporting little of interest to the US market. “There is a whole range of economic and investment projects being discussed with the American side that will be implemented,” Dmitriev told a Russian energy forum last week. “Our list of projects being discussed with the American side also includes various projects in the Arctic, energy projects, LNG [liquefied natural gas] projects and other areas.”



“More and more Americans, including within the administration, understand that sanctions harm the United States itself,” he added. In July – after years of Putin refusing to drop his maximalist demands in Ukraine – Trump finally seemed to side with Zelensky, telling reporters he was doing “an amazing job” and even backing Ukraine’s deep strikes on Russian oil refineries. Ukraine is expendable on strategic grounds, in Trump’s view, and it was standing in the way of a perfectly good campaign talking point. Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for Europe. “It’s an escalation, but it’s also an escalation that can help lead to an end” of the war, Trump said. But as the US conflict with Iran dragged on, keeping upward pressure on global oil prices, and as the midterm elections drew ever nearer, the Trump administration suddenly turned again.



After an August 31 meeting with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a Group of 20 (G20) event in Asheville, North Carolina, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries as the reason for surging fuel prices – rather than the war in Iran. It was then easy for Putin to recruit Trump into sharing that viewpoint, some observers said. Loading “The simplest explanation is that Trump was simply interested in having a talking point for the midterms on diesel, that he has a deal to lower it,” said Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for Europe during George W. Bush’s administration. “I think it is just Trump lashing out because he’s feeling cornered and unhappy with the midterms, and Zelensky stood in his way,” Fried said, especially after Zelensky publicly derided Trump as “weak” after he announced the diesel deal.



“Trump then extended his frustration to add pressure and try to force a settlement based on a great power deal with Putin, who is skilled at playing his more gullible interlocutors,” he said. That Trump and Putin share a view that strongmen should dominate a world divided into spheres of influence made it even easier for Putin, Fried added. Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump share a view that strongmen should dominate a world. AP “Trump appears to have been attracted to this view for decades,” he said. “And therefore, Ukraine is expendable on strategic grounds, in Trump’s view, and it was standing in the way of a perfectly good campaign talking point.” Trump’s latest swing toward Putin was hardly surprising, said a former senior US intelligence official.



“It almost doesn’t matter what he says, because Trump just seems like he’s very eager. He’s a very receptive audience,” the former intelligence official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. “If you look at the longer-term trends, he has clearly a preference for Putin over Zelensky, and that transcends any kind of temporary relaxation of the tensions that he has with Zelensky.” “He likes strong authoritarian leaders,” the official said. “And deep down, there is this underlying belief on his part that Ukraine cannot win this war, that Russia is bigger, Russia is stronger, Russia is going to crush Ukraine if that’s what it takes.” Related Article US midterms Long lines, late nights, adulation: What it’s really like inside Trump’s midterm election rallies Signs point to Trump seeking to strong-arm Ukraine into a deal by December, when Trump has invited Putin to join him at the G20 leaders’ summit in Miami, said Andrew Weiss, a Russian expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.



“The only way I can explain it is that it’s connected to the milestones leading up to the meeting of the G20 in December,” Weiss said. “I feel like what’s going on here is not really about diesel or refinery long-range strikes. It’s really about Trump thinking that he can push the Ukrainians into some sort of political settlement.” The Russians have “tried to use the administration as a battering ram to get the Ukrainians to surrender Donbas,” Weiss said, referring to the swatch of eastern Ukraine coveted by Putin. “But then that only opens up a subsequent conversation about constraints on Ukrainian military capabilities” he added, or other underlying Russian demands. “The administration has repeatedly misdiagnosed what the Russians want, and the Russians don’t make that easy because they don’t say exactly what they want.” Washington Post Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Cheaper rent, brightest minds: Why Melbourne is about to become Australia’s boom city
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAustralian economy Opinion Cheaper rent, brightest minds: Why Melbourne is about to become Australia’s boom city Aruna Sathanapally Grattan Institute CEO October 21, 2026 — 11:44am

October 21, 2026 — 11:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Another day, another bleak assessment of the state of Victoria, and its capital, Melbourne. Since the pandemic, it has been hard to avoid them. Even walking around the city centre has been a reminder of vibrancy lost. For the city hardest hit by the pandemic, the road back is a long one. Melbourne is building again towards a new cultural and economic boom. Wayne Taylor This is clearest in the state’s finances. All budgets (save Western Australia’s) are under pressure. But Victoria has gone from a relatively rich state to a relatively poor state, ahead of only Tasmania and South Australia. And with healthcare spending on the rise, infrastructure investment still at record levels, and the threat of a difficult bushfire season ahead, budget pressures aren’t likely to ease any time soon. But that is not the full story of Melbourne’s fortunes: the city could be on the cusp of an economic renewal.



Melbourne has long held a strong position in the battle of Australian cities when it comes to quality of life. It has consistently ranked as Australia’s most liveable city, and during much of the 2010s as the most liveable in the world. This year it was voted Time Out’s best city worldwide. Culture, sports, food, trams, and green spaces have made Melbourne marvellous. But right now, the real ace Melbourne has up its sleeve is its housing market. The view of Melbourne’s CBD along the Yarra. Joe Armao The steep – and damaging – climb in the cost of housing seen across Australia since the pandemic has not hit every city evenly. Today, median rents in Melbourne are the second lowest among capitals cities, after only Hobart. In fact, median rents for houses are the lowest of all capital cities. This makes a material difference to the cost of living for Melburnians. And it is particularly important for young people, and those in the early stages of their careers. In Melbourne, median rents for newly advertised dwellings are around 40 per cent of the median full-time wages of those aged 25-34. This is the lowest of any capital city. In Sydney, median rent chews up half of the equivalent median wage.



Not only does your wage go further in Melbourne, but affordable housing – particularly homes for rent – is a vital support to a healthy labour market. It supports mobility and allows people to take a chance and try new things. If you are a young professional looking to build your career, say in a national firm, there are very good reasons to take a job in the Melbourne office. Liveability and affordability in the one place. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent If you are an employer in Melbourne, the wage pressures you face at each salary review are not as acute as Sydney, Brisbane or Perth. If you are creative, or a freelancer, you will have a better shot building your base out of Melbourne. And the more skilled, creative or otherwise entrepreneurial people move to Melbourne, the more the city benefits from “agglomeration”, reaching a critical mass where networks form and exciting things happen. This has happened in cities down on their luck before: Montreal in the late 1990s, setting the stage for the creative boom in the early 2000s. Austin, Texas, is another recent example. It’s hard to disentangle how much of weaker house price growth in Melbourne is down to supply growth, a weaker economy or reforms to land taxes. But when it comes to slower growth in rents relative to incomes, the picture is clearer: in Melbourne there has been a steadier supply of housing to meet demands of population growth and smaller households.



Of course, even in Melbourne, housing costs are still punishingly high in many of the city’s most desirable areas. But Victoria’s land use planning reforms are changing that. These reforms are more substantial than those in NSW, and well ahead of Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth where restrictive low-density zones still cover most residential land. The Grattan Institute estimated last year that Victoria’s reforms will increase zoned capacity equivalent to 70 per cent of the existing housing stock, compared with 40 per cent for NSW. This arises predominantly from the state’s new “Townhouse Code”, but also the much-publicised Activity Centre Program; both examples of measures to boost gentle and medium density in the places people most want to live, and close to jobs. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly None of this is cause for complacency: the Victorian government needs to stay the course on reforms to allow more homes in the places Melburnians want to live. Construction productivity desperately needs a shot in the arm. Nor is it only about housing – you also need good transport networks, effective measures to bust congestion, and planning that makes the most of existing infrastructure rather than enabling more sprawl. Institutions like top-tier universities and globally leading firms also play a key role in agglomeration of knowledge workers and innovators, particularly through attracting the world’s best and brightest here. Melbourne’s story is still being written. And a commitment to remaining the most affordable city to rent in Australia will make it even more marvellous.



Dr Aruna Sathanapally is chief executive of the Grattan Institute. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Power protests light fuse on $2 billion data centre implosion, as NextDC shares plummet
World.content:
PoliticsFederalInvestigations Power protests light fuse on $2 billion data centre implosion, as NextDC shares plummet Clay Lucas October 21, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What began as a community protest in Melbourne’s inner west over enormous electricity poles being installed on narrow residential streets has now rocked the nation’s highest-profile data centre developer, as it scrambles to find a new way to supply energy to its flagship centre. On Wednesday, ASX-listed NextDC told investors it would slash its expected profits and construction spending as it dealt with delays in supplying energy to its M3 centre in West Footscray, triggering a share price plummet. NextDC’s M3 data centre in West Footscray. Joe Armao NextDC came out of a two-day trading halt on Wednesday warning investors that the final stages of the politically contentious development would also not be approved until after next month’s state election. The delays are the result of a community blockade in September, revealed by this masthead, against electricity distributor Jemena’s rollout of 15-metre tall 66,000-volt residential power poles. The protests prompted Jemena to halt construction until at least February.



The delays have left NextDC saying it now lacks the extra grid capacity needed to power its expanding data halls at West Footscray. The market reaction against the data centre developer was sharp: NextDC shares collapsed to $5.46 on Wednesday, down more than 40 per cent from their Monday closing price of $9.57. The crash wiped billions off the company’s valuation, driving its stock to its lowest point since 2019 – a far cry from its peak of $17.22 a year ago. Jemena power lines in a Yarraville residential street, with the NextDC data centre in the background (left). Joe Armao NextDC on Wednesday also revealed it was putting the brakes on its wider construction pipeline, in a move which could alarm state and federal governments as data centre construction is one of the few bright spots in the sluggish Australian economy. NextDC slashed its construction budget for the coming financial year from up to $5.75 billion to between $4.5 billion and $5 billion, pausing developments without client contract commitments. Previously, the company had built new data centres without having tenants contracted to go into them.



NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said the company had paused expectations from its West Footscray project, and would halt speculative expansion projects and land buys not already locked in by paying clients. “With [West Footscray] revenue deferred, we have paused projects not backed by customer contracts and put that capital behind the capacity our customers have already contracted,” he said. Yarraville resident Milco Bogoevski was among those who led the community protest to stop Jemena installing its enormous power poles in his residential street. He said while he was sympathetic to data centre operators – “No one here wants to see industry fail; we want industry to succeed” – what had happened was the direct result of power companies and business not listening to the community.



“These power lines, this material, it was going to be in our street, we were going to have to deal with it for decades after they left – power operators like Jemena, and [businesses like NextDC], they’re going to need to engage more with the community.” Bogoevski said the community opposition to the enormous West Footscray data centre and the impact of other data centres in Melbourne’s inner west could help swing seats in the November 28 election. A sign in Sanderson Street, Yarraville, on Tuesday. Jason South “The state government is responsible for power – it comes down to them. There is a good chance that an issue like this could flip this seat away from Labor; we’ve got a couple of issues like this that Labor hasn’t paid attention to,” he said. NextDC’s market shock represents the clearest evidence yet that Victoria’s rapid push to attract power-hungry artificial intelligence infrastructure has run into severe grid constraints and suburban backlash.



The M3 facility in West Footscray is designed to eventually span 10 hectares in an industrial pocket adjacent to residential homes. The site already occupies five hectares and was undergoing a $750 million expansion. However, feeding the expanding site required Jemena to replace standard wooden electricity poles with 15-metre concrete poles carrying 66,000 volts along residential streets in West Footscray and neighbouring Yarraville. A typical residential power pole carries about 400 volts. A Maribyrnong City Council spokeswoman noted that some poles in the rollout rise as high as 22 metres, which is equivalent to seven storeys.



The rollout ground to a halt in Yarraville last month following direct action by residents, who blockaded contractor trucks with parked cars, ignored door-knocks and filled excavation pits to stop high-voltage lines reaching the NextDC site. Jemena bowed to pressure and paused work to consult further, leaving the high-capacity route unfinished. Related Article Data centres Labor facing internal revolt over data centre spree NextDC said a state a planning permit decision for its next stages of its West Footscray project had also been delayed. With the Victorian government entering caretaker mode on November 3 ahead of the election, a planning decision for the site is now not expected until 2027. The mounting political and community friction creates a growing challenge for the election. As premier, Jacinta Allan and her then-economic development minister Danny Pearson aggressively courted hyperscale data operators, using fast-tracked planning schemes to bypass municipal councils and grant approvals in as little as 28 days.



Data centres consume about 2 per cent of national grid power, but the Australian Energy Market Operator has forecast that share could rise to 9 per cent by 2035 as AI adoption accelerates. To address growing concerns, Premier Ben Carroll last month introduced new rules requiring data centre developers to supply their own renewable energy, use recycled water, and maintain a minimum 150-metre buffer from homes. Community pushback is now hitting projects nationwide. Developer Green Square was recently forced to pull a proposed project in Western Australia, Goodman Group shelved a $1.2 billion facility in the Sydney suburb of Lane Cove, and private developer Firmus was forced to abandon a planned $44 billion stock market float. World.title: I protected politicians and presidents. It used to be easier to tell who the bad guy was
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Opinion I protected politicians and presidents. It used to be easier to tell who the bad guy was Rob Albert Former police close personal protection officer October 21, 2026 — 11:30am

October 21, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of my first jobs when I joined the NSW Police Protection Operations Unit was to provide a security escort to then prime minister John Howard through the Sydney CBD. A young man spotted the “C1” number plates and the little Australian flag fluttering as the PM’s white saloon car rolled by. So he ran up to the window, stuck up his middle finger, shouted a few expletives and stood down. A very minor incident, but I point it out because Australians have always had the larrikin tendency to feel they have the right not only to tell their mates what they think of them and where to go but also their elected representatives – in this case Australia’s 25th prime minister in 2005. Rob Albert has protected everyone from politicians to presidents, with some royalty thrown in. Marija Ercegovac Fast-forward two decades and things are radically different. I am deeply saddened by the attack on Helen Haines and wish her a full recovery, although I wonder if it’s possible to fully recover from an attack such as this – physically or psychologically.



But what about politically? Things are different. People are polarised. There’s anger at a level beyond a middle finger at a consulate car window. Many are stressed personally, financially and, regrettably, sometimes those with strong emotional connections to an ideology react violently towards those who don’t agree with them. Rob Albert protecting William and Kate on a royal visit to Sydney. Keeping our politicians safe has never been harder for police. At Counter Terrorism Command we always figured an attack could come at any time, from anywhere and from anyone. The result of a spontaneous decision or a finely tuned, pre-planned event. What’s changed is that anything is a weapon now. We used to think of weapons as firearms we had a register for, but now a Toyota Land Cruiser or any vehicle can inflict as much if not more damage than a gun. And in a rural area on a suburban street where politicians like Haines would have prided themselves on informal links to the communities they served, well, the basic security measures are fewer and further between.



I’ve provided close personal protection over the years to presidents, kings and queens, prime ministers, premiers, as well as various members of the military or spy agencies from Australia and abroad. Related Article Updated

Haines attack Suspect in Haines attack clashed with neighbours as his health unravelled Many of those people I admired and respected, and would willingly have risked my life to protect them in the office they held. I also looked after people for whom I had, let’s just say, less respect for and with whom I strongly disagreed politically, but I still would have risked my life to protect them. That was the job I signed up for. The question I ask myself and I ask the nation is how have we become a country where an everyday person would seek to attack, maim or kill another person they disagree with when I was willing to lay down my life for someone I disliked? When I escorted that car carrying Howard through Sydney in 2005, sure, people were divided on many topics. People disagreed. But the right and the left didn’t seem as deeply entrenched and diametrically opposed as they are now and any attack we anticipated came more from organised terror or crime groups rather than “Joe Citizen” who’d been blowing up on social media.



The indoctrination or radicalisation of people, whether it be through educational institutions, clubs, online through the dark web or through social media platforms has generated a subculture of people who are unable to live peacefully with others who might disagree with them or think differently. Their response to this conditioning is too often violent or hostile, heightening the threat and risk to high office holders. Rob Albert protecting William and Kate in Sydney. It used to be easier to tell who the bad guy was. Crime wore a balaclava and carried a gun, it didn’t dress in civvies in broad daylight while driving down the main street of Wangaratta. What’s the solution? It would be impossible and impractical to provide protection for every politician. Budget restraints, manpower, intelligence, surveillance … there is too much to do at too big a cost.



Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing My view from the news chair: the worst of the mob is coming for us Hugh Riminton Journalist and author Haines. Bondi. Whatever else is happening or about to happen in Australia, how do we stop it from happening or, worse still, becoming a common occurrence? It must start from the top, so my first appeal is to those leaders I would have “taken a bullet for”. Everyone I talk to has one common complaint – people no longer feel heard. People no longer feel cared about. People no longer feel safe, and it’s driving many of them to more radical solutions, radical politics and radical actions. So don’t play politics like a game because its consequences flow on to us. Bipartisan approaches may be required on some occasions. Rise above political point scoring and come together on the big issues for the sake of the country, the sake of its people, and the sake of Helen Haines. If all we see is you disagreeing, all we will do is disagree.



My second appeal is to the people of Australia. Maintain the larrikin! Debate. Disagree. But violence is never an option. Its consequences are catastrophic and rather than changing what you want it to change, history shows it usually has the opposite effect. Rob Albert is a former NSW Police close personal protection officer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Elon Musk’s $5 trillion monster: Tesla and SpaceX exploring the biggest merger in history
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions Elon Musk’s $5 trillion monster: Tesla and SpaceX exploring the biggest merger in history Richard Clough and Ed Ludlow Updated October 21, 2026 — 11:26am ,first published October 21, 2026 — 9:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, a preliminary step toward what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time. Musk has in the past tantalised shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive officer of both companies, said on SpaceX’s earnings webcast. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” Elon Musk says that a merger isn’t certain and would require shareholder support. AP Photo/Matt Rourke Musk said he isn’t participating in the committee discussions because he is a conflicted party, and that the committees have yet to agree on terms.



A blockbuster deal would unite Tesla’s electric vehicle, energy and robotics businesses with SpaceX’s rocket launch and satellite internet operations. Underpinning it all are the companies’ shared ambitions in artificial intelligence — or what some in the industry are now calling superintelligence — fuelling investments in areas such as data centres and driverless cars. SpaceX shares surged 8.1 per cent in post-market trading after reporting robust quarterly results, while Tesla climbed 1.8 per cent. Tesla is scheduled to release its third-quarter results on Thursday morning (AEDT). Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The scope of a potential merger is staggering, with both SpaceX and Tesla among the largest companies in the world and holding dominant positions in their respective industries. SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, has a market value of about $US2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly $US1.5 trillion. SpaceX and Tesla already have numerous business ties, overlapping investor bases and even some shared personnel. The rocket maker has purchased more than $US100 million worth of Tesla Cybertrucks, while xAI is a major customer of Tesla’s utility-scale batteries.



A combination has been widely expected since SpaceX rode a wave of investor enthusiasm to a record initial public offering this year, giving the company both currency and an implicit green light from shareholders to make a play for Tesla, making Musk the world’s first trillionaire. Bloomberg News reported in January that SpaceX had weighed a Tesla merger before ultimately deciding to acquire xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence startup. Musk cautioned that a merger isn’t certain and would require shareholder support. He said Tesla would need approval from 50 per cent of all shareholders, rather than simply a majority of those voting. “I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said. SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, has a market value of about $US2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly $US1.5 trillion. Bloomberg “Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty. I think that would be overstating it.”



SpaceX earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said it was tracking an annual revenue run rate of up to $US1 trillion. SpaceX’s revenue climbed 161 per cent to $US14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $US7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-centre capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Reflection AI rather than from its own models. Related Article Opinion

Future technology Why Elon Musk’s new Roadster will fly off the shelves Michelle Cazzulino Writer “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity and superintelligence,” Musk said on the call. He ended his portion of prepared remarks with a seemingly off-script remark: “In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of ’27 is somewhere between $US500 billion and a trillion.” The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous — capital expenses nearly tripled.

World.content:
City of Sydney deputy mayor Jess Miller is talking about Sydney’s success in developing Parramatta as a second CBD.

The idea of Melbourne’s becoming a “polycentric” city – rather than one where jobs are all in the CBD – is a big focus today.

Miller says two key moves were improving transport to Parramatta with the new Metro rail line, and shifting government offices there.

“Which meant that there was actually jobs close to where people lived, and that really mattered because all of a sudden, you have whole departments… located there,” she said.

“The planning controls changed to allow for a huge amount of uplift that brought the development sector with it, made housing more affordable.”

World.title: Is it a bus? Is it a Metro? Brisbane will investigate small Metro vehicles
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandBrisbane Metro Is it a bus? Is it a Metro? Brisbane will investigate small Metro vehicles Felicity Caldwell October 21, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Brisbane will investigate buying mini Metro vehicles to speed up services across the city as new data shows peak-hour speeds on major roads are slower than they were six years ago. The vehicles would be smaller than the current Brisbane Metro, which the council said was designed for busways. The council has not committed to the power source of the potential new buses, instead saying: “smaller vehicles powered by several possible fuel sources suitable for high-frequency operational requirements, including battery electric buses and other sustainable energy solutions, could bring bus rapid transit services closer to thousands more residents”. A Brisbane Metro vehicle. Courtney Kruk Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said building new busways and tunnels through established suburbs could cost billions and take years to deliver, causing significant disruption.



“We know we can use our existing road corridors in smarter, more efficient ways to get more people on public transport,” he said. Related Article Public Transport Back to diesel: LNP dumps Queensland’s electric bus program The council has not yet revealed more details, including whether a tender will be released, a delivery date, or how smaller Metros would differ from existing buses. A Metro can carry 150 people, or up to 170 in “event mode”, standard buses have a capacity of 79 people and bendy buses can hold more than 110. Labor opposition leader Jared Cassidy said Brisbane needed a public transport shake-up, not a new type of bus.



“Brisbane’s bus network is not working. We need more services connecting more people to more places,” he said. The RACQ floated the idea of “Metro Glider” services – smaller, more agile electric buses modelled after the Metro – last year. In October 2025, RACQ general manager advocacy Joshua Cooney said Metro Glider buses could act as suburban connectors, channelling passengers onto main, high-frequency routes, servicing key corridors leading into the city that larger Metros could not access. A leaked document obtained by this masthead in May showed the proposed expansion of the Brisbane Metro, including 22 new stations and stops to the north, south, east and airport, was unlikely to be finished before the 2032 Olympic Games. It suggested the council would instead partner with the state government to give buses priority on Old Cleveland Road and Gympie Road, with a staged rollout of future corridors from late 2032.



However, Schrinner argued without federal funding there would be no expansion of the Metro. Related Article Traffic On these Brisbane roads, riding a scooter would be faster than driving The $36 million expansion business case is due to be finished by August next year, and will look at how existing corridors could be used as well as future options, such as the proposed Gympie Road tunnel. Exactly two years ago, the first Metro rolled out, almost nine years after then-lord mayor Graham Quirk announced his Metro plan. Meanwhile, more than 70 per cent of south-east Queensland’s road sections were slower in 2025 during peak hour than in 2019, according to the RACQ’s annual travel speeds report.



On the Gateway Motorway between Nudgee and Pine River Bridge, motorists lost an average of 15.34 minutes each trip during the afternoon peak, the equivalent of more than 2.5 days a year extra spent in traffic. On Gympie Road, drivers averaged 25.2km/h in the afternoon peak between Kedron and Beams Road at Carseldine, adding almost nine minutes to the trip. The Centenary Motorway between Ipswich Motorway and Fig Tree Pocket Road averaged 32.8km/h during the morning commute, adding nearly eight minutes. World.title: Photos only a part of 'overwhelming' case against Scott Watson, Crown says
World.content:
Crown lawyers in the Supreme Court today say a photo montage at the heart of Scott Watson's appeal is only one piece of evidence in an "overwhelming" case against him.

Watson is appealing his conviction for the murders of Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in Marlborough Sounds on New Years' Day in 1998.

His lawyers argue the evidence of water taxi driver Guy Wallace - used in the original trial - who picked out Watson in "Photo Montage B" as the man seen boarding a boat with the young pair, is inadmissible.

Crown lawyer Madeleine Laracy said the Crown always relied on a "large volume of evidence" - not just a photo montage.

"This was and is an overwhelming case."

Laracy referred to the Court of Appeal's judgment in 2024 - which rejected a previous bid by Watson to quash his convictions.

The Court of Appeal had found there were just too many factors pointing to Watson, Laracy said.

"If Mr Watson was not the man on the Naiad, then the lone man, like Mr Watson, happened to be alone, happened to have a yacht, happened to have moored his yacht out from the jetty, happened to be in the same age range, late twenties or early thirties, happened to have an appearance that was so like Mr Watson's as to mislead Mr Wallace into thinking it was the same man."

Crown lawyer Stuart Baker said Wallace's evidence did not solely rely on picking him out of a photo montage.

"This was not a case of a fleeting glance by Mr Wallace, rather Mr Wallace observed the male at the lodge for some time throughout the evening, both in the main bar and the garden bar."

Baker said Wallace gave descriptions of the "lone man", prior to going to the wharf, including who was on the naiad, where exactly they went, what was said, and a description of rafted boats in the bay, where the three people disembarked.

Watson's Court of Appeal bid sought to overturn his convictions on the question of reliability of DNA evidence of two blonde hairs found on Watson's boat, as well as the photo montage evidence.

World.title: PNG Chiefs unveil logo and jersey in Port Moresby
World.content:
The PNG Chiefs, the NRL's newest franchise, has launched its logo and jersey in Port Moresby ahead of its 2028 debut.

The club, which is locked in a legal battle with New Zealand Rugby (NZR) over trademark rights to the "Chiefs" name, revealed its brand identity and kit on Wednesday morning.

The launch went ahead after New Zealand's High Court declined an urgent application by NZR for an interim injunction to stop the unveiling.

PNG Chiefs logo launched on Wednesday, 21 October 2026. Screengrab / Facebook/TVWAN Online

PNG's Prime Minister James Marape said the PNG Chiefs gives every child in the country a dream.

"Every child in PNG, this is your moment in the logo and the team colour that we are unveiling. You are in that focus," he said.

PNG Chiefs identity and jersey reveal. 21 October 2026 Screengrab / Facebook/TVWAN Online

PNG Rugby Football League chairman Sandis Tsaka said it has been a long road but all the sacrifice has been worth it.

"It's been a collective effort from a lot of people, partners, sponsors, people in rugby league, the Australian government, the Papua New Guinea government," said on TV Wan.

"It's been a team effort to get this far and finally get the nod for the bid and since then it's grown in leaps and bounds," he said.

"It has snowballed the work that everyone has done to make this dream come true and today to actually officially launch the Chiefs as a franchise for 2028 is a testament to a lot of work, a lot of sacrifices, commitment from a lot of people, partners, friends.

"We are just excited that the Chiefs brand has brought together all of Papua New Guinea basically to get behind this franchise and build a team that is truly Papua New Guinean."

Australian Minister for the Pacific Pat Conroy said the Chiefs is more than just sport, with its importance strengthening the relationship between PNG and Australia.

"This team is not just about sport," he said at the launch, where he represented the government of Australia.

"It will drive social cohesion, unite those thousands tribes, it will also drive powerful education and gender outcomes throughout the Pacific through the rugby league partnerships."

Conroy said the Australian government is committed to ensuring the PNG Chiefs will be a success, with its grant of AU$250 million geared to help the sport grow in the Pacific, with AU$90 million for PNG rugby league grassroots programs and development.

ARL commissioner general Peter Beattie said the PNG Chiefs is a partnership between PNG and Australia and will count on all partners working together as a team.

He said seeing the logo and club identity launched was an inspiration, especially with questions raised by New Zealand Rugby in court around the Chiefs brand.

Beattie said the ARL is not compromising as the PNG Chiefs name was decided by the people of PNG.

He added they will continue to fight the push by NZR and the Chiefs of Waikato to stop the club from using the name.

"We said no, we will not compromise. We won but it is not finished and we will continue," he said.

PNG Chiefs chief executive Lorna McPherson said the unveiling of the logo and jersey is the fruition of many Papua New Guineans belief and dreams that one day there will be a PNG team they can cheer for in the NRL.

World.title: Sale of Wellington Kāinga Ora houses sparks local backlash
World.content:
Community activists and politicians have only hours left to stop the sale of a Kainga Ora-owned social housing development in Wellington.

The sale of the Strathmore social housing at 4,6,8 Nuku St ends at 4pm on Wednesday.

It has sparked local backlash over concerns for community spirit and affordable housing - with the Labour and Green parties calling for the sale to be put on hold until after the election.

Kainga Ora regional director Sarah Willson told RNZ the agency had no plans to review the sale.

"We understand the strength of feeling in the Strathmore community about the Nuku St site and recognise how important public housing is to Wellington."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407154290112

Real estate agency Bayleys declined to comment on the sale of this property, or the sale of public land in general.

Minister of Housing Chris Bishop declined to comment saying the sale was an operational decision for Kāinga Ora.

The property's listing on the Bayleys website, described it as an "exceptional development opportunity".

When RNZ visited on Tuesday while the community protest was occurring, the buildings appeared run down with boarded up windows and in darkness.

Inside, mould dotted the flaking ceilings, peeling paint was visible, puddles of rainwater collected on the floor, and joinery and other interiors were broken.

A prospective buyer at the scene told RNZ he would rebuild affordable housing there and, "the government can rent them back off me".

"The government don't deserve to own these if they don't look after them. I'm a taxpayer, and look at the state what they've left it at."

Former tenant Christina Paese said she was disappointed the properties were being sold.

She believed the buildings had deteriorated because they had been left vacant for years.

She described fond memories of raising her children there safely.

"It's a good thing as a mum, you know, seeing my kids growing up healthy."

"But this is where they start from."

The sale of the Strathmore social housing at 4,6,8 Nuku St ends at 4pm this afternoon. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

She said she would have been living on the streets without the social housing on Nuku St.

She said selling the land to private buyers would be a loss for families struggling with the cost of living and low wages.

"This is a place where they're supposed to raise their family before they find a proper place," she said.

"So where are they going to end up?"

Willson said the housing agency remained committed to building more homes, with 37 planned on the nearby Ngatiapa Street site.

"We explored several options for redeveloping the Nuku Street site for social housing, but none proved financially viable, which is why we made the decision to sell the property."

Willson said the proceeds from the sale would be reinvested in new social housing that better met tenants' needs.

The housing agency sold more than 900 homes during its 2026 financial year, creating $417 million, according to its financial results released on Tuesday - its strongest in a decade.

Strathmore Housing Action organised a sit-in on Monday night, with locals sleeping in tents overnight in protest of the sale.

About 100 people gathered at the Nuku Street site in Strathmore Park on Monday evening, sharing a barbecue, speeches, hula dancing and a football game.

Organiser Lizzie Pringle said the gathering was about restoring a sense of community to the site, which had been vacant for about three years.

"We were bringing life back into Nuku Street," she said

Lizzie Pringle RNZ / Baz Macdonald

She said Wellington had more than 600 households on the public housing waiting list, and people at Monday's gathering included those waiting for homes and those living in overcrowded conditions.

"We know that there's just a desperate need for houses in Wellington," she said.

Pringle said the site's proximity to Kahurangi School and a major bus route made it well suited to public housing.

She said the closure of the homes also displaced some former tenants from the Strathmore community, disrupting their children's schooling and their access to work.

Labour MP Craig Renney RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Pringle delivered a banner with other locals carrying the message "Do not sell this land" to Kainga Ora's offices on Tuesday morning.

Labour's spokesperson for housing Kieran McAnulty wrote to Kainga Ora asking for the sale to be paused until after the election.

Standing before Kainga Ora's offices in Wellington, Labour MP Craig Renney said it was "nothing short of a disgrace" to sell state housing land before an election.

Green MP Julie Anne Genter said she and Tamatha Paul had launched an open letter weeks ago calling on ministers and Kainga Ora to hold off any land sales until after the election.

World.title: Lake Omapere gets $3 million boost to tackle algal bloom
World.content:
An ambitious project to restore Northland's largest - and most polluted - lake has received a $3 million boost from the government's Regional Infrastructure Fund.

Regional Development Minister Shane Jones made the announcement at Lake Ōmāpere, just north of Kaikohe, on Wednesday afternoon.

Jones said the funding would pay for consents, road access, a weir to regulate lake levels and design work for future water storage infrastructure.

He said the project would "go a long way" towards improving Northland's water and economic resilience while also restoring the lake's health.

The 1200-hectare lake was once regarded as the food bowl of Ngāpuhi for its vast numbers of eels and freshwater mussels.

However, deforestation in the 1800s, followed by expansion of farming, triggered a steady decline in water quality.

Lake Ōmāpere, north of Kaikohe, is Northland’s largest lake. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Since the 1980s the lake, which is little more than two metres deep, has been blighted by regular algal blooms, killing aquatic life and making the water unusable for drinking, recreation or irrigation.

Jones said local communities had long regarded Lake Ōmāpere as a taonga.

"Restoring the lake's health is about honouring that connection while supporting communities, businesses and future development. This investment is an important step towards realising that long-term vision."

Associate Minister Mark Patterson said a reliable water supply was critical if Northland was to remain productive during dry periods.

"By helping advance this project, we're supporting the long-term resilience of the region and its ability to respond to future water challenges, as well as helping revive a precious taonga," he said.

"A healthy Lake Ōmāpere has the potential to support local communities by enabling strengthened food production and creating opportunities for Māori economic development."

The first stage of the project was expected to cost around $5.9m with funding from multiple partners.
