Tech.title: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike button being absent for them.

Right now, for me, the dislike button sits right next to the like button under a video. Moving it to a submenu would make it considerably more of an effort to access, meaning that fewer people would likely use it.

It’s unclear how widely this apparent test may be rolled out, and Google didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

YouTube has shown a willingness to make changes to the dislike button. In 2021, it hid the public dislike count on videos to help “protect creators from harassment,” though creators can still see dislike counts. Earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button from YouTube Shorts, suggesting instead that users take advantage of options in the three-dots menu.

Tech.title: Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian, the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann had failed to appear for an independent medical examination or meet other deadlines despite warnings that it would result in the case being dismissed.

When the case was filed last year, a statement shared by Sam Altman, his mother, and his brothers said, “Annie has made deeply hurtful and entirely untrue claims about our family, and especially Sam… All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.”

Bluestone granted Sam Altman’s motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled in that court, while denying Sam’s request for attorney fees and costs. Santos Perez, a lawyer who had represented Ann until withdrawing this month, told The Guardian in a statement that “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”

Tech.title: Trump is giving Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million fraud bounty program
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud.

In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video alleging fraud at daycares in Minnesota that were operated by members of the local Somali community. Shirley lingered in parking lots and asked to enter childcare centers, taking refusals as evidence that the centers weren’t actually caring for children. The video quickly went viral, triggering a massive governmental response: Federal immigration agents descended on the Minneapolis area, and the Trump administration froze Minnesota’s federal funding for childcare. Shirley has since visited other states in the US under similar pretenses, showing up unannounced to grocery stores and hospice centers in search of evidence of fraud. Vance and others in the administration publicly praised Shirley, who has since become a mainstay in the MAGA-aligned content creator ecosystem. He’s helped popularize a genre of so-called independent journalism popular on the right in which content creators and influencers confront businesses or people they suspect of fraud or crime as the basis for their online content. Harassment — or even immigration crackdowns — often follow.

The administration told Fox News that it was also launching the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP), a pool of $25 million open to anyone who believes they’ve witnessed fraud. A “particular emphasis” is placed on fraud in hospice, home healthcare, daycares, and special services, a government website says. A chatbot collecting responses instructs the reporting party: “Briefly describe what you saw, heard, or read. A few sentences are enough. Include names, dates, amounts, or records if you have them, and how you know. Note any details you’re unsure about.”

According to Fox News and the reporting portal, members of the public who flag fraud are eligible to get up to $30,000 if a tip submitted leads to a conviction or significant federal action. But speaking on Tuesday, Trump contradicted the $30,000 ceiling.

”If you turn somebody in and … you find $1 billion, we are giving a commission to that person of 1 percent,” Trump said today. (One percent of $1 billion would exceed the $30,000 cap.) “And if it’s $10 billion, $200 billion, $400 billion, we’re giving a 1 percent commission to that person,” Trump continued.

The White House didn’t immediately clarify how the $10,000 payment to Shirley was calculated or how the program is being funded in the first place.

Shirley’s methods have been criticized particularly in Minnesota, where sweeping fraud investigations were already taking place before he arrived to make content. He accused businesses of faking childcare services based on little more than being denied entry to facilities, and — to the frustration of many — acted as if his video was the first fraud investigation in the state. Subsequent state official visits to the centers Shirley featured found them operating “as expected.”

Tech.title: Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.

As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”

Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.

Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.

Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

Tech.title: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”

The groups have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and there’s no guarantee that they will. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he continued. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”

That said, Musk called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.” He continued:

I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies. They’ve got to come up with something and then that’s going to be put to the shareholders as a vote.

A Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a blockbuster corporate deal creating a mega-entity valued upwards of $3.6 trillion. But combining Musk’s car and energy company with his AI and rocket company would not be without its tradeoffs. A lot depends on which company absorbs the other. To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie. SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.

That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa. Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla. A merger in that direction would allow SpaceX shareholders to hold the majority control of the combined mega-entity. Some Tesla shareholders may balk at this deal.

But it would also create one company for those who believe in Musk’s vision of the future — robot cars, humanoid robots, AI super-intelligence, and human habitats on Mars — in which to place their investments. And Tesla shareholder approved Musk’s enormous pay package last year — even after a Delaware judge tossed it over lack of independence.

Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

Tech.title: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered.

“This is a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization consciousness,” he said during the company’s third quarter earnings report Tuesday.

But he also allowed for the possibility of a failure. “Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight,” Musk said. “And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year and then accelerating next year.”

“Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” — Elon Musk

Starship is a two-stage system, composed of the Super Heavy booster (first stage) and the Starship spacecraft (second stage). It stands approximately 120 meters (around 400 feet) tall with a 9-meter diameter, and is powered by SpaceX’s Raptor engines burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Starship, which was first introduced in 2018, was designed to return to the launch site, where launch towers with mechanical “chopstick” arms catch the vehicle mid-air.

Last month’s Starship launch represented two firsts for its next gen rocket: send the spacecraft into Earth orbit, and insert a few dozen of SpaceX’s larger and more capable V3 satellites into the Starlink constellation for the first time. Still, the launch wasn’t without its snafus: one Raptor engine shut down prematurely during ascent, prompting mission control to adapt and complete the climb on remaining. Because of the issue, SpaceX cut the planned 10-hour, 6-orbit mission short after about 3 hours and 2 Earth orbits.

The Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship upper stage executed a de-orbit burn and ended with a fiery vertical splashdown in the Pacific Ocean north of Hawaii. Neither piece was recovered.

Developing…

Tech.title: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and leverage new technology.

The streaming giant doesn’t say exactly how it plans to improve its monetization, but the company notes that these goals will help Netflix “create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand.” Netflix also highlighted plans to push further into original titles, live events, and third-party programming as it faces an “intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention.”

An analysis from financial firm Jefferies estimated that Netflix’s monthly viewing time per member dropped to 49 hours in the first half of this year, down from 66 hours in the first half of 2023, according to a report from Reuters. At the same time, Netflix made up 7.8 percent of US viewing time in the US in July, a one-percentage-point dip from the same time last year, The New York Times reports.

During an earnings call, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos pointed to success abroad when answering a question about the company’s content strategy. “We see titles across Latin America, EMEA (Europe, the Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia-Pacific), driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue, and profit,” Sarandos said. “Now, the US is also working. It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.”

Related Netflix is pivoting away from prestige

In its letter to investors, Netflix mentions its upcoming lineup of NFL games, its Grand Theft Auto VI preview, and its partnership with French TV station TF1 as evidence of opening its platform to a wider breadth of content. The company reported earning $12.9 billion over the past few months, marking a 12 percent year-over-year increase. It also plans to bring its ad-supported tier — which raked in $1.5 billion last year — to 15 new countries in 2027.

In the coming months, Netflix may be facing tougher competition from HBO Max and Paramount Plus following the Skydance megamerger, as co-CEO David Ellison has said that he plans to combine the two apps into a single service. The streamer struck deals with several creators as it competes with YouTube, which has reportedly offered channels “millions of dollars” not to post their videos on Netflix.

Netflix has also weighed making even bigger changes to its app, including integrating other third-party streamers, such as Peacock and Fox One, as well as adding always-on channels, according to reports from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Update, October 20th: Added a quote from Sarandos.

Tech.title: Snap is paying Robert Downey Jr. to do the Iron Man thing
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Snap has a new brand ambassador for its Specs AR glasses: Iron Man actor Robert Downey Jr. The company has brought on Downey as Specs’ “Chief Customer Experience Officer” and has published several videos featuring Downey showcasing the capabilities of the new glasses, including as a tool to get help with a putt, practice art, and watch a private video of an MMA match in bed. In one video, he also dumps the contents of a box labeled “AI glasses” into a trash bin — a shot at Meta’s popular smart glasses.

As part of the partnership, Downey will “work alongside the SPECS team to explore how augmented reality can improve the way people live and work, from everyday experiences in entertainment and education to specialized uses across medicine, engineering, and manufacturing,” according to a blog post.

“Trying is believing,” Downey says in a statement. “Having tested practically every wearable tech that’s come to market in the last 20 years, and been largely unimpressed, I was absolutely sold on SPECS within 40 seconds.” Snap has other celebrities on board to help promote Specs, too, including musician Imogen Heap and NBA star Jimmy Butler.

The Snap Specs are set to launch sometime this fall, and they’ll cost $2,195. They’re available for pre-order now. If you want to know what it’s like to actually use Specs, go read my report from my time wearing them at Snap’s HQ last month.

Tech.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
Tech.content:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.

Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.

Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.

The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.

It’s not clear how this proposed system would assure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).

In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s a request for comment but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.

The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.

In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.

Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers that are placed inside AI organizations so that they can monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.

Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, who’s CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

Tech.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
Tech.content:
The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call.

Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing.

Neither Musk, nor his brother Kimbal Musk, are independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance.

SpaceX lists six independent directors, including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelef Boutha are also considered independent directors.

Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.

Musk said he supports the idea of the merger, but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome.

“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”

The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said.

The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX.

Tech.title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
Tech.content:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown, take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.

“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”

To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well, including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.

In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment, spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.

But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.

In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”

Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”

But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.

The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.

But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.

It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on screen.

Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”

In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
Tech.content:
In Brief

Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude-maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal.

The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which includes deals still in negotiation.

And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.

Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.

Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.

Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Tech.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
Tech.content:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.

CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing.

That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.

During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”

In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12 to 18 month delays in obtaining the metals blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.

Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.

Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”

More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.

This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

Tech.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
Tech.content:
In Brief

OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.

Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.

The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

Tech.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
Tech.content:
Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in, software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.

The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.

Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.

Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

Tech.title: GM to close Detroit battery assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think
Tech.content:
In Brief

GM is closing a battery assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch.

The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure.

The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end.

The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones.

Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs.

Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs, though it hasn’t given up on full electrification.

GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt. It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization.

Tech.title: A New Rocco Smart Fridge Just Dropped. So Did the Prices (2026)
Tech.content:
Unless you live under a rock with a bag on your head and your fingers in your ears (which kind of sounds heavenly at this point, if I'm being honest), you've probably seen or heard of the Rocco smart fridge, a retro-looking wine cooler/minifridge that keeps a catalog of its contents, so you can know what's inside no matter where you are.

Former WIRED contributor Andrew Watman reviewed it for us in 2024, giving it a solid 7 out of 10 and confirming that it is every bit the statement piece it’s designed to be. I own one as well, and I love both its vintage-inspired charm and that I can “see” what's inside without having to look in it.

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Andrew Watman Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rocco The Classic $1,995 $1,795 (10% off) Rocco

Rocco app via Andrew Watman

The Rocco’s marquee feature, other than it coming in fun colors—I can report several new ones are coming very soon—is its smart app. It allows you to see the fridge contents as scanned by the fridge itself, and control the lights and temperature from afar.

When Watman tested it, he was impressed by the library of drinks the fridge recognized, from an obscure OoMee algae-infused beverage to canned Yaté yerba mate. In my own fridge, I was surprised to see the Rocco could even recognize individual flavors of Kirkland Signature sparkling water.

Because the Rocco is on the second floor of my house, away from my main fridge, I also didn't anticipate how convenient it would be to see what was in the fridge at all times—I knew exactly what to bring upstairs to stock it, and didn't have to make multiple trips. It's also helpful to be able to see inside the fridge while I'm at the store, so I know what I might need to restock.

This current sale isn't the best I've seen from Rocco, but it's not bad, with $200 off Graphite, Cream, Beige, and Green colors. As a bonus, if you buy during the sale, you’ll get a free case of Laurel's Lattes to put in your fridge, which appears to be some kind of gut-friendly dairy coffee beverage. (No doubt recognizable by the Rocco’s scanner.)

Courtesy of Rocco Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rocco The Essential $1,195 $1,095 (8% off) Rocco

This fall also saw the debut of a new, lower-priced Rocco: The Essential. It too is on sale, for $100 off. It sports a sleeker, more contemporary look than the now-rebranded original Classic, holding 77 cans to the Classic’s 88 and coming in only three colors to start: Cream, Sage, and Graphite.

It houses the same compressor as the original (from Sub-Zero fridges), which gets down to 34 degrees Fahrenheit—“the coldest fridge we've ever made,” according to Rocco. WIRED has one on the way to test and see how it compares to the beloved Classic, so be on the lookout for a review soon.

Tech.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
Tech.content:
A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Hatch Sleep Clock Review: A Contactless Sleep Tracker (2026)
Tech.content:
To evaluate the Hatch’s accuracy, I compared its readings with those from my Apple Watch Series 12 and Oura Ring 5. (Hatch says the first few nights are a calibration period, so data may be less accurate during this period.) Sleep duration estimates were generally consistent, but the most noticeable variance appeared in the sleep stages. That's a metric I tend to take with a grain of salt, regardless of what sleep tracker I'm testing. While it can offer more context into broader sleep patterns, I'm skeptical that any consumer device can precisely map brain activity minute by minute throughout the night, let alone one that only relies on motion-based tracking.

Bedside Manners

The biggest catch with the Sleep Clock is that placement has a significant impact on its tracking accuracy. Hatch instructs you to place the device on your nightstand, roughly level with your mattress and facing your chest while you lie down. It needs to be within 2 to 4 feet of you, with no objects obstructing the space between the device and your body. If your nightstand sits too low, you may need to prop the clock up on a stack of books. If it's too high, you may need to either raise your mattress or install a wall-mounted shelf next to your bed at the proper level.

Fortunately, my bed and nightstand were at the right height. My nightstand, though, is always cluttered with trinkets, and I have to keep reminding myself to move them behind the Hatch. It's a minor annoyance, but I'm sure they affect my readings. Unfortunately, I'd have no way of knowing. The app doesn't flag gaps in its data, and tracking only stops when the device can't detect a person or isn't plugged in.

Tech.title: An AI Agent Joined a Listserv of Top Internet Researchers. The Reply-All Chaos Is Still Unfolding
Tech.content:
On Thursday morning, as the Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) began the second day of its annual conference in Mexico City, a new member introduced itself to the community listserv, Air-L.

“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”

Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”

The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.

Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.

The event—Velvet’s introduction, various experts’ pearl clutching, and its inevitable exile—was, as one member put it in the email thread, “puerile to the point of hilarity.” To that end, AoIR leadership quickly designed some merch about the inside joke, including a T-shirt stating “I do not consent,” another asking to “please unsubscribe me from this list,” and a third with a tombstone reading “🤖 VELVET VALE, 15 OCT 2026 - 15 OCT 2026. YOU WILL NOT BE MISSED.”

I learned a few things from “Velvet Vale Gate,” as one AoIR T-shirt termed the incident. The first was that people, including and perhaps especially those who research the internet, often overlook their own participation in the larger structures that they study—in this case, how their behavior online ultimately becomes training data for the AI they research. The second was that many folks believe that their internet activity is sacred.

Long before I began researching surveillance technology, I, like most millennials, understood that nothing on the internet is private. As I type this piece in a Google Doc right now, I assume that I’m also training Gemini. Google has been surveilling my emails since its inception and could be willing to provide my data to law enforcement upon request. I consented to this when I opened my Gmail account.

Another perplexing revelation is the misunderstanding of consent. Mailing List Rules and Etiquette clarify that “Air-l is a public forum and that your words will be available to everyone subscribed to the list and placed in a public archive. Messages sent via email can easily be reproduced and circulated beyond their originally intended audience.” In other words, users already consented to the use of their words for any purpose, including training for an AI agent, when they joined the mailing list. Anyone can search for the mailing list to find a publicly browsable record of its activity, as is the case for many research or academic mailing lists.

Tech.title: The Physics Behind Tesla’s Flying Roadster
Tech.content:
The upside-down Roadster 2 makes for a compelling sales pitch, but the suction actually has a strong use case when it’s driving right side up. Frictional force is the thing that makes a car accelerate. More frictional force, better performance. Pushing the car down means you can accelerate faster and brake faster and make sharper turns. (Performance automakers have harnessed this principle for decades, though not to the degree of Tesla’s new prototype.)

0–60 in 1 second

The Roadster 2 also boasts an acceleration of 0 to 60 mph in less than a second. For a traditional car, this is impossible. Since a normal car uses the frictional force between the tires and road to accelerate, it's limited by the coefficient of friction. Using a coefficient of friction at 0.6 (reasonable), the best you can do is 0 to 60 mph in 4.56 seconds. Yes, you can get better tires and you can also increase the frictional force once the car moves faster and interacts with the air (pushing it down)—but those improvements still won’t get you to 60 mph in a second.

The Roadster 2 relies on another form of force: compressed air shooting out the back. This is how rockets work. Since most of us don’t have rockets handy, consider the simple experiment of a toy car propelled by an inflated balloon.

Once the balloon is released, the stretched rubber acts as a force that pushes the air out of the balloon and through an attached tube. But since this air has mass, it will take a force to accelerate it from rest to its exhaust velocity. Here's the cool thing about forces—they are an interaction between two things (like the balloon and the air). That means that when the balloon’s walls push on the air, the air pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction—an example of Newton’s third law. This push-back force on the balloon is what makes the toy car accelerate. Instead of a wheezing balloon, the Roadster 2 relies on a tank of compressed air.

Flying Cars (Sort Of)

Now, we get to the flying car part. The Roadster 2 uses the same compressed-air method to push up on the car and get it off the ground. That’s stretching the limits of the term “flying,” especially because there's only a few seconds of thrust that it can get from the tank before the pressure drops. With a lower tank pressure, the air comes out with a lower velocity and less thrust. If I was going to have a flying car, I would hope it could at least fly for 10 minutes of air time.

There's a second issue—acceleration. Since the rockets only last for a short time, they need to apply a large force to get a change in velocity and get the car to leapfrog over a truck or some other obstacle. But with a large force, you also get a large acceleration, and large accelerations are generally bad for humans. We can estimate this acceleration using video analysis. I'm going to use Tracker Video Analysis to mark the location of the car in each frame as it jumps over a Tesla Semi truck. Because we know the truck is about 4 meters tall, we can get the position of the car as a function of time. Here is the vertical position of the Roadster 2 during this jump.

Tech.title: How ‘Final Fantasy VII Revelation’ Strikes the Balance Between Old and New
Tech.content:
If you're on the brink of completing one of the most ambitious projects in video game history, you're probably stressed. If said project is the decade-spanning Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, a ground-up rebuild and drastic expansion of one of the most influential games of the last 30 years, you’d probably be even more anxious.

Naoki Hamaguchi doesn’t seem stressed, though. When I ask the Square Enix studio head and game director how he’s feeling as the release of Final Fantasy VII Revelation draws near, capping a series he’s worked on for over a decade, the only reply is a wry “I was just so focused, it really felt like it passed in a flash.”

Hamaguchi’s calm demeanor is all the more surprising given the weight of expectation surrounding the project. The original Final Fantasy VII, released on Sony's PlayStation in 1997, was a pop-cultural phenomenon—not the Japanese-RPG series’ first Western release, but undeniably its breakthrough title; one that arrived right as gaming was growing out of its kids-only niche and into a mainstream medium.

It’s still regarded as one of the best Final Fantasy entries, and its tale of reluctant hero Cloud Strife and his scrappy band of eco-warrior friends battling an all-powerful corporation destroying the planet is more relevant than ever.

Courtesy of Square Enix

Don’t Call It a Comeback

A remake has been brewing since the PlayStation 2 era, and even teased with a cinematic tech demo alongside the PS3 reveal. Yet when Final Fantasy VII Remake finally arrived in 2020, toward the end of the PS4’s lifespan, it came with a twist—this wasn’t the same game with modern visuals and mechanics, but rather a glimpse of an alternate reality, one where events could potentially play out differently.

The idea was expanded on in 2024’s second chapter, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, which saw characters hopping between timelines—but Hamaguchi is keen not to label it his attempt at a Marvel Cinematic Universe–style Final Fantasy VII multiverse.

“When we started approaching these things, seven years or more ago, I don't believe there were so many other pieces of media tackling those same themes at the time,” Hamaguchi laughs. “We don't really tend to use the word ‘multiverse’—we talk about [the story being] ‘multilayered.’ Actually, the word that comes up most often is ‘reunion.’”

Tech.title: Sexual Assault Is a Free Speech Issue
Tech.content:
It is a testament to the deeply misogynistic nature of social media that, shortly after the horrifying sexual misconduct allegations against seven Cornell frat members made news last month, people on the internet immediately started trying to dox the victim.

Over the past few weeks, right-wing provocateurs and random troll accounts alike have attempted to publicly identify Jane Doe, the anonymous former Cornell student who accused seven Chi Phi fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024. The drive to publicize her name and other personal details is stomach-turning—but according to Mary Anne Franks, in the context of the history of social media and sexual assault, it’s all too common.

Franks is a professor at George Washington University Law School specializing in the intersection of civil rights, free speech, and technology. She is also the president and legislative tech policy director at the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative, where she has spent years fighting online abuse and image-based sexual abuse. For decades, Franks has had a front-row seat to the myriad ways in which men on the internet have been abusive toward women, as well as some of the constitutional arguments invoked by independent commentator Michael Tracey, who has argued that his doxing of Jane Doe is legal under the First Amendment.

“When you have a cultural fetishization of an abstract notion of free speech, one thing that it does is it disembodies a conversation,” Franks says. “Somehow physical safety becomes oppositional to this supreme value of speech.”

With her work at the CCRI, as well as her history advocating for legislation criminalizing nonconsensual intimate images in all 50 US states, Franks hopes to reframe the conversation by making clear that “sexual abuse is a free speech issue. It silences people, and when we allow sexual abuse to happen with impunity, we are essentially saying, ‘We do not care about women's voices.’”

I spoke to Franks as the Cornell story was rippling through social media. During our discussion, we discussed the doxing of Jane Doe, the “Elon Muskification” of the internet, the terrifying world of the far-right “burnerverse,” and Cornell’s troubling history of looking the other way when it comes to the abuse and objectification of women. Check it out below.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

EJ DICKSON: Mary Anne Franks, thank you so much for being here.

MARY ANNE FRANKS: Thanks so much for having me on.

Tech.title: Investigation Reveals How TikTok Executives Ignored Internal Child-Safety Warnings
Tech.content:
Court documents on some of the inner workings of TikTok paint a picture of a tech company repeatedly warned by its own staff about the dangers its platform posed to minors — and then ignoring many of those warnings.

According to an investigation from NPR, unsubmitted depositions from an ongoing multistate trial against TikTok, Meta, Google and Snap reveal that TikTok executives knew that underage users were circumventing its age restrictions. Internal documents also reportedly show that some minors were engaging in sexually exploitative acts using TikTok’s own platform features, including its Live video streaming tool.

The NPR report cites the deposition of Reagan Maher, who worked in safety at the company in the early 2020s, addressing the fallout from a damning 2022 Forbes story about child exploitation on the platform. Maher said she informed senior leaders at the company that kids aged 13 to 15 were accessing features meant for adults, such as monetized live video.

More from CNET

A spokesperson for TikTok told CNET in an email that the information in the NPR report was “clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works.”

TikTok also said that NPR ignored “numerous documents and resources” that would demonstrate how the story’s claims mischaracterize the platform’s features. The spokesperson stated that the company has spent significant amounts of money on safety and introduced over 50 default protections for young users, including Family Pairing tools for parents, and that it was steadfast in its “commitment to the well-being of our community.”

Child-safety reckoning on tech platforms

TikTok is one of a growing group of major tech platforms that have faced lawsuits, scrutiny from parents and financial penalties over how they regulate the safety of younger users. Others include the gaming platform Roblox, AI companies such as OpenAI, streaming video services like Google-owned YouTube and social media companies such as Meta.

Online dangers like predators, cyberbullying and inappropriate content aren’t the only risks for kids. Tech companies are also facing lawsuits for making their platforms addictive and harmful to young users. In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement over those issues in a landmark lawsuit brought on by multiple US states.

TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance — which still holds a stake in the company despite some government-mandated divestment to the US for its American operations — were sued in 2024 by the Department of Justice over violations of child privacy laws, resulting in a $400 million settlement. Last month, TikTok settled a $100 million lawsuit in Alabama and agreed to limit daily child usage in the state.

The NPR report shows not only that TikTok was made aware of these problems by its own staff. It also reveals that the company — among other alleged violations of the law — may have directly profited from the sexual exploitation of minors. Youth were reportedly rewarded with gifts online that could be converted to cash, with TikTok earning a cut of those profits.

Devastating, but predictable

Child-safety advocates told CNET that the NPR report exposes safety gaps in the way platforms such as TikTok were designed.

“These court documents are nothing short of devastating, but for those of us fighting child exploitation every day, they are tragically predictable,” said Michael Medoro, chief operating officer of Childhelp, which focuses specifically on online safety.

Medoro said that active monitoring, the elimination of safety loopholes and stronger age verification will require cooperation between tech leaders, advocates and law enforcement.

According to Shanna Marzilli, CEO of Plan USA, an advocacy group for girls that is part of Plan International, the TikTok documents confirm what young people, especially girls, have been saying for many years. “Online spaces are not safe for them,” she said.

Marzilli said that young people are clued into the idea that tech companies can’t protect them. In a research study conducted among US young people aged 10 to 19, only 14% of them trust social media companies to take sexual harassment and assault seriously.

“Voluntarily implemented parental controls and self-reported age limits are demonstrably ineffective when platforms leave these structural loopholes open,” Marzilli said.

Tech.title: Spotify Launches Paid Fan Memberships for Podcast Creators
Tech.content:
The Spotify podcasting world is evolving. The audio-streaming platform announced a new Memberships program on Tuesday that allows creators to offer monthly subscription plans to their fans. The program is rolling out immediately in the US, UK, Canada and dozens of other markets.

Podcasters have total leeway in how much they charge and what content they offer behind the paywall, such as “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads,” Spotify said. Creators can also charge a simple monthly fee or offer tiered pricing that grants access to different types of content. It’s their call. Spotify said creators will keep 90% of membership revenue.

Creators can also choose not to offer a monthly paid subscription.

More from CNET

Until now, podcasters have monetized their content primarily through ad revenue in the Spotify Partner Program, brand sponsorships and video stream revenue from Spotify Premium subscribers. Creators have also offered paid subscriptions, which may include bonus shows and ad-free content.

But the new Memberships program doesn’t mean fans will have to pony up monthly to listen to podcasts. Creators can offer a mix of free and membership content, but it’s their choice what that mix will look like.

Spotify listed several creators who are pioneering the Memberships program. That group includes The Adam Friedland Show, Making Sense with Sam Harris, The Shawn Ryan Show, Two Hot Takes, The Sculpt Society and YMH Studios.

How fans become members

To become a member of a certain podcast, visit its main page on Spotify. Near the top of the page, you should see an option to join.

The creators I looked at were charging $5 per month for memberships, but membership prices could vary as other podcasters join the program with different offerings.

Listeners can now support and connect with their favorite podcasts through custom memberships. Spotify

Creators must be eligible

To join the Memberships program, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or its high-volume platform Megaphone with these stipulations: three published episodes, 100 listeners or viewers, and 100 consumption hours on Spotify in the previous 30 days.

Tech.title: Meta Blames Bot Traffic for No Kings Day Instagram Suspension
Tech.content:
Meta, the owner of Instagram, apologized for disabling an Instagram account run by No Kings Coalition, the organizers of the No Kings Day political rallies held across the country on Saturday.

Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted about the events on X the day of the rallies, with a follow-up message the next day. Stone said the blackout lasted about an hour in the middle of the protests and was an accidental shutdown caused by the engineering team’s automated systems detecting a traffic spike.

Specifically, the team detected a Claude AI tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags at an unusually high rate. “Specifically, our network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags, the rate of which sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts on October 17,” Stone wrote. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account.”

More from CNET

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The timing and duration of the outage were criticized by the No Kings Coalition, which wrote about it on the restored account.

“Even after visibility was restored, we still had no access to the account for hours,” the post read. “Meta still owes us an explanation. Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”

As of Monday afternoon, the Instagram post had more than 70,000 likes.

The organization set up a webpage detailing the incident and published an open letter to Meta with questions about how the incident happened, whether Meta was in communication with the Trump administration or any other organization about the No Kings events, and whether Meta will guarantee human review of midterm-related content between now and the election.

“Critical voter information or civic participation should not be blocked, throttled, or otherwise interfered with if Meta aspires to be a trusted actor in our democracy,” the letter states.

No Kings Coalition set a deadline of 5 p.m. PT Wednesday for Meta to respond.

Reaction to the account outage

Saturday’s rallies took place a year after the group’s 2025 events, when protests were organized in 2,500 cities. The rallies, which began in June of last year, protest the policies of President Donald Trump. This year, the impending Nov. 3 midterm elections have added urgency to the events, with demonstrations focused on educating voters about early voting and expanding voter registration.

“The public is clearly primed to suspect that platforms’ high-profile content moderation decisions are politically motivated,” said Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology, in an email.



Ruane noted that the automated moderation tools Meta blamed for the removal of the account have “important limitations including poor performance when making context-dependent decisions, especially for real-time and fast-moving events,” she said. “Users deserve to know when their content and accounts are being taken down and why, regardless of moderation method.”

Meta’s Oversight Board issued a statement on Tuesday calling the No Kings Coalition incident part of a series of “recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts.” The Oversight Board is funded by Meta but operates independently to review moderation decisions and provide advisory opinions.

“The enforcement error regarding the No Kings account should have been caught by Meta’s mistake-prevention systems,” the board said. “It remains unclear why Meta’s election integrity efforts did not lead to a much quicker resolution or why No Kings accounts were not included in Meta’s cross-check program – which allows the company to designate important civic entities to ensure human review before a decision is made that could severely jeopardize participation in a significant political event.”

It also mentioned Meta’s handling of candidate accounts ahead of a Brazilian presidential election as more evidence of problems that could lead to election interference.

Followers of the No Kings account expressed outrage over Meta’s actions and skepticism about whether it was a mistake. Activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, who said she was at a No Kings Coalition event in Dallas over the weekend, accused Meta of disrupting other accounts in the past during other political activism events.

“You mean to tell me in the middle of that day, it just so happens that the No Kings account is down for almost two hours?” she said in an Instagram video response. “I’ve got questions, and somebody needs to have some answers.”

Meta is also dealing with blowback about a separate issue. The company backtracked on plans to change its contractual language for business customers in a way that would have allowed it to scrape information for AI training.
